feed.title: Building with AI & Azure

entry.content:
TL;DR

After Ignite, five layers have a say in an agent’s MCP tool call: the registry, the gateway, Entra identity, the network and the agent runtime. Most of the new controls are preview, and several of them overlap.

Don’t switch them all on and hope. Give each decision one owner and one enforcement point: the registry records which servers exist, the gateway decides which tools each agent can reach, identity decides whether this agent gets a token right now, the network catches traffic that skips the gateway, and the runtime checks the arguments before anything runs.

In a hurry? Jump to the five layers, the ownership split or the default for a new agent, then come back for the gaps.

Ask a team which tools their agent can call and you’ll usually get a list from the developer’s code. Ask who decided, and the room goes quiet.

After Ignite there’s a different problem. Microsoft has tool controls in Agent 365, Entra, Global Secure Access, AI Gateway, Foundry and Azure Policy. Several can block the same call, and many are still in preview. More controls don’t make it obvious who owns each decision.

This post extends my Governance for AI Agents series. Part 1 put a deterministic policy check in front of every tool call, and AI Agent Containment on Azure built stop buttons and containment around the agent. This one is about the decision itself: which layer owns which tool decision, and what a sensible default looks like for the next agent your teams ship.

Australia’s rapid review of an AI-driven cyber incident shows what’s at stake. The Australian Signals Directorate found that the agent wasn’t properly contained and lacked timely human oversight. The government accepted all 18 recommendations. Containment and oversight both need someone who owns them.

The product details below were checked against Microsoft, GitHub and Model Context Protocol sources on 26 November 2026.

Five layers, one tool call

Each layer answers a different question. Trouble starts when two layers try to answer the same one, because then nobody knows which allow list is authoritative. The diagram shows one possible call path. The identity decision happens when a token is issued or refreshed, not on every call.

As at 26 November, Agent 365 plugin and skills governance, AI Gateway MCP federation and tool lists, and Foundry’s managed hosted-agent egress controls are generally available. The layer-by-layer guide below calls out previews and cases where announcements and docs disagree.

Layer 1: the registry records which servers exist

The registry answers “which MCP servers are we prepared to use in this organisation?” It records the decision; the runtime enforces it. The Agent 365 tools inventory shows supported servers and their consumers. Blocks take effect in experiences that use the Agent 365 Tooling Gateway or through a connected gateway, not on every MCP client in the organisation.

Look before you block. The registry helps identify who would lose access when a server goes dark.

What admins can do today:

  • Block or unblock a whole MCP server, which disables all its tools, and see the plugins that use it so they can block those too.
  • Turn individual tools on or off. This is still rolling out and only works for supported server types.
  • Approve or reject MCP server registration requests on the Requests tab, which is preview. The flow needs the AI Administrator or Global Administrator role, Entra consent is a separate step after approval, and a server can take up to 30 minutes after consent to appear in Copilot Studio.
  • Decide who can use each plugin, and which publisher categories are allowed.

Foundry has a private tool catalogue in preview. Admins register remote MCP servers in Azure API Center, and developers need the Azure API Center Data Reader role, which can take up to 24 hours to propagate. It’s a discovery list, not a fence. Back it with project tool controls and configure the route in AI Gateway or API Management; Foundry doesn’t register the server with a gateway for you.

Coding agents have their own registry

GitHub Copilot uses GitHub’s enterprise managed settings, not the Agent 365 registry. The allowedMcpServers and deniedMcpServers lists govern supported server configurations. A deny takes precedence; built-in servers aren’t restricted by those lists. The older registry restriction is in preview and can also block Copilot connectors.

GitHub announced strictPluginOnlyCustomization on 16 November. For the categories you choose, it keeps skills, custom agents, Copilot hooks, MCP servers or executable Copilot extensions from loading from standalone user and project settings. Eligible plugins and managed settings can still supply them. This is for GitHub Enterprise Cloud users with eligible Copilot Business or Enterprise licences. Plugin-only isn’t a marketplace allow list, so pair it with strictKnownMarketplaces.

One caution from the same week: VS Code 1.147 lets admins allow the Claude and Codex harnesses through vscode.allowedHarnesses, but those sessions don’t inherit Copilot’s managed permission, sandbox, MCP and plugin controls. Check the controls each harness actually enforces before allowing it.

Layer 2: the gateway decides which tools each agent can reach

The gateway enforces which tools an agent can reach at run time. In AI Gateway, MCP federation and tool lists are GA. A tool outside the allow list doesn’t appear in tools/list and can’t be called. A blocked tool can still appear but won’t run. Shape what agents see with the allow list and keep the block list as the backstop.

Those lists apply to the gateway’s MCP server, not to an individual agent. To give two groups different toolsets, expose separate gateway MCP endpoints with their own lists and scope each group’s AI Gateway Tools User role to the relevant server.

Two newer controls sit on top, both preview:

  • Agent Hooks ask your own decision service for an allow or deny verdict before a tool runs, after it finishes, or both. They fail closed by default but can be configured to fail open. Discovery calls such as initialize and tools/list don’t trigger a hook. The gateway doesn’t offer a transform or approval verdict here.
  • Tool threat protection uses Defender and Purview to evaluate tool requests and results. It’s one policy per server, runs after the gateway’s existing policies and requires a delegated user token. An evaluated invocation without a usable token fails; don’t rely on this control for app-only agents. Defender’s Block mode fails closed, while Audit doesn’t block.
sequenceDiagram    accTitle: One tool call checked by the runtime, the gateway and an Agent Hook    accDescr: The agent's host asks agent controls about the proposed call at pre_tool_call and gets allow, deny or transform. If allowed, the call reaches AI Gateway, which checks its tool lists and then asks an Agent Hook decision service, which can allow or deny. Only then does the MCP server run the tool. After the tool runs, a post-call hook can still withhold the result.    autonumber    participant AG as Agent host    participant AC as Agent controls    participant GW as AI Gateway    participant HK as Agent Hook service    participant S as MCP server    AG->>AC: pre_tool_call with name and arguments    AC-->>AG: allow, deny or transform    AG->>GW: tools/call    GW->>GW: Tool allow and block lists    GW->>HK: Before the call    HK-->>GW: allow or deny    GW->>S: Run the tool    S-->>GW: Result    GW->>HK: After the call    HK-->>GW: allow or deny the result    GW-->>AG: Result or error

A deny after the call can withhold the result, but the tool has already run. Put any check meant to stop a write before the call.

When you connect Agent 365 to AI Gateway, Agent 365 boundaries become gateway policy. A one-time tenant consent grants the A365 MCP Gateway Policy Operator role. Blocking a server returns HTTP 403. Blocking a single tool needs a static list of tools and returns HTTP 200 with isError: true, so watch tool errors rather than HTTP status alone.

The status needs care. The API Management Ignite announcement calls the integration GA, while the Agent 365 announcement still lists AI Gateway support as preview. Verify the exact gateway and governance action before relying on it in production.

The catch is in one line of the docs: Agent 365 doesn’t automatically route agents through a customer-hosted gateway. Point each agent at the gateway’s MCP endpoint and stop direct access at the backend. For app-only tools, allow only the gateway identity. Where a tool requires a delegated user token, validate that token at the server and restrict the network path to calls from the gateway.

API Management can host MCP servers too, in the Developer, Basic, Standard and Premium tiers and the v2 tiers, but not in workspaces. Agent 365’s integration covers only the v2 tiers, where it can block whole servers. My earlier post, Azure AI Gateway Is GA, covers where each gateway fits.

Layer 3: identity decides whether this agent gets a token

Identity is where the agent stops being “the app” or “the user” and becomes something you can make a decision about. An Entra agent identity is a special kind of service principal. It’s created from a blueprint, which holds the credentials, and it can have a sponsor: the person or group accountable for it. Agent ID is available to all Entra customers, but extending Entra’s security features to agents needs Agent 365.

With Conditional Access for assistive agents (preview), a policy can say no to the agent without saying no to the person it works for.

What changed at Ignite:

  • Defender and Global Secure Access discover local agents. Defender discovery is GA and network discovery in Global Secure Access is preview. Automatic Agent IDs start with GitHub Copilot CLI and Claude Code, in preview.
  • Conditional Access for assistive agents can block a risky local agent without blocking the employee’s own access.
  • Lifecycle policies can check sponsorship and recent activity. Microsoft’s Entra Ignite post calls them GA and describes disabling agents at 60 days. The Learn guidance for the default inactivity policy still says preview and lists notification at 60 days, disabling at 90 and deletion at 455. The default policy doesn’t require a licence, but check whether it’s enabled and applies to the agent in your tenant.

Three details from Conditional Access for agents matter for design. First, policies evaluate token issuance or refresh. Don’t expect a new block to stop a session with an existing valid token unless the resource and scenario support Continuous Access Evaluation. An API key doesn’t use this token flow at all.

Second, Conditional Access evaluates the token’s resource audience, not an arbitrary MCP URL or tool name. It can stop token issuance for a server registered as its own Entra resource. When the caller requests a token for AI Gateway, however, Conditional Access sees the gateway audience. Gateway RBAC and tool policy distinguish the MCP servers and tools behind it. A downstream OBO exchange can trigger another Conditional Access evaluation for the backend resource.

Finally, target each token subject you use. Delegated access evaluates policy for the signed-in user, app-only access for the agent identity, and agent-user access for the agent’s own user account through the separate Agent Users assignment. A policy targeting the agent identity doesn’t cover those other subjects. Check licensing for the specific policy, especially agent-risk policies. Microsoft’s preview for sensitive actions and destinations isn’t evidence that Conditional Access can govern arbitrary calls on your own MCP server.

The server has a say too

Don’t forget the last hop. The MCP HTTP authorisation spec builds on OAuth 2.1. MCP authorisation is optional, but a server that implements this flow must publish Protected Resource Metadata and validate that each token was issued for it. Clients identify the intended resource, and the server must not pass the received token through to downstream services. The tools spec calls for input validation, access controls and rate limits on the server, and recommends keeping a human able to refuse tool calls.

The MCP Events extension makes a point worth repeating: receiving an event doesn’t authorise an action. Follow-up calls still need ordinary MCP authorisation, and clients should evaluate policy before turning an event into a tool call.

Microsoft’s Work IQ announcement describes a tenant-wide ceiling on actions, for example allowing read, create and update but not delete. Per-agent policy can only narrow that ceiling. For agents registered in Agent 365, Work IQ checks their policy on each call under the agent’s identity. This applies to traffic through Work IQ, not to every route to Microsoft 365 data. Check availability of this policy for your tenant.

Layer 4: the network catches what skips the gateway

The network layer is your backstop for agents that talk to servers nobody put behind a gateway. There are two controls, one for devices and one for hosted agents.

The network can catch a request to an unapproved remote server. It can’t see the local stdio exchange. A local server process can still initiate its own outbound connections, which need their own controls.

Managed devices: MCP firewall in preview

Global Secure Access rules can match server URLs, tools, resources, prompts and other MCP request metadata. They can block unencrypted HTTP but don’t match tool arguments. The firewall covers supported remote HTTP traffic, not stdio or JSON-RPC batches. Check the Entra Internet Access licence, device join, TLS inspection and Conditional Access requirements before counting on it.

Hosted agents: egress rules

Foundry’s managed hosted agent egress controls are GA, with Transform rules still in preview. An agent references a guardrail that holds an ordered list of rules. One guardrail can serve many agents, so treat write access to it like write access to every agent that uses it.

Rules match on host and path, and the first match wins. That doesn’t distinguish two MCP tools served at the same endpoint. Foundry enforces the rules outside the agent’s sandbox. Start in Audit with a default of deny, inspect what would be blocked, then switch to Enforce and deploy a new agent version. Test rewrites and header changes outside production: they’re applied in Audit mode too.

Layer 5: the runtime checks the call before it runs

The runtime is the earliest point that can see the arguments before a tool runs, which makes it a natural place for “this tool, but only like this”. In Foundry there are three checks, at three different moments.

flowchart TB    accTitle: Three tool checks inside Microsoft Foundry    accDescr: Azure Policy checks agent and toolbox configurations when they're saved, first in Audit mode and then Deny. The project's tool controls enforce an allow list at run time. Agent controls evaluate each proposed call, including its arguments, at pre_tool_call and return allow, deny or transform.    C1["Azure Policy · when saved
approved tool types, MCP endpoints, connectors"]:::design    C2["Project tool controls · at run time
default deny, explicit allowed tools"]:::rt    C3["Agent controls · per call
name and arguments: allow, deny or transform"]:::percall    C1 --> C2 --> C3    classDef design fill:#cce5ff,stroke:#1f6feb,color:#000    classDef rt fill:#e6ffed,stroke:#2da44e,color:#000    classDef percall fill:#fff4c2,stroke:#b7950b,color:#000

With Deny assigned, Azure Policy stops a non-compliant configuration being saved where the policy applies. Project tool controls restrict supported runtime tool use. Agent controls can judge the specific call and its arguments.

Save time: Azure Policy

The approved and denied tool definitions accept tool types, MCP endpoints and MCP connectors, with Audit, Deny or Disabled effects. Don’t approve the broad mcp type if you need to restrict individual servers. Microsoft documents up to 30 minutes for enforcement changes and up to 12 hours for compliance results. These preview policies check toolboxes and Responses API prompt agents without the Copilot harness. They don’t inspect hosted agent code.

Run time: project tool controls

Set toolControls.defaultAction to Deny and list the allowed tools in allowedTools. This preview control has no audit mode, so try it in a non-production project. An Azure Policy assignment doesn’t change the list. Both controls can restrict endpoints and connectors rather than individual tools on a server. Scope those tools at the gateway, and don’t assume tool controls constrain outbound calls made directly by hosted agent code.

Per call: agent controls

Agent controls is a preview policy service built on the Agent Control and Agent Hooks specifications. Policies combine a Rego module with a manifest that binds evaluation to intervention points. The hosted service evaluates input, output, and before and after tool calls. Your host enforces the verdict. This example follows Microsoft’s authoring schema. It allows ticket reads and filters close requests to arguments that name the service desk queue. The ticket service still needs to authorise the write against its own records.

And the manifest that binds it to the moment before a tool call, with the tool arguments as the target. YAML is the authoring format here. For the hosted service, convert it to a JSON object in properties.acs and reference the separately uploaded Rego resource in properties.acsRegos, as the linked authoring guide describes.

Enforce this result before dispatch using the exact arguments that were evaluated, and deny the call on a failed or invalid evaluation. The queue string is a request argument, not proof of where the ticket lives. Resolve the ticket and check its actual queue and the caller’s authority in trusted code. The policy is a preflight filter, not an authorisation decision on its own. If you use the Agent Governance Toolkit, an open-source Microsoft project I work on, its policy layer also uses the Agent Control Specification from version 5.0. Check the manifest format for whichever runtime you use.

Toolboxes make the runtime layer easier to own. A toolbox gives supported tools, skills and agents a versioned surface and centralises downstream authentication. Prefer agent identity or user delegation over shared keys where the tool supports it.

Gaps and overlaps

The layers overlap on purpose, but they also leave holes. These are the ones I’d raise in a design review.

  • Preview doesn’t mean absent, but it also doesn’t mean safe to depend on alone. Where Microsoft pages disagree, notably on Agent 365 gateway governance and Entra lifecycle policies, use the more cautious interpretation and verify your exact feature.
  • Allow lists see destination or tool names, not arguments. Agent controls and Agent Hooks can apply your rules to arguments. Tool threat protection looks for threats. The server still has to validate inputs and authorise writes.
  • Know what falls outside each control. That includes stdio, other coding harnesses, MCP servers defined in repository custom agents outside the managed lists’ scope, hosted agent code outside Foundry’s save-time policies, and app-only callers outside tool threat protection.
  • Check the real path. Workspaces can’t host MCP servers, and Agent 365 won’t send traffic through your gateway automatically.
flowchart TB    accTitle: Where each control sits, by timing and owner    accDescr: Design-time controls are the Agent 365 registry and the Foundry private catalogue, owned by security, Azure Policy for approved tools, owned by the platform team, and GitHub managed settings, owned by the developer platform team. Run-time controls are Conditional Access for agents and the MCP firewall, owned by security, hosted agent egress rules and AI Gateway tool lists and hook policies, owned by the AI platform team, Foundry project tool controls, owned by the platform team, and agent controls, owned by application teams.    subgraph DT["Design time"]      R1["Agent 365 registry
security"]:::sec      R2["Foundry private catalogue
security"]:::sec      R3["Azure Policy for approved tools
platform team"]:::plat      R4["GitHub managed settings
developer platform team"]:::dev    end    subgraph RT["Run time"]      T1["Conditional Access for agents
security"]:::sec      T2["MCP firewall
security"]:::sec      T3["Hosted agent egress rules
AI platform team"]:::ai      T4["AI Gateway tool lists and hook policies
AI platform team"]:::ai      T5["Foundry project tool controls
platform team"]:::plat      T6["Agent controls
application teams"]:::app    end    classDef sec fill:#ede9fe,stroke:#6d28d9,color:#000    classDef ai fill:#e6ffed,stroke:#2da44e,color:#000    classDef plat fill:#cce5ff,stroke:#1f6feb,color:#000    classDef dev fill:#f1f5f9,stroke:#334155,color:#000    classDef app fill:#fff4c2,stroke:#b7950b,color:#000

The owner isn’t always the team enforcing the decision. For example, security can own a server block that a gateway operated by the AI platform team enforces.

One owner per decision

This is the split I’d agree before the next agent goes live. By platform team I mean the team that runs your Azure landing zone, which may or may not also run API Management.

  • Security owns the approved server inventory, Agent IDs and Conditional Access. It sets device policy in the MCP firewall and owns emergency blocks in Agent 365 for covered gateways and clients.
  • The AI platform team owns the toolsets exposed via gateway MCP servers, scoped access to those servers and the egress rules for hosted agents.
  • The cloud platform team owns the Foundry project’s tool list, keeping Azure Policy and the runtime tool controls aligned.
  • The application team owns rules about the arguments a tool may receive. The AI platform team can operate the decision service. Pick one primary enforcement point for a rule: the agent host before dispatch or an AI Gateway Agent Hook.
  • The developer platform team owns what coding agents may load, through GitHub managed settings. Microsoft 365 admins own the separate ceiling on actions through Work IQ.

The rule I apply when two rows seem to overlap: the owner is whoever carries the risk, and the enforcement point is the coarsest layer that can see what the decision needs and can’t be routed around. If the decision needs only the server, the registry records it and the gateway or Foundry’s tool policy enforces it. If it needs the tool name, the gateway. If it needs the arguments, agent controls or an Agent Hook.

A default for a new agent

This is the baseline I’d hand a team shipping its next agent on Azure.

  1. Register each server with a named owner. Enforce the approved inventory in the gateway and in the Foundry or GitHub controls that apply to the agent.
  2. Give the agent its own identity and a human sponsor. Set up a way to disable idle or orphaned identities where lifecycle controls are available.
  3. Route remote MCP through AI Gateway, or API Management where the workload needs it. Prefer exact tool names for writes and close direct paths to the servers.
  4. Default to deny in Foundry. Use an explicit runtime allow list and start the save-time policy in Audit before moving it to Deny.
  5. Check arguments before writes with pre_tool_call or a fail-closed Agent Hook. Keep resource authorisation at the server.
  6. Lock down outbound paths. Start hosted-agent egress rules at default deny, and use device controls for managed clients. Don’t rely on a preview control alone.
  7. Where supported, connect Agent 365 so security can block a server or tool without a deployment.
  8. Test what each layer should deny in a non-production environment, and repeat those tests after policy changes.
flowchart TB    accTitle: Rolling out tool policy, audit first and then deny    accDescr: Start with an inventory from the registry and gateway logs. Turn on policies in audit mode, review what would have been blocked, fix it or grant a time-limited exception with an owner, then switch to deny and enforce, keeping logs and the exception register as evidence and reviewing exceptions on a schedule.    I["Inventory
registry and gateway logs"]:::step    AU["Audit mode
Azure Policy audit, egress audit"]:::audit    RV["Review what would
have been blocked"]:::step    EX["Fix it, or grant an exception
with an owner and an expiry"]:::warn    EN["Deny and enforce"]:::enforce    EV["Evidence
logs and the exception register"]:::step    I --> AU --> RV --> EX --> EN --> EV    EV -. "review on a schedule" .-> EX    classDef step fill:#f1f5f9,stroke:#334155,color:#000    classDef audit fill:#cce5ff,stroke:#1f6feb,color:#000    classDef warn fill:#fff4c2,stroke:#b7950b,color:#000    classDef enforce fill:#e6ffed,stroke:#2da44e,color:#000

Start in Audit where it exists. Where it doesn’t, such as project tool controls, test the actual deny in a non-production project. Give any exception an owner and an expiry.

My take

Don’t mistake overlap for depth. Five layers that can all block the same tool call sound like defence in depth, but without owners they become five allow lists that drift apart, and an incident turns into an argument about which one was right. I’d rather have each decision live in one place and have the other layers act as backstops.

Enforce where the decision can be seen and can’t be routed around. Server-level decisions are recorded in the registry and enforced at the gateway or in Foundry’s tool policy. Tool-level decisions belong in the gateway. Anything that depends on arguments belongs in agent controls or an Agent Hook. The gateway is the natural home for most of it, which is why I’d put every remote MCP server behind one and make the servers refuse everything else.

Be honest about where the arguments are. A gateway allow list can’t tell “close this ticket” from “close every ticket”. Agent controls and Agent Hooks provide custom argument-policy hooks in this comparison; tool threat protection sees the arguments but looks for threats, not business rules. The server can enforce those business rules too. Agent controls only work where your host actually calls them, so for write tools that interception code is the control, and you should test it like one.

Treat preview as preview. Gateway tool lists can still restrict names if a hook isn’t ready for production, and egress rules can restrict destinations if project controls aren’t ready. Neither decides whether a particular write is authorised. For that, the MCP server’s own validation and authorisation remain the backstop.

Where I’d start: pick one production agent, register its servers, put them behind AI Gateway with exact tool names, give the agent its own identity and sponsor, add one argument check on its riskiest write tool, and then try to break each layer on purpose with the owners in the room.

Key takeaways

  • Five layers now have a say in an MCP tool call: registry, gateway, identity, network and runtime. Each answers a different question.
  • Give every tool decision one owner and one enforcement point, and use the other layers as backstops.
  • Put remote MCP behind a gateway and prevent direct access. Agent 365 doesn’t route callers there for you.
  • Check arguments before writes, deny on evaluation failure, and authorise the operation against trusted data at the server.
  • Keep independent controls behind preview features and test what each layer denies, not just what it allows.

References

  • Microsoft: Agent 365 at Ignite 2026 and Agent 365 enforcement in AI Gateway
  • Azure AI Gateway Labs: Tool lists and Agent Hooks
  • Microsoft Learn: Conditional Access for agents and Global Secure Access MCP firewall
  • Microsoft Learn: Govern tools in Foundry and author agent controls policies
  • GitHub: Enterprise managed settings
  • Model Context Protocol: HTTP authorisation and tool requirements
  • Australian Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet: Rapid Review incident findings

Related posts

  • AI Agent Containment on Azure: Stop Buttons, Identity and Network Controls: containment and stop buttons around the agent.
  • Azure AI Gateway Is GA: When to Use It, When to Keep APIM, and Who Should Own It: where the gateway layer should live and who owns it.
  • Your Agent SDK Carried the Payload: Hardening Agent Build Pipelines After the Mastra npm Compromise: MCP servers launched with `npx -y` are package installs too.
  • GitHub Copilot Harness Security: Patch, Pin and Govern Your Coding Agents: MCP and customisation policy for coding agents.

entry.summary: Assign each MCP tool decision to an owner, from registry and gateway to Entra, network and runtime controls, and build a default deny baseline for Azure agents.
entry.title: Who Decides Which MCP Tools an Agent Can Call? Registry, Gateway, Identity and Network After Ignite

entry.content:
TL;DR

In June, an attacker Microsoft attributes with high confidence to Sapphire Sleet took over a maintainer’s npm account and republished more than 140 packages of Mastra, a TypeScript framework for building agents, each with one new dependency: a dayjs lookalike whose postinstall script dropped a remote access implant. Any laptop or build agent whose install pulled in one of those versions could be hit, whether or not its code ever imported Mastra.

Install from a lockfile, make new releases wait, turn off unreviewed install scripts and reject provenance downgrades where you can. Keep deployment credentials and unrestricted network access out of the build job.

In a hurry? Jump to what happened, the response runbook if you think an affected version reached you, or the five controls, then come back for the why.

Agent teams pull fast-moving frameworks onto machines that hold model keys, deployment identities and package feed credentials. That makes a routine install worth treating as a security boundary.

Microsoft Threat Intelligence analysed the Mastra compromise and, two days later, attributed it with high confidence to Sapphire Sleet, a North Korean state actor that primarily targets the financial sector.

I’m writing about it five months on for two reasons. It’s still the clearest example I know of an agent SDK used to deliver a payload, and the tooling has moved on. pnpm 11 defaults to a one-day release age, npm 12 stopped running unapproved dependency install scripts, and Dependabot added a default three-day cooldown for version updates.

The incident details come from Microsoft’s analysis, Mastra’s own incident report, Socket’s registry timeline and the public advisories. The product guidance was checked on 26 November 2026.

What happened in June

Researchers found the change in the registry, not in Mastra’s source repository: a stolen publishing credential, a lookalike package and a dependency range that admitted the poisoned version.

The way in was the npm account of a Mastra maintainer with publish rights across the @mastra scope. Mastra’s incident report says the maintainer’s machine was compromised after phishing from a hijacked LinkedIn account. The scope required two-factor authentication but allowed tokens that bypassed it. A token tied to that account republished the packages.

On 16 June, the day before the republishing, a different npm account published easy-day-js, a copy of the popular dayjs library that even claimed dayjs’s author and repository. Version 1.11.21 was clean bait. Version 1.11.22, published at 01:01 UTC on 17 June, added a postinstall script that ran an obfuscated dropper.

Eleven minutes later the hijacked account started republishing Mastra packages: more than 140 by Microsoft’s and Socket’s count, 116 by Mastra’s own. Each new version added a dependency on easy-day-js@^1.11.21, which resolved to the poisoned 1.11.22, and for the mastra CLI Microsoft found that was the only change. Every poisoned version was tagged latest, and nothing in Mastra’s GitHub repository matched it.

flowchart TB    accTitle: Timeline of the Mastra compromise in UTC    accDescr: On 16 June at 07:05 UTC a clean bait version of easy-day-js was published. At 01:01 on 17 June the poisoned version 1.11.22 followed. From 01:12 to about 02:36 the hijacked account republished more than 140 Mastra packages with the new dependency, including mastra 1.13.1 at 01:20. Mastra learned of it at 03:45, had unpublished or deprecated the affected versions it identified by 06:57 and published clean versions at about 08:00. Microsoft attributed the campaign to Sapphire Sleet on 19 June.    T1["16 Jun 07:05
easy-day-js 1.11.21, clean bait"]:::prep    T2["17 Jun 01:01
easy-day-js 1.11.22 adds the postinstall dropper"]:::bad    T3["17 Jun 01:12 to about 02:36
140+ Mastra packages republished,
mastra 1.13.1 at 01:20"]:::bad    T4["17 Jun 03:45
Mastra learns of it"]:::resp    T5["17 Jun 06:57
Mastra's identified versions
unpublished or deprecated"]:::resp    T6["17 Jun about 08:00
clean versions published"]:::fixed    T7["19 Jun
Microsoft attributes it to Sapphire Sleet"]:::fixed    T1 --> T2 --> T3 --> T4 --> T5 --> T6 --> T7    classDef prep fill:#cce5ff,stroke:#1f6feb,color:#000    classDef bad fill:#ffd6d6,stroke:#c0392b,color:#000    classDef resp fill:#fff4c2,stroke:#b7950b,color:#000    classDef fixed fill:#e6ffed,stroke:#2da44e,color:#000

Within about six hours of the first poisoned Mastra publish, Mastra had unpublished or deprecated the affected versions it identified. That’s the early exposure window an age gate helps with. Deprecation doesn’t prevent installation, though, so the deprecated versions could still reach an install later.

The publishing metadata gave it away. Microsoft says its monitoring spotted the anomaly within minutes, and it wasn’t the only one watching: Socket flagged easy-day-js within six minutes of publication. Up to 1.13.0, mastra releases came out of the project’s own GitHub Actions workflow, authenticated with OpenID Connect. Then 1.13.1 appeared, published outside that workflow from the maintainer’s account, with an anonymous email address on the publisher record. Keep that detail in mind, because one of the controls below checks for it.

OSV records a separate malicious clone of the mastra CLI published the day before. That looks like a rehearsal, but the advisory doesn’t establish a link to the same operator. Microsoft separately attributes the earlier Axios npm compromise to Sapphire Sleet.

What the payload did

The postinstall hook ran a dropper that left markers in the temp directory and fetched a second stage. The code ran with the install process’s permissions, not inside a separate agent sandbox.

The second stage persisted across Windows, macOS and Linux, using names that resembled Node version-manager files. Microsoft observed remote task execution, browser-history collection and wallet-extension inventory. Socket’s recovered sample didn’t copy wallet secrets, saved passwords or cookies, but follow-on code could still steal them. On some hosts Microsoft also observed a PowerShell backdoor and a service running as SYSTEM. The runbook below focuses on what to look for rather than the payload mechanics.

For pipelines, this is the part of Microsoft’s write-up that matters most. The dropper fired during installation, so exposure had nothing to do with whether your code used Mastra. If a laptop or build agent installed or updated a project that resolved one of the bad versions while they were up, directly, through another dependency or through npx, treat it as exposed.

Why agent teams should care

Mastra isn’t a stray utility. It’s a popular framework for building agents and workflows in TypeScript, so it lives in the same repositories and build agents that hold model keys and deployment rights.

It could reach developer machines a second way. Mastra’s MCP docs server setup shows npx -y with no pinned version. @mastra/mcp-docs-server 1.1.47 was affected, so starting a coding agent could have pulled in the compromised server if it needed to resolve or install the package. That puts dependency installation on the agent’s start-up path, even if a cached copy means nothing is downloaded that time.

Automation made it worse. In an early incident report, a team reported that their dependency bot pulled the poisoned versions within minutes of publication, and a failing CI install is how they noticed.

Install time is the blast radius

A postinstall script runs as the build user with the install process’s environment. A scanner later in the job can’t prevent code that’s already run.

On a build agent, that reach usually includes:

  • Pipeline secrets in environment variables, including anything an earlier step exported.
  • OIDC token requests in a GitHub Actions job with id-token: write. Cloud trust policy still determines which requests can be exchanged for cloud access. In Azure Pipelines, anything mapped into the step’s environment, including System.AccessToken, is readable by the processes that step starts.
  • The cloud metadata service on a runner with a reachable managed identity endpoint.
  • Feed credentials. Azure Pipelines’ npmAuthenticate@0 adds credentials to the specified .npmrc for the build. For an in-organisation feed this uses the build identity. Limit that identity’s permissions as well as the feed role.
  • The checked-out source, signing material and SSH keys readable by the build user.
  • Network destinations reachable from the worker. That matters both for fetching a payload and sending data out.

On a developer machine, add browser profiles, crypto wallets, cloud CLI sessions and the coding agent’s own credentials. Wallets were this actor’s main interest, but nothing stops the next one wanting your Azure session.

So I treat the install step as untrusted code execution, because that’s what it is.

If an affected version reached you

flowchart TB    accTitle: Response runbook for a poisoned npm dependency    accDescr: Stop suspect builds, isolate affected machines and revoke exposed access. Establish scope from lockfiles, caches, feeds and logs. Preserve evidence, quarantine bad packages and issue fresh credentials from a trusted host before resuming on clean runners.    S["Stop suspect builds, isolate hosts
and revoke exposed access"]:::bad    F["Establish scope
lockfiles, caches, feeds, CI logs"]:::step    P["Preserve evidence
and quarantine bad versions"]:::step    R["Issue replacements
from a trusted system"]:::step    B["Rebuild
clean runner, known-good versions"]:::ok    S --> F --> P --> B    S --> R --> B    classDef step fill:#cce5ff,stroke:#1f6feb,color:#000    classDef bad fill:#ffd6d6,stroke:#c0392b,color:#000    classDef ok fill:#e6ffed,stroke:#2da44e,color:#000

Contain and revoke first. Don’t wait for a positive malware scan or a cache purge to revoke access. Keep replacement credentials away from affected jobs, and don’t resume builds until you have a clean runner and dependency inputs.

  1. Stop suspect jobs, isolate affected hosts and revoke credentials the install could reach. For managed identities and federated credentials, check sign-in and activity logs and restrict or remove suspect grants or trust relationships. There’s no stored identity secret to rotate.
  2. Establish scope. Compare lockfiles, caches and CI logs against Socket’s affected-package list and the advisories. The poisoned versions include mastra and create-mastra 1.13.1, @mastra/core 1.42.1 and @mastra/mcp-docs-server 1.1.47. Search for easy-day-js in Git history with git log --all --oneline -S easy-day-js and check developers’ npx caches.
  3. Check 01:00 to 08:00 UTC on Wednesday 17 June: 13:00 to 20:00 in New Zealand and 11:00 to 18:00 in Sydney. Look for later installs from caches too. Old logs may have expired. GitHub Actions defaults to 90 days, and Azure Pipelines uses the project’s retention settings.
  4. Preserve forensic evidence and look for the implant. Microsoft’s indicators include temp markers, unexpected JavaScript files, persistence changes and network connections. Rebuild an affected runner from a known-good image rather than cleaning it in place. Review artefacts produced by exposed builds before trusting them.
  5. Quarantine or purge the bad versions from caches and upstream-enabled Azure Artifacts feeds. A feed can still serve a saved copy after npm takes it down. Issue replacement credentials from a trusted system, then rebuild from a reviewed lockfile on a clean runner.

These checks cover the main markers and persistence Microsoft and Socket documented. A miss doesn’t prove a machine is safe, so treat the result as one input rather than a verdict. Run them on developer machines and on any self-hosted build agent that could have installed the packages; on a build agent, the Run key sits in the hive of the account the agent runs as.

For network evidence, use retained telemetry. Defender advanced hunting defaults to 30 days of native Defender data, or up to 90 days of supported data with an eligible ISOC licence. Neither reaches June from November. This example uses a Microsoft Sentinel workspace that still has DeviceNetworkEvents for the period and uses its TimeGenerated column. Check firewall or flow logs for runners that aren’t onboarded to Defender for Endpoint. An empty query without the right data is not evidence that the runner was unaffected.

Five controls for agent build pipelines

Each check breaks a different link. A lockfile controls what you install, while the script and runner controls limit what the installed code can do.

1. Install only from a lockfile

Commit the lockfile and install with npm ci, pnpm install --frozen-lockfile or yarn install --immutable. npm ci fails if the lockfile and package.json disagree and doesn’t rewrite either. A trusted lockfile from before the poisoned versions would have kept CI on the versions it already used.

A lockfile pins dependencies, not trust. Review lockfile changes, and don’t assume npx some-tool is covered by the project lockfile if it has to fetch the package. Pinning the requested tool version helps. Installing it as a locked dependency and invoking that local binary also locks its transitive dependencies.

2. Make new versions wait

Poisoned releases rarely last long. GitHub’s cooldown analysis cites a review of 21 widely reported incidents from 2018 to 2026 that found a cooldown could have filtered out most of them, and that’s why Dependabot now waits three days by default. Mastra fits the pattern: easy-day-js 1.11.22 was eleven minutes old when the first poisoned Mastra package was published, and Mastra reported unpublishing or deprecating the 116 affected versions it identified within about six hours. A strict one-day gate on fresh resolution would have kept the new versions out during those first hours. It isn’t the whole answer, though: npm wouldn’t let Mastra unpublish six of them, so they were only deprecated, which is one more reason to keep install scripts off as well.

Several clients and update bots have an age gate. Package managers can enforce it during resolution; update bots only delay their own proposals. The units differ, so check them.

  • npm 11.10 and later: min-release-age in days. Off by default, including in npm 12.
  • pnpm 10.16 and later: minimumReleaseAge in minutes. Defaults to 1,440 minutes (one day) from pnpm 11.
  • Yarn 4.12 and later: npmMinimalAgeGate as a duration. Defaults to 1d.
  • Bun 1.3 and later: minimumReleaseAge in seconds under [install] in bunfig.toml. Off by default.
  • Dependabot: cooldown in days. Defaults to three days for version updates on github.com.
  • Renovate: minimumReleaseAge as a duration. Off by default; security:minimumReleaseAgeNpm enables a three-day wait for npm updates.

In npm, min-release-age filters fresh resolution. It won’t stop npm ci from installing a version that’s too new if it’s already pinned in the lockfile. Apply the gate when you create or update the lockfile, and review newly resolved packages before committing it.

pnpm 11’s built-in 1,440-minute gate isn’t strict. It can fall back to a newer version if nothing in the requested range is old enough. Set the age and strict mode explicitly so resolution fails instead.

And for Dependabot, if you want a longer wait for major versions:

Dependabot’s security updates skip the cooldown. GitHub announced the three-day default for github.com version updates and GitHub Enterprise Server 3.23. A gate also needs the real publish time. Azure Artifacts users report seeing cache-insertion timestamps instead of the original registry timestamps. pnpm can skip checks when timestamps are missing unless you set minimumReleaseAgeIgnoreMissingTime: false. Test the configured behaviour against your own feed rather than assuming it mirrors npm metadata.

If you’re on GitHub Enterprise Cloud, the GitHub package firewall is in public preview for npm. Its default minimum age is one day, and it only applies to requests routed through the firewall.

3. Turn dependency install scripts off

The dropper only ran because npm ran a stranger’s postinstall script. That’s no longer the default in most clients:

  • npm 12 skips dependency lifecycle scripts unless they’re approved. npm approve-scripts --allow-scripts-pending lists what needs review without changing package.json. After reviewing the installed version or versions, npm approve-scripts <package> records the approval there, pinned to the installed version by default. Set strict-allow-scripts if unreviewed scripts should fail the install rather than be skipped.
  • npm 11 still runs dependency scripts by default. Use npm ci --ignore-scripts. If a package really needs a build step, review it and rebuild only that named package in an isolated job.
  • pnpm blocks dependency build scripts by default from version 10. Version 11 uses the allowBuilds map and fails on unreviewed scripts by default.
  • Yarn 4.14 and later turn off third-party postinstall scripts by default.
  • Bun ships a curated default allow list. Setting trustedDependencies replaces that list; an empty list disables it entirely.

Check which npm your build agents actually run. The npm that ships with your Node.js version may be older than 12, and hosted runner images can lag behind the latest npm. The GitHub package firewall also blocks newly introduced install scripts by default.

4. Fail when provenance goes backwards

This is the signal Microsoft says it used to spot the attack. Earlier Mastra versions were published by a GitHub Actions workflow through npm’s trusted publishing, with provenance attestations. The poisoned ones were published outside that workflow with a personal token, and carried none.

The pnpm trust policy can turn that into a failed install. With trustPolicy: no-downgrade, pnpm refuses weaker trust evidence than an earlier release of the same package. Review any exception before adding it to trustPolicyExclude. The GitHub package firewall blocks missing attestations on packages that previously had them. npm audit signatures verifies registry signatures and available attestations; it isn’t an install-time downgrade check or a requirement that every package have provenance.

The limits are real. Provenance tells you where a package was built, not that it’s safe. A brand-new package like easy-day-js has no history to downgrade from. One Azure Artifacts user reports that upstreams don’t pass through the provenance metadata pnpm needs. If your feed strips that evidence, don’t count on the policy to distinguish an ordinary release from a downgrade.

If you publish packages, internal tools and MCP servers included, trusted publishing doesn’t switch off alternate publishing credentials. Configure npm’s two-factor authentication and token policy to disallow publishing tokens on packages that publish through OIDC. That would have closed the token route Mastra identified. npm’s current token guidance says that since August 2026, bypass-2FA tokens can’t perform account-identity or account-governance actions. They can still publish directly where package policy permits it; npm documents January 2027 for removing that ability. Verify the rollout status before planning a publishing migration around that date.

5. Keep the install step poor

Split building from deploying. The build job has no deployment secrets, cloud identity or OIDC permission. If it needs a private registry credential, use a short-lived feed credential with only the access it needs. Restrict egress to the registry and CI service endpoints. The separate deployment job takes an artefact from the trusted build, runs behind an approval and uses federation without installing project dependencies.

These are pipeline templates, not deployment test results. For GitHub Actions, replace each <commit-sha> with a reviewed action commit and scope Azure trust to the intended repository and deployment environment. The job split doesn’t configure runner egress or make a tainted artefact safe.

The Azure Pipelines version has the same shape. Provision the named pools and configure the production environment’s checks and the workload identity federation service connection separately. The build pool needs Node.js, npm, zip, an .npmrc pointing to the feed and outbound access to the feed and required Azure DevOps endpoints, but not a managed identity. The deployment pool needs Azure CLI. Both pools use Linux workers in this example.

On the network side:

  • Azure DevOps: Run Managed DevOps Pools in your own virtual network and route egress through an FQDN-aware firewall or proxy. Allow the feed and required Azure DevOps endpoints. An NSG on its own can’t filter by host name.
  • GitHub Actions: Azure private networking for larger runners lets you apply your network rules in a supported region. Australia East is listed; New Zealand North isn’t. GitHub’s native egress firewall is in early access for Linux runners, including standard runners. Until that is available to you, use larger runners with private networking or tightly controlled self-hosted runners for jobs that require enforced egress.

Test that the build works with only those destinations. Keep the restriction on during compilation and tests, where dependency code can still run even if install scripts are disabled.

Agents install things too

Agents pull packages outside your pipelines too. Three habits matter for agent teams.

  • Pin and lock MCP servers. A version on npx -y some-mcp-server pins the requested server, not its transitive dependencies when it needs to install. Put the server in a tools project with its own lockfile or bake it into the agent’s image.
  • Package at build time. Apply the controls in CI, then run that container image in production without resolving packages at start-up.
  • Apply the same rules in agent sandboxes. A repository-level .npmrc travels with the code, but for pnpm 11 use pnpm-workspace.yaml for the dependency policy. Keep sandbox egress restrictions outside the agent’s control.
flowchart TB    accTitle: Runtime installs versus build-time packaging for agents    accDescr: If an agent resolves dependencies at runtime, it can pick up a newly published version. With build-time packaging, CI installs from a lockfile behind an age gate with scripts off, builds and scans one image, and production agents run it without resolving packages.    subgraph RUN["Runtime installs"]      R1["Agent starts"]:::agent      R2["npx or npm install
may resolve versions at start-up"]:::bad      R3["New releases can run
before anyone reviews them"]:::bad    end    subgraph BLD["Build-time packaging"]      B1["CI: lockfile, age gate,
scripts off"]:::ok      B2["One image, built and scanned once"]:::ok      B3["Agent runs the image
and installs nothing"]:::agent    end    R1 --> R2 --> R3    B1 --> B2 --> B3    classDef agent fill:#cce5ff,stroke:#1f6feb,color:#000    classDef bad fill:#ffd6d6,stroke:#c0392b,color:#000    classDef ok fill:#e6ffed,stroke:#2da44e,color:#000

My take

The Mastra attack wasn’t clever code. It was clever logistics: one stolen publishing token, one lookalike dependency and one caret range. The defences that would have stopped it look boring on a slide, which is why they get skipped.

The biggest change this year is that defaults have started to flip. Don’t assume the package manager on your build runner has those defaults. Check its version and settings, then review each dependency that needs an install-time exception.

My order: lockfile installs and scripts off first, a resolution age gate and an update-bot cooldown next, then split installs from deployments and remove cloud identities from build pools. Introduce provenance checks once you’ve confirmed your registry or proxy preserves the evidence they need.

Know the limits. A cooldown does little against a backdoor that sits quietly for months or a compromised build system, and GitHub says as much. Provenance proves origin, not innocence. And if your npm traffic goes through Azure Artifacts or any other caching proxy, test your age gate and trust policy against it before you count on them, and lean harder on scripts off and egress control until you’ve confirmed they work.

Key takeaways

  • Treat dependency installation as untrusted code execution, even if application code never imports the dependency.
  • Stop suspect jobs and revoke access before rebuilding on clean runners. Check caches, feeds and previously published artefacts, not just the current lockfile.
  • Keep installs locked, delay new releases and block unreviewed scripts. Reject provenance downgrades where supported; no one control covers everything.
  • Give builds only the feed access they need, restrict egress and deploy from a separate job. Lock packages that agents would otherwise resolve at start-up.

References

  • Microsoft Threat Intelligence: Mastra npm supply chain compromise and advanced hunting retention
  • Mastra: Incident report
  • Socket: Registry timeline and affected packages
  • GitHub Advisory Database: Mastra CLI, Mastra core and MCP docs server
  • npm: Version 12 security defaults and min-release-age configuration
  • pnpm: Version 11 release notes
  • Yarn: Default script policy and age gate
  • Bun: Lifecycle script policy
  • GitHub: Dependabot cooldown and package firewall

Related posts

  • GitHub Copilot Harness Security: Patch, Pin and Govern Your Coding Agents: the same patch and pin discipline, applied to the coding agents themselves.
  • AI Agents Exploit Leaked Keys in Minutes: Go Keyless on Azure: getting rid of stored secrets, the step before this one.
  • AI Agent Containment on Azure: Stop Buttons, Identity and Network Controls: default-deny egress and short-lived identity for running agents.
  • Governance for AI Agents (Part 1): The Gap, the OWASP Agentic Top 10, and Where AGT Fits: the governance gap that pipelines sit inside.
  • AKS Static Egress Gateway: Per-Namespace Static Egress IPs: controlled egress when workloads share a cluster.

Image Credits

  • Cover image generated by Copilot
entry.summary: The Mastra npm compromise showed what a dependency can reach at install time. Learn how to respond and harden agent builds on GitHub Actions and Azure DevOps.
entry.title: Your Agent SDK Carried the Payload: Hardening Agent Build Pipelines After the Mastra npm Compromise

entry.content:
TL;DR

Azure AI Gateway went GA on 17 November as its own Azure resource, in 17 regions including Australia East but not New Zealand North. Paid billing starts on 1 January 2027, preview-tier gateways must be re-created before 15 January, and private networking works but is still in preview.

If you already run an enterprise API Management front door, my default is two lanes with two owners: API Management for business APIs, and AI Gateway, run by the AI platform team, for model and tool traffic. Keep API Management when the gateway must sit in New Zealand North or a workload needs unsupported API routes, A2A, semantic caching or format translation. API Management workspaces still won’t carry MCP.

In a hurry? Jump to the decision path, the three topologies or the ownership split, then come back for the detail.

For most of this year my answer to “should we use the new AI Gateway?” was “not for production yet”. Now the more useful question is who owns it and what stays on API Management.

flowchart TB    accTitle: Deciding which gateway a workload should use    accDescr: Business APIs stay on API Management. Model and tool traffic goes to AI Gateway unless the gateway itself must run in New Zealand North, or the workload needs unsupported API routes, A2A, semantic caching or format translation, in which case it stays on API Management v2 for now.    Q1{"Business API, or model
and tool traffic?"}:::q    APIM1["API Management
front door"]:::apim    Q2{"Must the gateway itself
run in New Zealand North?"}:::q    Q3{"Needs missing API routes, A2A,
semantic caching or format translation?"}:::q    APIM2["API Management v2
for this workload, for now"]:::apim    AIG["AI Gateway"]:::aig    Q1 -- "business API" --> APIM1    Q1 -- "models and tools" --> Q2    Q2 -- "yes" --> APIM2    Q2 -- "no" --> Q3    Q3 -- "yes" --> APIM2    Q3 -- "no" --> AIG    classDef q fill:#f8fafc,stroke:#334155,color:#000    classDef apim fill:#cce5ff,stroke:#1f6feb,color:#000    classDef aig fill:#e6ffed,stroke:#2da44e,color:#000

AI Gateway was a preview tier of API Management, and its resource type changed during the preview in October. It now has its own roadmap. API Management shipped its own AI features to GA on the same day.

So the question I keep getting has moved on. A platform or integration team runs the enterprise API Management (APIM) estate. An AI platform team wants its own gateway for models and MCP tools, without raising a ticket every time it adds a model alias. Both have a point. This post is how I’d place the two gateways, and who I’d make accountable for each.

Product details in this version reflect the 26 November 2026 source check. AI Gateway has two sets of docs, the product docs at ai.gateway.azure.com and Microsoft Learn. I’ve noted where they disagree. The topologies and correlation policy below are design guidance, not the results of a deployment test.

What went GA on 17 November

AI Gateway started as the AI Gateway tier of API Management. Microsoft’s product comparison describes the standalone service as built on the same gateway foundation but with a different scope and roadmap. It keeps the Microsoft.ApiManagement provider but uses Microsoft.ApiManagement/aigateways (API version 2026-11-01) and runtime endpoints under *.ai.gateway.azure.com.

flowchart TB    accTitle: From an API Management tier to a standalone service    accDescr: AI Gateway began as a preview tier of API Management. On 14 October 2026 it moved to its own resource type. It became generally available on 17 November 2026. Paid billing starts on 1 January 2027, and resources of the old preview type are retired on 15 January 2027 and then removed.    A["Preview
AI Gateway tier of API Management"]:::past    B["14 Oct 2026 · New resource type
Microsoft.ApiManagement/aigateways"]:::change    C["17 Nov 2026 · Generally available
17 regions, AI-only roadmap"]:::ga    D["1 Jan 2027 · Paid billing starts"]:::date    E["15 Jan 2027 · Old preview resources retired"]:::risk    A --> B --> C --> D --> E    classDef past fill:#f1f5f9,stroke:#64748b,color:#000    classDef change fill:#cce5ff,stroke:#1f6feb,color:#000    classDef ga fill:#e6ffed,stroke:#2da44e,color:#000    classDef date fill:#fff4c2,stroke:#b7950b,color:#000    classDef risk fill:#ffd6d6,stroke:#c0392b,color:#000

Two dates matter more than the GA date. Paid billing starts on 1 January 2027, and two weeks later the old preview resources are retired, then removed. There’s no in-place conversion.

The GA announcement lists 17 regions, including East US 2 EUAP. The Learn region table leaves that early access region out and lists 16. Australia East is the only one in Oceania. New Zealand North isn’t on either list.

The announced price above the free allowance is US$500 per gateway per month, billed hourly, with 10 million requests included. Extra requests cost US$20 per million, billed in increments of 10,000. Microsoft says regional prices will be available when billing starts. Confirm how the free allowance applies before budgeting: the GA announcement says 10,000 requests per gateway per month, while the API Management Ignite post says per Azure subscription.

Here’s what I’d pin up before a design review.

CapabilityStatus on 26 November
Model aliases across providers, with priority, weighted and conditional routing and failoverGA
OpenAI-compatible chat completions, Responses and embeddings, plus Anthropic MessagesGA
Token, request and cost limits, IP filtering and managed identityGA
Entra ID authentication with Azure RBAC runtime roles, and on-behalf-of authentication for toolsGA
MCP federation with tool allow and block listsGA
OpenTelemetry export of metrics, logs and tracesGA
Model Router and per-request model selectionPreview
Private networking: Private Link for inbound calls, VNet integration to reach private backendsSupported, in preview (private endpoints need preview approval)
Agent Hooks and tool threat protectionPreview
The az aigateway CLI extensionPreview
Content safety screening of prompts and responsesTwo answers: the GA announcement, the product docs and Microsoft’s labs show it, but the Learn migration page says it isn’t supported
Semantic caching, A2A agents and translating between API formatsNot offered in AI Gateway’s docs today

The last row surprises people. AI Gateway routes each protocol natively. API Management’s Unified Model API handles translation.

OpenAI-compatible doesn’t mean the whole OpenAI API surface. Microsoft’s workload migration guidance lists only /openai/v1/chat/completions, /openai/v1/responses, /openai/v1/embeddings and /v1/messages. Keep unsupported operations, such as audio, images, Assistants, threads and vector stores, on API Management; a model API may need to be split rather than moved wholesale. The same guidance keeps A2A agents on API Management for now.

API Management’s documentation still uses “AI gateway” for its own AI features: the llm- policies, semantic caching, MCP servers and the Unified Model API. When someone in a design review says “the AI gateway”, ask which one.

API Management didn’t stand still

The API Management team also announced two features as GA, but the documentation doesn’t agree on the second one’s status.

The Unified Model API is GA in supported v2 tiers. Clients call one OpenAI Chat Completions endpoint and API Management translates for supported OpenAI Chat Completions and Anthropic Messages backends. You can use model aliases and fail over across providers. Classic tiers can try it through the AI Gateway Early release channel.

Agent 365 discovers registered MCP servers and can block them. On API Management v2 that means inventory and server-level blocking. Standalone AI Gateway adds per-tool blocking and activity, as well as separately previewed tool threat protection. The API Management Ignite post calls the integration GA, but the Agent 365 announcement lists AI Gateway support in preview and Learn’s guidance still describes preview limitations. I’d verify support for the exact gateway and action before relying on it in production.

The API Management regional table lists Basic v2, Standard v2 and Premium v2 in New Zealand North, but not dedicated workspace gateways. Microsoft’s comparison frames the two products as complementary. API Management still supports existing AI workloads. I read Microsoft’s guidance as a signal that new AI features are likely to reach standalone AI Gateway first, not that anyone needs to migrate already working APIs.

API Management can expose REST operations as tools or proxy a remote MCP server. It supports MCP tools, not prompts or resources, and neither mode is available in workspaces. For private connectivity, check the exact tier: Standard v2 and Premium v2 support inbound private endpoints and outbound VNet integration, while Premium v2 also offers VNet injection. API Management v2 pricing depends on the tier and number of units. Basic v2 and Standard v2 include monthly request allowances, while Premium v2 includes unlimited requests.

A decision path

Ask the three questions in order: what kind of traffic is it, where must the gateway run, and which features does the workload need? Most model and tool traffic ends at AI Gateway. The exceptions are a hard New Zealand North requirement for the gateway, API operations it doesn’t expose and the features it doesn’t have yet. A security standard that bans preview features on production network paths is another reason to stick with API Management.

Private networking isn’t absent. Microsoft’s private networking lab covers inbound Private Link and outbound VNet integration, both in preview. Private endpoints require subscription approval. Turn off public network access explicitly if you need private ingress; creating a private endpoint doesn’t do that for you. Entra authentication and IP filtering are GA controls for a public endpoint, not substitutes when policy requires a private path.

Three topologies

These are the three shapes I see working for an organisation that already has an enterprise API Management front door. Each diagram carries one idea.

A: API Management only

One gateway and one owner make this simple to run. It can live in New Zealand North, but the platform team also owns the queue for AI changes.

I’d pick this when AI traffic is a small share of the estate, when the gateway must run in New Zealand North, or when a workload depends on unsupported API routes, A2A, semantic caching or the Unified Model API. What you give up: the AI team doesn’t own its policy, Agent 365 stops at server-level blocks on v2, and you don’t get Agent Hooks or MCP federation.

B: Two lanes, two owners

Business calls and AI calls each have one governed route. When an agent needs a business API as a tool, AI Gateway can publish it from API Management as an MCP tool. Test that the call goes through the API Management gateway so its policies still apply, and check which identity API Management sees. That depends on the backend authentication you configure, including whether the tool uses the caller’s delegated identity.

This is the shape I recommend for most organisations, and it matches Microsoft’s positioning: keep business APIs in API Management, and send model and tool traffic through AI Gateway. The platform team keeps the estate it knows. The AI platform team owns aliases, routing, limits and tools, and can move at the speed models change. The price is a second gateway to run, a second set of logs, and a clear rule about which lane a new workload uses.

One rule makes the lanes hold: prevent direct calls to model deployments and MCP servers. For app-only backends, authorise only the gateway’s managed identity and turn off alternative credentials where supported. For delegated tools, keep the user’s identity but restrict the network path so a caller can’t reach the backend directly. Azure Policy can enforce settings such as turning off key access on Foundry resources, but it won’t route traffic through a gateway on its own.

C: API Management in front of AI Gateway

Use two hops when policy says every inbound call enters through the enterprise front door. Keep each policy in one place: the front door authenticates and correlates, and AI Gateway applies model and tool policy.

I haven’t found a Microsoft reference design for this chain, although Microsoft’s migration guidance does mention keeping a translating layer in front of AI Gateway, which is one documented reason to chain them. Treat it as your own pattern and test it. Settle five things before you build it.

  1. Decide which identity AI Gateway sees. If API Management uses one managed identity for all callers, AI Gateway can’t use that identity to distinguish them. User delegation and tool threat protection require a delegated token. Where you need those features, have the front door validate and forward the caller’s token for AI Gateway. Verify the supported audience for your gateway and client before configuring validation; product guides and older lab examples might differ.
  2. Block direct access. A valid forwarded token is also valid if it arrives on a direct path. Don’t assume the API Management v2 gateway has a fixed outbound IP to allow. For a private path, let the front door reach an AI Gateway private endpoint through outbound VNet integration, and disable AI Gateway’s public access. Private Link is in preview for AI Gateway.
  3. Use trusted headers. If AI Gateway routes on a header set by the front door, overwrite whatever value the caller supplied.
  4. Put each policy in one place. Token limits in both gateways mean two places to debug and two numbers to explain.
  5. Test MCP through the chain. API Management can proxy an MCP server, but every tool call then crosses two policy engines. Keep tool policy in AI Gateway.

What about the AI Gateway Landing Zone?

The similar names don’t help. Microsoft’s AI Gateway Landing Zone is the API Management accelerator that started as AI Hub Gateway and now ships as Citadel Governance Hub. If you’ve built on it, it maps to topology A or C. The standalone service is a new option rather than a requirement to replace it.

Region and residency from New Zealand

In this design the prompt crosses the Tasman either way. Putting API Management in New Zealand North doesn’t keep a call to a Foundry deployment in Australia East onshore. The region you create a gateway in, where inference runs and where telemetry lands are separate decisions.

For a New Zealand organisation, three facts shape this.

  • Model inference: New Zealand North isn’t listed for the Foundry model deployments in this comparison. For Foundry serverless model deployments, Global can process in any Azure region, Data Zone stays inside the selected US, EU or Asia Pacific zone, and Standard or Regional Provisioned stays within the deployment’s Azure geography. A region for a gateway isn’t a guarantee about model inference.
  • Gateway payloads: I couldn’t find a statement covering request processing and storage beyond the gateway’s chosen region. Leave payload capture off for regulated prompts until you’ve confirmed residency and what gets captured or redacted.
  • Telemetry: AI Gateway sends OpenTelemetry signals to the endpoint you configure. In Microsoft’s monitoring lab, logs and traces land in the linked Log Analytics workspace, while metrics land in an Azure Monitor workspace. For onshore telemetry, verify regional support for OTLP ingestion and the location of each workspace, not just the Application Insights resource.

If you already use the pattern from my Foundry cross-region post, with data at rest in New Zealand North and inference in Australia East over private endpoints, AI Gateway fits the same shape. Its inbound private endpoint can sit in your New Zealand North virtual network even though the gateway runs in Australia East, while outbound VNet integration needs a dedicated subnet in the gateway’s own region and subscription. Both are in public preview.

Plan a dedicated integration subnet in the gateway’s region and subscription. Microsoft’s lab demonstrates changing private routing on an existing gateway, while Learn’s migration page says you can’t change the virtual network or subnet after creation. Don’t make the design depend on changing it later. Verify the private connection and DNS from the New Zealand client network as well as from the gateway to the backends.

Workspaces won’t carry MCP

The tempting compromise is to give the AI platform team a workspace in the enterprise API Management instance: their own APIs, products and policies, while the platform team keeps the service. Workspaces are good at that, but read what they don’t support before you promise it.

  • MCP servers aren’t supported in workspaces.
  • There’s no self-hosted gateway or credential manager, and Defender for APIs doesn’t cover workspace APIs.
  • Workspaces get the internal cache only, and semantic caching needs an external one.
  • Request metrics can’t be split by workspace in Azure Monitor.
  • Dedicated workspace gateways have no inbound private endpoints or custom hostnames. Gateways created after 15 April 2025 can host up to 30 workspaces by default; support can raise the limit. Dedicated capacity costs extra. It isn’t offered in New Zealand North, and Australia East shows new workspace gateways as temporarily unavailable.

In the v2 tiers a workspace can use the instance’s managed gateway instead of a dedicated workspace gateway, which helps with cost but not with MCP.

Who owns what

Two gateways only work with one owner per decision. This is the split I’d start with.

flowchart TB    accTitle: Ownership zones for two gateways    accDescr: The platform team owns the API Management front door, business APIs, WAF, DNS and certificates. The AI platform team owns AI Gateway, including aliases, routing, limits, MCP federation and tool allow lists. Security owns Entra ID, Conditional Access and Agent 365 blocks, and its blocks override the gateway. Application teams own their agents and request runtime roles on the aliases and MCP servers they need.    subgraph APP["Application teams"]      X1["Agents and apps
request roles per alias or MCP server"]:::app    end    subgraph PL["Platform team"]      P1["API Management front door
business APIs, WAF, DNS, certificates"]:::apim    end    subgraph AIT["AI platform team"]      A1["AI Gateway
aliases, routing, limits,
MCP federation, tool allow lists"]:::aig    end    subgraph SEC["Security"]      S1["Entra ID, Conditional Access,
Agent 365 blocks"]:::sec    end    X1 -- "business calls" --> P1    X1 -- "model and tool calls" --> A1    S1 -. "a block overrides" .-> A1    classDef app fill:#f1f5f9,stroke:#334155,color:#000    classDef apim fill:#cce5ff,stroke:#1f6feb,color:#000    classDef aig fill:#e6ffed,stroke:#2da44e,color:#000    classDef sec fill:#ede9fe,stroke:#6d28d9,color:#000

The platform team owns the front door, the AI platform team owns model and tool policy, security can override with a block, and application teams ask for the access they need.

  • Platform team: decides which business APIs to publish and to whom. API Management products and subscriptions enforce that decision.
  • AI platform team: owns aliases, routing, failover and consumption limits. It agrees the exposed toolset with security and enforces it in AI Gateway.
  • Security: owns emergency blocks of servers and tools via Agent 365 on supported gateways.
  • Application teams request access; the AI platform team approves and assigns scoped runtime roles to aliases or MCP servers.
  • Foundry owners: own model deployments and their quotas.

A few details make this split work in practice.

  • Use runtime roles, not shared keys. The broad scope is the default workspace, labelled All assets in the portal. AI Gateway Models User can also be scoped to a model alias, and AI Gateway Tools User to an MCP server. AI Gateway User covers both. Give application teams the narrower grants so they can’t reach a model outside their alias and miss the alias limits.
  • Set a policy floor at the gateway and tighter limits at narrower scopes. Foundry quota still applies at the backend. Registering a deployment doesn’t change who owns it.
  • Agree that a security block wins. Agent 365 integration requires tenant consent for the A365 MCP Gateway Policy Operator role. The integration can discover resources in existing and future subscriptions and write scoped policies. Server blocks return HTTP 403. Tool blocks require a static list of exposed tools and return HTTP 200 with isError: true, so alert on tool errors rather than HTTP status alone. Point agents at the gateway explicitly and make sure infrastructure deployments don’t remove Agent 365’s managed policies.
  • Keep policies in infrastructure as code. Audit or deny changes with Azure Policy where it supports the relevant resource properties. Treat estimated cost limits as guardrails, not exact budgets: a limit can return LlmCostQuotaExceeded, and concurrent activity can overshoot briefly. Reconcile estimates from public prices with actual billing.

Correlation IDs across both gateways

I use the same rule for every gateway: honour the caller’s correlation ID end to end into Log Analytics, and if there isn’t one, create it and return it. With two gateways, you need a second ID as well.

sequenceDiagram    accTitle: A correlation ID and a W3C trace across both gateways    accDescr: The caller sends x-correlation-id. API Management keeps it if it's valid or creates one, and sends it on to AI Gateway with a W3C traceparent. AI Gateway calls the model. API Management returns the correlation ID to the caller. Both gateways send their records to the same Log Analytics workspace.    autonumber    participant C as Caller    participant A as API Management    participant G as AI Gateway    participant M as Model    participant L as Log Analytics    C->>A: Request with x-correlation-id    A->>A: Keep a valid ID, otherwise create one    A->>G: Forward with x-correlation-id and traceparent    G->>M: Inference call    M-->>G: Response    G-->>A: Response    A-->>C: Response with x-correlation-id    A->>L: Gateway logs, LLM logs, request telemetry    G->>L: OTelSpans and OTelLogs

The correlation ID ties the call to the caller’s logs. W3C Trace Context lets you follow the same request across services. Microsoft’s lab says AI Gateway continues an incoming trace; confirm that API Management sends it and that you can find it in telemetry before relying on a join.

At the front door, keep a valid caller ID, otherwise create one, and send it back on the response. This sketch checks the format so a caller can’t push arbitrary text into your logs:

The on-error section means calls that fail with a policy error carry the ID too (a return-response in a parent scope still skips it), and the choose block keeps AI Gateway’s own ID when it sends one, which it does on some responses such as Agent 365 blocks, so the two can still be matched. In Bicep or ARM templates, match the format to the policy text: use xml for the escaped example above and rawxml for policy text with unescaped expressions. Then:

  • Set the HTTP correlation protocol for API Management’s Application Insights diagnostic to W3C so it sends Trace Context to the backend.
  • Configure OTLP ingestion and the appropriate signal endpoints; a connection string alone isn’t enough. Microsoft’s monitoring lab documents the Monitoring Metrics Publisher grant on the data collection rule and shows OTelSpans and OTelLogs in Log Analytics.
  • Query both gateways’ telemetry in the same Log Analytics workspace where your residency rules permit it. API Management’s ApiManagementGatewayLlmLog shares a CorrelationId with ApiManagementGatewayLogs for its own request and token records. That’s distinct from your application header.
  • Send a test request with a known traceparent and x-correlation-id. Confirm the trace ID in OTelSpans matches the Application Insights operation ID before joining on it. Don’t assume AI Gateway records your custom header. If it doesn’t, log the gateway’s returned ID alongside your own when present, or retain an explicit mapping in trusted telemetry.

A correlation ID is a label, not proof of who called. Don’t use it for authorisation.

If you built on the preview tier
