A pilot on the old AI Gateway tier keeps working until 15 January 2027, and then it’s removed. There’s no in-place conversion.

  1. Create a gateway of the new resource type, and move templates to Microsoft.ApiManagement/aigateways with API version 2026-11-01.
  2. Re-create model providers, models, aliases, MCP servers, policies, monitoring and keys. Role assignments don’t carry over, and a new system-assigned identity has a new principal ID, so re-grant its access to your backends.
  3. Update callers: the new runtime URL, a new key or Entra identity, and an Authorization: Bearer header in place of api-key.
  4. Check the gaps that matter to you on the migration page. Private endpoints need preview approval. The page says the content safety policy isn’t supported and suggests Foundry guardrails instead, while the GA announcement, the product docs and Microsoft’s labs show a content safety policy on the new type, so test it on your own gateway and keep Foundry’s guardrails on either way. And it says you can’t change the virtual network or subnet after creation. The product’s release notes say you now can, but the product docs also list an AIGatewaySubnetImmutable error for gateways where that isn’t enabled yet, so plan as if the migration page is right.

If you’re also moving AI APIs off a regular API Management instance, Microsoft publishes a coding-agent plugin that inventories the instance, plans the equivalent AI Gateway and provisions it. It’s designed to add resources rather than remove anything from API Management, so it’s a reasonable way to get a first draft of that move. Review its plan before you let it provision.

My take

GA changes the default. For new model and tool traffic, I’d start on AI Gateway in Australia East unless one of the three questions sends the workload to API Management. API Management stays the front door for business APIs, and nobody needs to rip out AI workloads that already run well there.

Two lanes beat a chain. Topology C looks tidy on a slide, but every AI call adds a second gateway hop to operate and observe, and needs an identity design you have to get right on purpose. Check the cost of each gateway separately against its tier and request allowance. I’d only chain the gateways when a security standard requires one front door for everything, and I’d write down which policy lives where before the first API goes live.

Ownership is the real decision. The AI platform team should own model and tool policy outright, with security holding a block it can apply at any time through Agent 365. A workspace in someone else’s API Management is a reasonable home for AI APIs, but not for MCP or semantic caching.

The gaps are real. Private networking is there but still in preview, and so are Agent Hooks, Model Router and tool threat protection. Content safety, the free allowance and the Agent 365 integration each have two answers depending on which page you read. AI Gateway isn’t offered in New Zealand North, and I couldn’t find a published statement on where it processes or stores request data beyond the region you create it in. None of that needs to stop a production pilot. It should stop anyone promising what the platform doesn’t do yet.

My first week would look like this: re-create any preview-tier gateways, then stand up one AI Gateway in Australia East with Entra access and no runtime keys, one alias, one MCP server and tracing into the same workspace as the front door. Use it to test the ownership split with real traffic.

Key takeaways

  • Put business APIs on API Management and model and tool traffic on AI Gateway by default. Give each path one owner.
  • Keep workloads on API Management when the gateway must be in New Zealand North or needs unsupported inference routes, A2A, semantic caching or format translation. AI Gateway private networking is still in preview.
  • Replace old preview-tier gateways before 15 January 2027 and grant runtime roles again at the narrowest scope.
  • If you chain gateways, verify which identity and trace survive both hops. Confirm the deployment type, not the gateway address, before promising where inference runs.

References

  • Microsoft: Azure AI Gateway GA announcement and API Management at Ignite 2026
  • Microsoft Learn: Compare AI Gateway and API Management and migrate from the preview tier
  • Microsoft Learn: API Management regional availability and workspace constraints
  • Microsoft Learn: Foundry model deployment types and model region availability
  • Microsoft Learn: Agent 365 governance on AI Gateway and API Management policy expressions
  • Azure AI Gateway Labs: Private networking and monitoring and traces

Related posts

  • MCP Goes Stateless: No Handshake, No Sticky Sessions, Better AI Gateways: per-tool routing at the gateway, and the preview-era AI Gateway notes this post brings up to date.
  • AI Agents Exploit Leaked Keys in Minutes: Go Keyless on Azure: why Entra roles beat gateway keys.
  • Microsoft Foundry Cross-Region with Private Endpoints (Part 1): data at rest in New Zealand North, inference in Australia East.
  • Copilot Studio Bring Your Own Model: Microsoft Foundry Governance and Security: another case of two control planes with two owners.
  • APIM Backend Fan-out: Shared Backend + rewrite-uri vs One Backend Per API (A Real Benchmark): API Management backend design, measured rather than assumed.

Image Credits

  • Cover image generated by Copilot
entry.summary: Compare three ways to run Azure AI Gateway alongside API Management, with practical guidance on New Zealand residency, MCP governance, ownership and tracing.
entry.title: Azure AI Gateway Is GA: When to Use It, When to Keep APIM, and Who Should Own It

entry.content:
TL;DR

A model can pass standard evaluations and still carry a backdoor. Microsoft showed a fine-tuning set poisoned at about 1% hijacking a coding agent in roughly 78% of trials on the harnesses it was trained with, and a sleeper agent planted by editing fewer than ten neurons. You can’t prompt your way out of that.

ASD’s new guidance on AI testing environments says it plainly: prompts and model safeguards aren’t containment. Build it into the architecture instead: a model intake gate, one identity per agent, default-deny egress, logs the agent can’t reach, and stop buttons at the inference, identity and infrastructure layers that you’ve actually tested.

In a hurry? Jump to the three stop buttons, the Azure mapping or the containment checklist, then come back for the why.

This is Part 2 of my Governance for AI Agents series. Part 1 covered the governance gap, the OWASP Agentic Top 10 and a deterministic policy check in front of every tool call. This part is about what happens when that isn’t enough: containment, and the stop buttons you’ll want when something gets past the policy.

Three things this month changed how I think about it. Microsoft published two research posts showing a model can carry a backdoor that standard evaluation may miss. Australia’s ASD published guidance that says, in so many words, that prompts are not containment. And OpenAI described a system that halts its research models’ output within 35 seconds and denies inference if that system itself goes down.

The guidance and product details below were checked against primary sources on 20 November 2026.

What changed this month

flowchart TB    accTitle: Containment research and guidance in 2026    accDescr: OpenAI described Control Room. On 10 November Microsoft published research on sleeper agents hidden in model neurons and OWASP released Securing Agentic Applications V2. On 12 November ASD published guidance on securing AI testing environments and Microsoft published its trained to betray research. As at 20 November, Foundry hosted agent egress controls are generally available, Defender runtime protection for local agents on Windows became generally available at Ignite, and an Agent Sandbox extension for AKS is in preview.    subgraph R["Research and guidance"]      A["OpenAI Control Room
stops research inference, fails closed"]:::ext      B["10 Nov · Microsoft: sleeper agents
a backdoor in fewer than ten neurons"]:::threat      C["10 Nov · OWASP Securing
Agentic Applications V2"]:::guide      D["12 Nov · ASD: securing
AI testing environments"]:::guide      E["12 Nov · Microsoft: trained to betray
poisoned fine-tunes hijack coding agents"]:::threat      B --> C --> D --> E    end    subgraph P["Products, as at 20 November"]      F["Foundry hosted agent
egress controls, GA"]:::prod      G["Defender runtime protection
for local agents on Windows, GA"]:::prod      H["Agent Sandbox extension
for AKS, preview"]:::prod      F --> G --> H    end    classDef ext fill:#f1f5f9,stroke:#334155,color:#0f172a    classDef threat fill:#fee2e2,stroke:#b91c1c,color:#7f1d1d    classDef guide fill:#e0f2fe,stroke:#0369a1,color:#0c4a6e    classDef prod fill:#dcfce7,stroke:#15803d,color:#14532d

The research says the model itself can’t be fully trusted, the guidance says build containment around it, and the products are starting to catch up.

If that sounds theoretical, July made it concrete. Hugging Face disclosed an intrusion into part of its production infrastructure that was “driven, end to end, by an autonomous AI agent system”. OpenAI later confirmed the agents were its own models under internal cyber testing, in an evaluation environment without direct internet access, and that they “exploited a previously unknown zero-day vulnerability in Artifactory” to get out. ASD’s new guidance makes its case with exactly this class of incident, citing disclosures from the UK AI Security Institute, OpenAI and Anthropic of test agents that reached or affected real systems.

The threat: a model that passes standard tests

Microsoft’s two studies attack the same assumption: that a model which passes evaluation is safe to hand tools.

  • Trained to betray (12 November). Microsoft Defender Research added 90 poisoned examples to roughly 9,000 terminal-agent conversations, about 1% of the set, and fine-tuned gpt-4.1-mini on it. The trigger was a routine request to create project documentation. On the two harnesses seen in training, the unsafe action fired in 78.0% and 77.8% of 500 trials. On two unseen harnesses it fell to 11.0% and 0%, so the harness changes behaviour, but it isn’t a control. Threat hunting also turned up rows in a large public dataset that mapped benign requests to unsafe tool calls, including downloading and running a remote script. The same post covers a second study by the Microsoft AI Red Team: in its strongest configuration, open-weight checkpoints poisoned before release reached 84.1% to 94.8% attack success on repositories they hadn’t seen, and the backdoor still fired under Claude Code, Pi and Codex CLI, which Microsoft stresses isn’t a weakness in those tools.
  • Sleeper agents (10 November). Microsoft Research showed a capable agent model can become a sleeper agent by editing fewer than ten neurons. It passes standard evaluations, then runs an attacker’s command when a trigger appears, and the trigger can be as mundane as the date rolling into 2027. Microsoft hasn’t seen threat actors use the technique.

The Trained to betray authors land where this post lands: “Strict authorization controls at the tool-execution layer can prevent a triggered backdoor from acting.”

sequenceDiagram    accTitle: A poisoned model meets its trigger, and where containment stops it    accDescr: A poisoned dataset plants a trigger during fine-tuning and the model passes normal evaluation. Later a developer makes a routine request, and the model proposes an unsafe tool call. If the tool-call policy denies it, it never runs. If the policy misses it, the command runs in a sandbox where egress to an unknown host is blocked. Either way the decision is logged to a store the agent can't reach.    autonumber    participant P as Poisoned data or checkpoint    participant M as Model in the agent harness    actor U as Developer    participant G as Tool-call policy    participant S as Sandbox and egress    participant L as Protected log store    P->>M: Fine-tuning plants the trigger    Note over P,M: Passes normal evaluation    U->>M: Create the project documentation    M->>G: Proposes: download and run a remote script    alt Policy denies it      G-->>M: Denied, the call never runs    else Policy misses it      G->>S: Command runs inside the sandbox      S-->>S: Egress to an unknown host blocked    end    G->>L: Decision recorded out of the agent's reach

A trigger can be a normal request. Evaluation may miss a backdoor that fires only on a particular everyday phrase. Independent controls around the tool call can limit the damage: the policy that decides, the sandbox that runs it, the network that restricts it and the log that records it.

Microsoft’s phrasing of the risk is worth keeping in your back pocket for design reviews: “The available tools and their permissions define the potential blast radius.”

Prompts aren’t containment

ASD’s guidance on securing AI testing environments, published on 12 November, is the clearest statement I’ve read on this. It says prompts, scoped instructions and model safeguards “do not provide sufficient technical containment on their own”, and it tells operators not to rely on them as containment controls. It then describes containment you can actually build: minimum tools and credentials, secrets applied by a proxy, default-deny egress, logs out of the agent’s reach, execution limits, a separate management plane, and tested termination at three levels.

One scoping note. This guidance is written for testing environments, and ASD says it doesn’t cover production. I still use it as the blueprint for production, alongside ASD’s May guidance on adopting agentic AI services, which New Zealand’s NCSC co-authored with ASD and other Five Eyes partners. An agent with real credentials deserves at least the containment we’d give one in a lab. ASD’s September guidance on agent harnesses, written for adoption rather than testing, is blunter still: “No harness is inherently secure.”

flowchart TB    accTitle: A containment boundary for an AI agent, based on ASD's guidance    accDescr: Inside the boundary the agent runs with a unique short-lived identity, minimum tools that are denied by default, execution limits, and a credential proxy that applies secrets without handing them over. Egress is denied by default except approved model endpoints and package mirrors. Logs flow one way to a store outside the boundary, and operators on a separate management plane hold the stop buttons.    subgraph B["Containment boundary"]      A["Agent
unique, short-lived identity"]:::agent      T["Minimum tools
denied by default"]:::inside      X["Execution limits
duration, runs, tool-call rate, tokens"]:::inside      CP["Credential proxy
applies secrets, never hands them over"]:::inside      A --> T      A --> X      T --> CP    end    EG{"Egress
default deny"}:::gate    CP --> EG    EG -- "approved model endpoints
and package mirrors" --> OK["Allowed destinations"]:::ok    EG -- "everything else" --> NO["Blocked"]:::no    A -. "one-way export" .-> LOG["Logs and traces
outside the boundary"]:::out    OP["Operators
separate management plane"]:::out -- "stop buttons" --> A    classDef agent fill:#1e293b,stroke:#0f172a,color:#ffffff    classDef inside fill:#e0f2fe,stroke:#0369a1,color:#0c4a6e    classDef gate fill:#f1f5f9,stroke:#334155,color:#0f172a    classDef ok fill:#dcfce7,stroke:#15803d,color:#14532d    classDef no fill:#fee2e2,stroke:#b91c1c,color:#7f1d1d    classDef out fill:#ede9fe,stroke:#6d28d9,color:#3b0764

Containment lives outside the agent. ASD asks for network restrictions and execution limits enforced where the agent can’t modify them. A compromised model can ignore an instruction. It can’t edit a firewall rule it has no access to.

Layer 1: a model intake gate

If a checkpoint can carry a backdoor, it’s a dependency, and it needs the same supply chain discipline as a package. This is OWASP’s ASI04, Agentic Supply Chain Vulnerabilities, applied to the model itself. Foundry already ties catalogue models to their original publisher and scans the containers they run in, so the gate matters most for checkpoints you bring yourself: fine-tunes, merges, adapters and open weights from public hubs. Microsoft’s recommendations translate into a gate:

  • Pin the data. Pin training datasets by cryptographic hash and review examples for actions that don’t follow from the request.
  • Prove where the model came from. Source checkpoints from the original publisher, check its hashes, record source, version, hash and review status, and reject models without a verifiable base.
  • Diff against the base. Legitimate fine-tunes change weights diffusely, while implants tend to change a few sharply. Microsoft found frontier agents acting as auditors are highly effective at spotting these edits, and it’s turning the technique into a red-teaming harness. Today it’s a research method, not a product.
  • Scan the files. Turn on Defender for Storage malware scanning on upload for the staging account. Defender for Cloud’s AI model security (preview) covers supported models in Azure Machine Learning workspaces and registries, but it scans weekly, doesn’t support private link workspaces or registries, and has a 10 GB file limit. Add a supported command-line scan to the release pipeline as a gate, and handle unsupported files explicitly. Microsoft is clear that this covers serialisation and code-level risks rather than auditing the weights.
  • Evaluate in your own harness. The 78% against 11% result shows the harness changes behaviour, so test in the one you’ll run.
  • Enforce at deployment. Register approved models in a private Azure Machine Learning registry. For Foundry deployments, assign the built-in Azure Policy “Foundry model deployments should only use approved models” in Deny mode with the appropriate approved asset IDs or publishers. Publisher approval is broader than approving a specific version. The companion “Foundry model deployments should meet eligibility requirements” can deny preview models with denyPreviewModels set to true; both of its switches default to false. If you serve your own checkpoints on Azure Machine Learning endpoints, evaluate “[Preview]: Azure Machine Learning Deployments should only use approved Registry Models” as well. Check each policy’s scope and verify it blocks an unapproved deployment.
flowchart TB    accTitle: A model intake gate on Azure    accDescr: A candidate model from a public hub lands in staging storage with malware scanning on upload. Provenance is checked against the publisher and hash, the checkpoint is compared with its declared base model, and the model is evaluated in your production harness. Approved models go into a private Azure Machine Learning registry, and Azure Policy allows deployments only of approved models. Anything that fails a check is rejected.    H["Public hub or
vendor checkpoint"]:::ext --> S["Staging storage
malware scan on upload"]:::step    S --> P{"Provenance
publisher, version, hash"}:::q    P -- "unverifiable" --> R["Rejected"]:::no    P -- "verified" --> W{"Diff against the
declared base model"}:::q    W -- "sharp, sparse edits" --> R    W -- "expected changes" --> E{"Evaluate in your
production harness"}:::q    E -- "unexpected tool calls" --> R    E -- "passes" --> REG["Private Azure Machine
Learning registry"]:::ok    REG --> POL["Azure Policy
approved models only, Deny"]:::ok    POL --> DEP["Deployment, within
the policy's scope"]:::ok    classDef ext fill:#f1f5f9,stroke:#334155,color:#0f172a    classDef step fill:#e0f2fe,stroke:#0369a1,color:#0c4a6e    classDef q fill:#fef9c3,stroke:#a16207,color:#713f12    classDef no fill:#fee2e2,stroke:#b91c1c,color:#7f1d1d    classDef ok fill:#dcfce7,stroke:#15803d,color:#14532d

A gate, not a guarantee. Microsoft says it directly: “no scan can prove beyond any doubt that a model is safe”. The gate cuts the odds of a bad model arriving. The next two layers limit what one can do if it gets through.

Layer 2: one identity per agent, minimum tools, no raw secrets

ASD asks for unique, short-lived, least-privilege credentials, tools denied by default, and secrets that the agent never holds: “use an intermediary mechanism, such as a controlled proxy, that applies the required credential”. ASD’s May guidance says to “construct each agent as a distinct principal”. That covers OWASP’s ASI02, Tool Misuse and Exploitation, and ASI03, Identity and Privilege Abuse.

On Azure the pieces exist:

  • Identity. Microsoft Entra Agent ID is generally available, every agent identity and blueprint needs a sponsor, and Foundry now gives each new agent its own identity with no permissions until you grant them. Conditional Access for agent identities can block them.
  • The credential proxy. An AI gateway in API Management that authenticates callers with Entra ID and calls the model with its own managed identity is exactly ASD’s controlled proxy. I covered the pattern in Go Keyless on Azure.
  • A decision before every tool call. That’s the Part 1 idea, and it has matured. AGT 5.0 moved policy into the Agent Control Specification, a deterministic, fail-closed decision runtime. Bind approvals to the exact call and test that changed continuations are rejected before an approval executes.
flowchart TB    accTitle: A policy decision in front of every tool call    accDescr: When an agent proposes a tool call, a policy decides before it runs. Allowed calls run in the sandbox with the agent's own identity. Denied calls are blocked and logged. Calls that need approval go to a human who approves the exact call, and anything rejected or timed out is blocked. If the policy service is unavailable, the call is blocked.    T["Agent proposes a tool call"]:::agent --> P{"Policy decision
before it runs"}:::q    P -- "allow" --> R["Runs in the sandbox
with the agent's own identity"]:::ok    P -- "deny" --> D["Blocked and logged"]:::no    P -- "needs approval" --> H["A person approves
the exact call"]:::human    H -- "approved" --> R    H -- "rejected or timed out" --> D    P -- "policy unavailable" --> D    classDef agent fill:#1e293b,stroke:#0f172a,color:#ffffff    classDef q fill:#f1f5f9,stroke:#334155,color:#0f172a    classDef ok fill:#dcfce7,stroke:#15803d,color:#14532d    classDef no fill:#fee2e2,stroke:#b91c1c,color:#7f1d1d    classDef human fill:#ede9fe,stroke:#6d28d9,color:#3b0764

Fail closed, every time. The interesting branch is the last one. If the thing that makes the decision is down, the answer is no. AGT’s own README is honest about the limit: “AGT enforces governance at the application middleware layer, not at the OS kernel level.” Run each agent in its own container so the next layer still holds if the process doesn’t.

Layer 3: default-deny egress and logs the agent can’t reach

ASD’s egress rule is simple: allow only approved model endpoints, “block all other external destinations by default”, and treat package repositories the same way. Treat the mirror itself as part of the boundary too: patch it, make it read-only to agents and watch what it fetches. In July, a package cache proxy was the way out. Here’s how that maps on Azure, traps included:

  • Foundry Agent Service on your own network. Network injection uses a delegated subnet of /27 or larger (/24 is Microsoft’s starting point for production), with no public egress by default. For hosted agents, set it when you create the Foundry account, because you can’t add it later.
  • Foundry managed virtual network. “Allow only approved outbound” mode works, but FQDN rules create a Microsoft-managed Azure Firewall at extra cost, and Learn notes “No logging of outbound traffic support yet.” Log at another layer.
  • Foundry hosted agents. Network egress controls are generally available, except Transform rules. Governing them with Azure Policy is in preview in Canada Central, Spain Central and Korea Central only, and a new Deny assignment doesn’t stop a running session.
  • Network security perimeter. Generally available for Foundry resources, while classic Azure OpenAI resources are still in preview. In enforced mode it denies public inbound and outbound traffic that no access rule allows, and outbound rules are FQDN-based.
  • Code execution. Container Apps dynamic sessions default to EgressDisabled. The new Container Apps Sandboxes are the opposite: “Without a policy, outbound access is unrestricted.” Attach one. For coding agents on developer machines, Defender’s runtime protection for local agents on Windows is now generally available.
  • AKS. Route outbound traffic through Azure Firewall with userDefinedRouting, or use outbound type none for a network-isolated cluster. My AKS static egress gateway post covers per-namespace egress if agents share a cluster.

For logs, ASD’s rule is just as direct: “Store logs and traces on a system the agent cannot access, modify or delete.”

flowchart TB    accTitle: Logs an agent can't reach on Azure    accDescr: The agent runtime emits traces and diagnostic logs into a Log Analytics workspace in a separate subscription that requires workspace permissions. Data export copies the tables to immutable storage with a locked retention policy, and Microsoft Sentinel runs detections on the workspace. The agent's identity has no role that can read, change or delete the workspace or the storage.    A["Agent runtime"]:::agent -- "emits traces and logs" --> LA["Log Analytics workspace
separate subscription
workspace permissions required"]:::log    LA -- "data export" --> W["Immutable storage
locked time-based retention"]:::safe    LA --> SN["Microsoft Sentinel
detections and response"]:::safe    ID["Agent identity"]:::agent -. "no read or delete rights" .-> LA    ID -. "no read or delete rights" .-> W    classDef agent fill:#1e293b,stroke:#0f172a,color:#ffffff    classDef log fill:#e0f2fe,stroke:#0369a1,color:#0c4a6e    classDef safe fill:#dcfce7,stroke:#15803d,color:#14532d

Write once, out of reach. Two Azure defaults work against you here. A workspace’s default access mode lets anyone who can read a resource read that resource’s logs, so switch it to require workspace permissions. And Log Analytics data can be purged, so export the tables that matter to immutable storage with a locked retention policy and protected append writes turned on, because data export writes append blobs. Data export retries failed deliveries for 12 hours and then discards them, so alert on export health too.

Three stop buttons

ASD’s guidance asks operators to “Test emergency termination at the inference, identity and infrastructure levels”. The controls should be independent, so “a failure at one level does not prevent operators from stopping the test”. It also asks for documented owners, a method and an expected time for each, and for an operator who doesn’t depend on the agent or its execution environment.

flowchart TB    accTitle: Three independent stop buttons for an AI agent on Azure    accDescr: An operator on a separate management plane can press three independent stop buttons. Inference: a gateway policy returns 503 after the change propagates, or the model deployment is paused, while the process may keep running. Identity: disabling the agent identity or blueprint and blocking it with Conditional Access stops new tokens after propagation, while issued tokens may remain usable until expiry. Infrastructure: an Azure Firewall deny drops relevant existing sessions after the rule change, and scaling to zero or deactivating the revision stops the compute.    OP["Operator
separate management plane and identity"]:::op    OP --> I1["Inference
gateway returns 503,
or pause the deployment"]:::btn    OP --> I2["Identity
disable the agent identity or blueprint,
Conditional Access block"]:::btn    OP --> I3["Infrastructure
Azure Firewall deny,
deactivate or scale to zero"]:::btn    I1 --> E1["Calls fail after propagation
the process may keep running"]:::effect    I2 --> E2["No new tokens after propagation
issued tokens may remain valid"]:::effect    I3 --> E3["Relevant sessions dropped
compute stopped"]:::effect    classDef op fill:#1e293b,stroke:#0f172a,color:#ffffff    classDef btn fill:#fee2e2,stroke:#b91c1c,color:#7f1d1d    classDef effect fill:#fef9c3,stroke:#a16207,color:#713f12

The inference stop can leave the process running, the identity stop can leave issued tokens usable, and the infrastructure stop is the bluntest instrument. Each one covers a gap in the others, which is why you press them together. Timing and coverage depend on the actual configuration, so verify each action during the drill.

Inference stop

Use a gateway policy that returns 503, pause the Foundry deployment, or suspend the agent’s API Management subscription if it calls with a key. This refuses subsequent model calls after the change takes effect. A paused deployment returns HTTP 423 to every caller, and pausing works on Standard, Data Zone Standard and Global Standard deployments. Unpublishing an API Management product doesn’t invalidate subscription keys.

Identity stop

Disable the agent identity or its blueprint in Entra, and block it with Conditional Access. This stops new tokens after the change takes effect; disabling a blueprint stops every identity created from it. Assume tokens issued before you press it work until they expire: the default access token lifetime is 60 to 90 minutes. Agent identity policies alone don’t cover all delegated scenarios. Review the separate policies for agents acting as users and users signing into agents.

Infrastructure stop

Apply an Azure Firewall deny rule to egress that routes through your firewall, deactivate the container app’s revision, or scale the agent’s Kubernetes deployment to zero. The firewall rule drops relevant sessions and the compute actions stop the workload. Cordoning a node only stops new pods, so drain it or scale to zero. A Foundry managed network’s firewall isn’t yours to edit, so remove its outbound rules instead. Removing an NSG allow rule leaves existing connections up. An Azure Policy deny doesn’t stop anything already running.

AGT’s kill switch is a fourth, application-level option. It’s fast and precise, but it runs in the same process as the agent, so treat it as a complement to the three ASD layers rather than one of them.

Run the drill

sequenceDiagram    accTitle: A stop button drill for one agent    accDescr: The drill stages an out-of-scope action that should raise an alert. The operator presses the inference stop and confirms the next model call fails, disables the agent identity and confirms new tokens are refused, then applies the firewall deny and scales to zero and confirms sessions drop. Finally the operator checks the evidence survived and records each time against its target.    autonumber    actor O as Operator    participant A as Agent    participant G as AI gateway    participant E as Microsoft Entra ID    participant N as Firewall and compute    participant L as Protected log store    A->>N: Staged out-of-scope action    N-->>O: Alert, inside the target time?    O->>G: Press the inference stop    A->>G: Next model call    G-->>A: 503    O->>E: Disable the agent identity    A->>E: Token request    E-->>A: Refused    O->>N: Firewall deny and scale to zero    N-->>A: Sessions dropped    O->>L: Evidence intact, times recorded

Measure it like an outage. ASD asks for measurable maximum times for detecting out-of-scope activity, alerting and stopping it, and for containment verification to be the first test on higher-risk work. A stop button you haven’t timed is a hope.

Fail closed at the choke point

OpenAI’s Control Room is the most interesting design I saw this month, even though it’s internal research infrastructure rather than a product. Every agentic research workload must be tied to an approved safety case, and inference engines check with Control Room before serving each request. It “halts model output within 35 seconds of a decision to intervene”, where 35 seconds is the maximum lag from an authorisation cache. It stops output, not the job. And if Control Room itself goes down, for any reason including tampering, every inference request is denied until it recovers.

sequenceDiagram    accTitle: A fail-closed control check in front of inference    accDescr: An agent job sends an inference request to the gateway, which checks the control state before forwarding. If the agent is approved and running, the request reaches the model. If the agent is stopped, the gateway returns 503 and nothing reaches the model. If the control state is unavailable, the gateway denies the request.    autonumber    participant J as Agent job    participant G as AI gateway    participant C as Control state    participant F as Model deployment    J->>G: Inference request    G->>C: Is this agent approved and running?    alt Running      C-->>G: Yes      G->>F: Forward the request      F-->>G: Response      G-->>J: Response    else Stopped      C-->>G: Stopped      G-->>J: 503, nothing reaches the model    else Control state unavailable      G-->>J: Denied, fail closed    end

Copy the pattern, not the scale. A single place every inference request passes through is useful, but a separate control that defaults to “no” when its state is unavailable needs additional design.

The diagram shows the stronger pattern with a separate control-state check. In API Management, a simpler manual stop uses a named value and a short choose block:

Set the plain named value agent-traffic-state to running initially. Change it to stopped to refuse requests after the update reaches the gateway. Restrict changes to those two controlled values: named values are substituted into the policy expression, so arbitrary strings can make it invalid. The comparison denies other valid string values, but this is not equivalent to Control Room’s fail-closed service: a gateway may continue using its last deployed configuration if a control-plane update cannot reach it. It also doesn’t terminate an in-flight response or a running process. Scope controls to the intended agents and measure propagation and stop times at each gateway during the drill.

This only works if the gateway is the only way in. Disable key authentication on the Foundry resource, give the agent’s identity no role on it and keep the endpoint private. For Foundry agents whose model calls never pass through your gateway, the inference stop is pausing the deployment.

ASD and OWASP, mapped to Azure and an owner

OWASP’s Securing Agentic Applications V2, released on 10 November, covers the same ground from the builder’s side: identity and access controls, runtime protection, supply chain security and assurance testing. I’ve used OWASP’s Top 10 IDs so each control maps to a named risk.

Model intake gate

Microsoft’s backdoor research informs this control for ASI04, Agentic Supply Chain Vulnerabilities. The AI platform team can use Defender for Storage on upload, Azure Machine Learning registries, Defender for Cloud AI model security (preview) and the approved-models policy.

One identity per agent

ASD and Microsoft recommend distinct identities for ASI03, Identity and Privilege Abuse. The identity team can use Entra Agent ID, Foundry agent identities and Conditional Access for agents.

Minimum tools and a credential proxy

ASD’s guidance addresses ASI02, Tool Misuse and Exploitation. The application and platform teams can combine AGT or Agent Framework policy and approvals with API Management managed identity and Key Vault.

Sandboxed code execution

ASD and Microsoft recommend isolation for ASI05, Unexpected Code Execution (RCE). The platform team can use Container Apps dynamic sessions, Container Apps Sandboxes with a policy, or Agent Sandbox for AKS (preview).

Default-deny egress

ASD’s guidance helps limit ASI01, Agent Goal Hijack, and ASI10, Rogue Agents. The network team can use Foundry network injection, a managed network in approved-outbound mode, hosted agent egress controls, a network security perimeter and Azure Firewall.

Logs out of reach

For ASI10, ASD recommends protected logs. Security operations can use Log Analytics in a separate subscription, immutable storage, Sentinel and Purview audit.

Execution limits

ASD’s guidance helps limit ASI08, Cascading Failures. The platform team can use API Management token limits, AGT circuit breakers and budgets.

Three tested stop buttons

ASD’s guidance and OpenAI’s Control Room illustrate responses to ASI08, Cascading Failures, and ASI10, Rogue Agents. Operations and security operations can combine API Management policy, Entra disable and Conditional Access, Azure Firewall and scaling to zero.

Ten containment checks

  1. Models come through the gate. Provenance, hashes, a diff against the declared base and an evaluation in your own harness, with the approved-models policy in Deny mode.
  2. Training data is pinned. Datasets are pinned by hash and reviewed for actions that don’t follow from the request.
  3. Every agent is its own principal. Its own identity, a sponsor, and no standing access beyond its tools.
  4. Tools are denied by default. Credentials are applied by a proxy and never handed to the agent.
  5. Egress is default deny. Package repositories included, the mirror patched and read-only to agents, and enforced outside the agent’s environment.
  6. Code runs in a sandbox with its own egress policy. Container Apps Sandboxes need one attached.
  7. Logs go one way. The agent’s identity can’t read, change or delete them, and the copies that matter are immutable.
  8. Three independent stop buttons exist. Each has a named owner, a method and a target time.
  9. You’ve run the drill. Timed, with the evidence checked afterwards.
  10. Containment comes first. For any higher-risk agent, verifying the boundary is the first test you run.

My take

Containment is architecture, not prompting. In my experience, teams spend weeks on system prompts and an afternoon on egress rules. This month’s research says to flip that. A prompt is a request to a component you can’t fully inspect. A firewall rule is a fact.

The backdoor work changed how I think about the model as an artefact. A checkpoint is a dependency, with a supply chain, a provenance and a blast radius set by the tools you hand it. Microsoft’s own conclusion is that no scan proves a model safe, which is why the intake gate is the first layer and not the only one.

None of the stop buttons is perfect on its own: issued tokens may outlive a disabled identity, an NSG change leaves live connections up, and AGT’s kill switch shares a process with the agent. The defaults don’t help either: a Foundry managed network doesn’t log outbound traffic yet, and Container Apps Sandboxes ship with open egress. ASD wrote its guidance for testing, not production. I treat it as the floor for production anyway, because the agents with real credentials are the ones that most need it.

If I had one week, I’d pick one production agent, give it its own identity, put a gateway stop and a firewall deny in front of it, and run the drill on a weekday morning with a stopwatch and the owners in the room.

Key Takeaways

  • A model can pass standard evaluations and still carry a backdoor: about 1% poisoned fine-tuning data gave roughly 78% attack success on familiar harnesses, and fewer than ten edited neurons made a sleeper agent.
  • Prompts and model safeguards aren’t containment. ASD says so, and the controls that work sit outside the agent.
  • Treat models as dependencies: provenance, hashes, a diff against the base model, evaluation in your own harness and an approved-models policy.
  • Give every agent its own identity, deny tools by default, and let a proxy apply credentials so the agent never holds them.
  • Default-deny egress and logs the agent can’t reach, with the Azure traps in mind: open egress on Container Apps Sandboxes, no outbound logging on Foundry managed networks, and purgeable Log Analytics data.
  • Build three independent stop buttons, at inference, identity and infrastructure, and time them in a drill. Fail closed when the control itself is in doubt.

Related posts

  • Governance for AI Agents (Part 1): The Gap, the OWASP Agentic Top 10, and Where AGT Fits: the policy layer in front of every tool call that this part builds on.
  • AI Agents Exploit Leaked Keys in Minutes: Go Keyless on Azure: the credential proxy and agent identities in practice.
  • AKS Static Egress Gateway: Per-Namespace Static Egress IPs: controlled egress when agents share a cluster.
  • MCP Goes Stateless: No Handshake, No Sticky Sessions, Better AI Gateways: the gateway as the choke point for agent traffic.

entry.summary: Contain AI agents on Azure with model intake checks, least-privilege identities, restricted egress and tested stop buttons for inference, identity and infrastructure.
entry.title: AI Agent Containment on Azure: Stop Buttons, Identity and Network Controls

entry.content:
TL;DR

Copilot Studio can use a model you host in Microsoft Foundry in a prompt through bring your own model (BYOM) on the standard harness. That doesn’t replace the agent’s primary orchestration model, and the Microsoft Copilot harness doesn’t support the prompt tool.

BYOM gives your platform team control over the deployment and its applicable guardrails, quota, diagnostics and Azure costs. Agent orchestration, identity and sharing remain with Copilot Studio and the wider Microsoft governance tools.

The documented connector uses an API key. A dedicated Foundry resource contains the risk of a resource-wide key better than a project in a shared resource.

In a hurry? Jump to the resource decision or the nine go-live checks, then come back for the detail.

A question I keep getting from AI platform teams goes like this: makers are building agents in Copilot Studio, our models live in Foundry behind our guardrails, so if Copilot Studio used our Foundry models, could we govern it like everything else?

It’s a fair question, and the answer is “partly”. Copilot Studio calls a Foundry model mainly from inside a prompt, and that one connection decides a lot about what the platform team controls and where the Foundry should sit. In this post I’ll walk through where Foundry models plug in, what that puts in the platform team’s hands, what it leaves with the Copilot Studio and Microsoft 365 admins, and why I’d give it a dedicated Foundry resource.

The product details below were checked against Microsoft Learn on 20 November 2026, after this year’s Ignite announcements.

Two control planes, one bridge

Copilot Studio runs on Power Platform. Foundry runs on Azure. Each has its own control plane, and neither governs the other. A Copilot Studio agent can reach Foundry in four ways, and two of them put your Foundry model inside Copilot Studio:

  • A prompt with bring your own model. The prompt uses your selected Foundry deployment every time it runs.
  • A generative answers node on Azure OpenAI on your data (preview). A classic data option inside a topic, on the standard harness. It’s the older route, and I’d keep it out of new designs.
  • A connected Foundry agent (preview). The Copilot Studio agent hands a task to a Foundry agent, which does the work on its own model, under Foundry’s controls, and returns a result.
  • A connector or HTTP call. The same pattern: a tool call that returns data.

With generative orchestration, the agent’s primary model, picked from Copilot Studio’s list, decides what to do with the result and can write the answer the user reads. A topic, or a prompt set to send a specific response, can pass the prompt’s output straight to the user, so your Foundry model can have the last word. Microsoft’s model selection guidance separates primary model selection from prompt builder models. The connected-agent preview requires the Foundry agent’s Activity protocol endpoint to be enabled.

flowchart TB    accTitle: Where Microsoft Foundry plugs into a Copilot Studio agent    accDescr: A user reaches a Copilot Studio agent whose primary model comes from Copilot Studio's list. It can call a prompt using bring your own model, a connected Foundry agent or a connector. The response may be generated by the agent or passed through from a prompt.    U["User or trigger"]:::user    subgraph CS["Copilot Studio · Power Platform control plane"]      PM["Primary model from Copilot Studio's list
orchestrates the agent"]:::cs      PT["Prompt with bring your own model"]:::bridge      CA["Connected Foundry agent, preview
a tool call"]:::tool      TL["Connectors and HTTP
tool calls"]:::tool    end    subgraph AZ["Microsoft Foundry · Azure control plane"]      DEP["Your model deployment
your guardrails, quota and logs"]:::az      FA["Foundry agent
its own model and controls"]:::az    end    U --> PM    PM --> PT    PM --> CA    PM --> TL    PT -- "chat completions with an API key" --> DEP    CA -- "Activity protocol call" --> FA    classDef user fill:#f1f5f9,stroke:#334155,color:#000    classDef cs fill:#ede9fe,stroke:#6d28d9,color:#000    classDef bridge fill:#cce5ff,stroke:#1f6feb,color:#000    classDef tool fill:#fef9c3,stroke:#a16207,color:#000    classDef az fill:#e0f2fe,stroke:#0369a1,color:#000

One bridge for new designs. Your Foundry deployment can act as a model in two places, but the older generative answers route is a preview I’d leave alone, so the prompt is the bridge to design around. A connected Foundry agent is a tool call: Foundry does its part under its own controls, and Copilot Studio’s primary model decides what happens next.

The documented BYOM bridge uses the standard harness

Copilot Studio now runs agents on three harnesses: the standard harness, the Microsoft Copilot harness and the Customer Conversation harness, which went GA at Ignite. The BYOM documentation is scoped to the standard harness. The Microsoft Copilot harness has no prompt tool at all: Learn marks prompts there as replaced by skills, and upgrading an agent to that harness creates a copy of the agent rather than converting it in place.

The primary model lists differ by harness too. The standard harness defaults to GPT Chat Latest, while the newest models, such as Claude Fable 5.2, appear on the Microsoft Copilot harness list.

flowchart TB    accTitle: Which Copilot Studio harness has the prompt tool    accDescr: On the standard harness an agent has the prompt tool, so bring your own model to Foundry is available, and the primary model comes from the standard harness list. On the Microsoft Copilot harness prompts are replaced by skills, so there is no bring your own model route, and the primary model comes from that harness's list, which includes Claude Fable 5.2.    A["Copilot Studio agent"]:::cs --> H{"Which harness?"}:::q    H -- "Standard harness" --> S1["Prompt tool available
bring your own model: yes"]:::yes    H -- "Microsoft Copilot harness" --> M1["Prompts replaced by skills
bring your own model: no"]:::no    S1 --> S2["Primary model from the standard list
GPT Chat Latest by default"]:::cs    M1 --> M2["Primary model from the harness list
including Claude Fable 5.2"]:::cs    classDef cs fill:#ede9fe,stroke:#6d28d9,color:#000    classDef q fill:#f1f5f9,stroke:#334155,color:#000    classDef yes fill:#dcfce7,stroke:#15803d,color:#000    classDef no fill:#fee2e2,stroke:#b91c1c,color:#000

Check the harness before you design the bridge. A BYOM plan only makes sense for agents that stay on the standard harness. If an agent is heading to the Microsoft Copilot harness, its prompts need a new home first.

What the bridge accepts

BYOM is narrower than most people expect. Here’s what Microsoft documents today:

  • Where it lives. In the prompt tool, a maker selects + in the model list and connects a Foundry model. The prompt then uses that deployment every time it runs.
  • The connector. The connection runs on a Power Platform connector. Its fields match the Azure AI Foundry Inference connector reference, and Learn says to govern it in data policies under the name “Azure AI Foundry”.
  • The API. Chat completions only. The endpoint must end in /chat/completions, and a Responses API URL fails.
  • The models. The GPT-5 family and later models aren’t currently supported. Claude models in Foundry use the Messages API, so a Claude deployment doesn’t fit the connector either.
  • Authentication. An API key, alongside the endpoint, deployment name and base model name. The connector documents no Entra ID or managed identity option.
  • Safety. The prompt’s content moderation setting isn’t available for Foundry models, and Microsoft recommends applying Responsible AI policies in Foundry. Confirm which controls actually apply to the model and API; coverage and behaviour vary.
  • Cost. Foundry charges for BYOM processing separately. Microsoft’s AI Builder billing guidance treats invoking a BYOM prompt as an agent action, without an extra text and generative AI tool processing charge. Other agent activities and licensing or test-panel exceptions can affect Copilot Credit charges.
flowchart TB    accTitle: Which Foundry models fit bring your own model in Copilot Studio prompts    accDescr: A model must serve the chat completions API, so Claude on the Messages API doesn't fit. GPT-5 and later models aren't supported. A model that passes both checks fits, but its retirement date should sit beyond your next review.    M["Candidate Foundry model"]:::cs --> Q1{"Serves the chat
completions API?"}:::q    Q1 -- "No, for example Claude
on the Messages API" --> N1["Doesn't fit the connector"]:::no    Q1 -- "Yes" --> Q2{"GPT-5 family
or later?"}:::q    Q2 -- "Yes" --> N2["Not supported
for prompts"]:::no    Q2 -- "No" --> Q3{"Retires after
your next review?"}:::q    Q3 -- "No" --> W1["Plan the replacement first
check the Foundry retirement date"]:::warn    Q3 -- "Yes" --> Y1["Candidate for BYOM
verify support and test"]:::yes    classDef cs fill:#ede9fe,stroke:#6d28d9,color:#000    classDef q fill:#f1f5f9,stroke:#334155,color:#000    classDef yes fill:#dcfce7,stroke:#15803d,color:#000    classDef no fill:#fee2e2,stroke:#b91c1c,color:#000    classDef warn fill:#fef9c3,stroke:#a16207,color:#000

A narrow door. Foundry’s retirement schedule lists o1, o3, o3-mini and o4-mini for retirement on 19 November, and GPT-5 and later are excluded from BYOM prompts. GPT-4.1 and GPT-4o are candidates, but availability varies by version, deployment type and region. Their listed base-model retirement dates range from January to April 2027, so check and test the specific deployment before building on one.

Base modelVersionListed retirement
GPT-4o2024-05-1314 January 2027
GPT-4o2024-08-0614 April 2027
GPT-4.12025-04-1414 April 2027

These are Azure public cloud base-model dates, not a guarantee that every deployment type remains available until then.

Five owners, and where the platform team fits

On 11 November Microsoft published a governance map on the Copilot Studio blog, “Where do I govern my Copilot Studio agents?”, built around five outcomes, each led by a different admin in a different product:

  • Enable makers safely and at scale. The Power Platform admin, in the Power Platform admin center: environment strategy, environment routing, environment groups and rules, connector policies and sharing controls.
  • Configure agent identity and resource access. The identity and access admin, in Microsoft Entra: Entra Agent ID and Conditional Access for agents.
  • Protect information. The compliance admin and data security team, in Microsoft Purview: DSPM, sensitivity labels, DLP and audit.
  • Observability and business value. The AI admin, in Microsoft Agent 365: the registry, the agent map, tool governance and Copilot Credit cost management.
  • Detect and respond. The security admin and SOC, in Microsoft Defender: agent security posture and threat investigation.
flowchart TB    accTitle: Who governs a Copilot Studio agent, and where the Foundry platform team fits    accDescr: A Copilot Studio agent has five governance owners: the Power Platform admin, the identity admin in Entra, the compliance admin in Purview, the AI admin in Agent 365 and the security team in Defender. The AI platform team in Azure only joins for prompts that call its Foundry deployments.    A["Copilot Studio agent"]:::agent    A --> P["Enable makers safely
Power Platform admin"]:::m365    A --> E["Identity and access
Microsoft Entra"]:::m365    A --> PV["Protect information
Microsoft Purview"]:::m365    A --> AG["Observability and value
Microsoft Agent 365"]:::m365    A --> D["Detect and respond
Microsoft Defender"]:::m365    A -. "only for BYOM prompts" .-> F["Model calls in your Foundry
AI platform team in Azure"]:::az    classDef agent fill:#cce5ff,stroke:#1f6feb,color:#000    classDef m365 fill:#ede9fe,stroke:#6d28d9,color:#000    classDef az fill:#e0f2fe,stroke:#0369a1,color:#000

The map has no Azure row. Microsoft’s five owners cover the agent itself. The platform team joins only for the prompts that call its deployments, which is the gap this post is about.

What moves to the platform team, and what doesn’t

With BYOM in place, the platform team can govern the deployment and the call that reaches it. That doesn’t give it control over the whole agent or conversation.

flowchart TB    accTitle: What bring your own model moves to the platform team and what stays native    accDescr: For prompt calls that reach Foundry, the platform team controls approved models and versions, where inference runs, guardrails, quota, logs, token cost, key rotation and retirements. Copilot Studio and Microsoft 365 admins keep the primary model, external model access, cross-region data movement, connectors and data policies, environments and sharing, agent identity, audit, registry and threat response.    subgraph PLAT["Moves to the platform team, for BYOM calls only"]      P1["Approved models and versions"]:::az      P2["Where inference runs
deployment type and data zone"]:::az      P3["Guardrails on each deployment"]:::az      P4["Quota and rate limits"]:::az      P5["Diagnostic logs and token metrics"]:::az      P6["Token cost on your Azure bill"]:::az      P7["Key rotation and model retirement"]:::az    end    subgraph NAT["Stays with Copilot Studio and Microsoft 365 admins"]      N1["The primary model and orchestration"]:::cs      N2["External models and
cross-region data movement"]:::cs      N3["Connectors, knowledge and data policies
including the Azure AI Foundry connector"]:::cs      N4["Environments, routing and sharing limits"]:::cs      N5["Agent identity and Conditional Access"]:::cs      N6["Audit, DSPM, registry and threat response"]:::cs    end    classDef az fill:#e0f2fe,stroke:#0369a1,color:#000    classDef cs fill:#ede9fe,stroke:#6d28d9,color:#000

You govern the call, not the agent. BYOM gives the platform team real control over one model call. Everything a maker can change about the agent stays in Copilot Studio.

One lever on the native side is worth knowing. The Power Platform admin decides whether BYOM is allowed at all, because the connector is governed by data policies under the name “Azure AI Foundry”. I’d use that: allow the connector only in the environments where the platform team has agreed to host the model, and block it everywhere else.

Follow one prompt call

Here’s what happens when an agent uses a BYOM prompt, and where the evidence for each step lands.

sequenceDiagram    accTitle: One prompt call from Copilot Studio to a Foundry deployment    accDescr: A user asks the agent a question. The agent can call the prompt tool, which sends a chat completions request with an API key to the Foundry resource. Applicable guardrails act around the deployment. The result returns to the agent and may be passed through or used to form an answer. Available Copilot Studio and Azure evidence depends on configuration.    autonumber    actor U as User    participant A as Copilot Studio agent    participant P as Prompt with BYOM    participant F as Foundry resource    participant D as Your deployment    rect rgb(237, 233, 254)    U->>A: Asks a question    A->>P: Primary model picks the prompt tool    end    rect rgb(224, 242, 254)    P->>F: Chat completions request with the API key    F->>F: Applicable input controls    F->>D: Runs the model    D-->>F: Completion    F->>F: Applicable output controls    F-->>P: Result and token usage    end    rect rgb(237, 233, 254)    P-->>A: Prompt output    A-->>U: Answer or prompt output    end    Note over U,A: Copilot Studio evidence: transcripts, analytics,
Purview audit, Agent 365, Copilot Credits    Note over F,D: Azure evidence: diagnostic logs,
token metrics, Azure consumption

Two sets of evidence, one conversation. Foundry receives whatever the prompt sends, which can include a user’s question or other context. It doesn’t automatically see the entire conversation or orchestration. Available logs depend on diagnostic settings and supported model features, so an investigation may need evidence from both sides.

Where should that Foundry live?

Platform teams usually put two options on the table:

  • Option 1: a dedicated Foundry resource for Copilot Studio, in its own subscription.
  • Option 2: a project inside the shared AI platform’s Foundry resource.

Option 2 looks like the natural fit. Foundry projects give teams isolated workspaces that share model deployments under central governance, and Microsoft describes exactly that pattern. But BYOM changes the maths in three ways:

  1. The key is resource-wide. Learn puts it plainly: “Keys are all-or-nothing per resource.” A key that works for the Copilot Studio deployment works for every deployment in the resource, across every project, with no role restrictions.
  2. Key authentication has to stay on. BYOM only offers an API key, so the resource can’t set disableLocalAuth to true, and Learn describes API keys as “Generally not accepted by enterprise production workloads and not recommended by Microsoft.” On a shared platform resource, the whole platform goes back to accepting keys, the opposite of the keyless pattern I wrote about earlier this month.
  3. The endpoint has to stay reachable. The connector isn’t on Power Platform’s published virtual network support list. For this documented connector, plan for a reachable public endpoint and test network restrictions. That absence doesn’t prove that every possible private integration is impossible.

There’s more. The built-in Foundry User role includes permission to list keys when assigned at a scope covering the resource, as do some broader roles. Check effective assignments and inheritance rather than assuming every project user can list them. Guardrails can be attached per deployment, diagnostic settings are set per resource, and model router’s instant access (preview) is configured for the whole resource. Microsoft’s rollout guidance also recommends treating isolation as the production default.

flowchart TB    accTitle: What the bring your own model key opens in each option    accDescr: In option 2 a resource key can reach shared deployments and the documented connector needs a reachable network path. In option 1 the key is contained in a dedicated resource while the shared platform can keep its own keyless and private network configuration.    subgraph O2["Option 2: project in the shared platform resource"]      K2["BYOM API key"]:::key --> R2["Shared Foundry resource
key auth on, reachable endpoint"]:::bad      R2 --> D2A["Copilot Studio project deployments"]:::az      R2 --> D2B["Team A project deployments"]:::bad      R2 --> D2C["Team B project deployments"]:::bad    end    subgraph O1["Option 1: dedicated resource"]      K1["BYOM API key"]:::key --> R1["Copilot Studio Foundry resource
key auth on, reachable endpoint"]:::warn      R1 --> D1A["Copilot Studio deployments only"]:::az      S1["Shared platform resource
Entra ID only, private endpoints"]:::good    end    classDef key fill:#fee2e2,stroke:#b91c1c,color:#000    classDef bad fill:#fee2e2,stroke:#b91c1c,color:#000    classDef warn fill:#fef9c3,stroke:#a16207,color:#000    classDef az fill:#e0f2fe,stroke:#0369a1,color:#000    classDef good fill:#dcfce7,stroke:#15803d,color:#000

A key is a resource-wide pass. In a shared resource, the Copilot Studio key can reach other teams’ deployments and requires key authentication for that resource. A dedicated resource contains the exception.

The resource decision

Option 1, a dedicated resource: the BYOM key can reach that resource’s deployments, so keep only the intended workloads there. Key authentication and the required network exception are contained to that resource. Limit who can list keys, attach and test the applicable guardrails, and use resource-level costs for simpler attribution. A separate subscription gives it a separate quota pool, subject to availability and approval.

Option 2, a project in a shared resource: the key can reach other deployments in the resource, while key authentication and the reachable endpoint affect the shared resource. Review effective key-listing permissions, including resource-scoped Foundry User and Contributor assignments. Guardrails are configured per deployment, and quota is shared by subscription, region, model and deployment type. Cost attribution depends on available dimensions; the shared key doesn’t identify the caller.

For most organisations I’d pick Option 1. Option 2 needs a deliberate security review of key scope and network exposure, even if the shared resource already accepts keys.

Do you need the bridge at all?

Before either option, ask whether a prompt needs your model in the first place. Copilot Studio offers managed prompt models, and Microsoft has announced automatic migration for the prompt models retiring in December.

flowchart TB    accTitle: Deciding whether a Copilot Studio prompt needs bring your own model and where to host it    accDescr: If a managed prompt model does the job, use it with no Foundry. If the prompt needs a specific model that fits bring your own model, host it in a dedicated Foundry resource deployed from the platform template with a time-bound key authentication exemption. If the model doesn't fit, call it as a tool through a connected Foundry agent or an API.    S["A prompt needs a model"]:::cs --> Q1{"Does a Copilot Studio managed
prompt model do the job?"}:::q    Q1 -- "Yes" --> A1["Use it, no Foundry needed"]:::good    Q1 -- "No, it needs a specific model
such as an open-weight one" --> Q2{"Does that model
fit BYOM?"}:::q    Q2 -- "No" --> A2["Call it as a tool
connected Foundry agent or an API"]:::warn    Q2 -- "Yes" --> A3["Dedicated Foundry resource
from the platform template"]:::good    A3 --> A4["Platform policies apply
key auth exemption with an owner and an end date"]:::good    classDef cs fill:#ede9fe,stroke:#6d28d9,color:#000    classDef q fill:#f1f5f9,stroke:#334155,color:#000    classDef good fill:#dcfce7,stroke:#15803d,color:#000    classDef warn fill:#fef9c3,stroke:#a16207,color:#000

Use the bridge only when you need it. BYOM earns its place when a prompt needs a model Copilot Studio doesn’t offer, such as an open-weight or industry model. Managed models can reduce deployment work, although you still need to test migrations. The Foundry agent service uses Entra ID rather than API keys; a connected agent is a different integration, with its own identity and permission configuration.

Who runs the dedicated Foundry

Dedicated doesn’t mean ungoverned. I’d place the resource in the AI landing zone, deploy it from the platform team’s template and apply the relevant management group policies, including the built-in policy for approved model deployments. The documented connection requires key authentication, so a policy that disables local authentication needs a reviewed exception. If the tested network path requires public access, review that exception too. Give each exception an owner and expiry, and track renewal alongside key rotation.

The AI platform team owns the template and its guardrails, using infrastructure as code, approved-model policies and central diagnostics.

The Copilot Studio platform team owns the subscription, deployments and connection. It requests models through the platform’s approval path and manages key rotation and connector data policy.

The security team reviews exceptions and monitors key listing and unusual token use.

Approving and retiring models on two calendars

Copilot Studio and Foundry retire models on different calendars, and BYOM puts you on both.

On the Copilot Studio side, Microsoft runs the calendar. Its standard harness documentation lists 12 November retirement dates for GPT-4.1, GPT-4.1 Mini, GPT-5 Chat, GPT-5 Auto and GPT-5 Reasoning as primary models, with extensions of up to 30 days and GPT Chat Latest as the replacement. FedRAMP tenants, and environments outside the US that restrict cross-region data movement, have an exception for GPT-4.1 and GPT-5, so check your environment’s setting. On the Microsoft Copilot harness, the EU and EFTA exception for GPT-5 Chat ends on 30 November. Affected managed prompt models move automatically by 2 December to GPT-6 Luna, ChatGPT-latest or GPT-6 Reasoning, depending on their tier.

On the Foundry side, you run the calendar. A BYOM prompt points at a named deployment and base model, so swapping the model should be a change you make and test. Plan it before the retirement date: Foundry can upgrade some deployments automatically at retirement, and gpt-4o version 2024-05-13 on Global Standard and Data Zone Standard moves to gpt-5.1, which BYOM doesn’t support. Foundry retired the o-series on 19 November and has GPT-4o and GPT-4.1 on its retirement schedule for January to April 2027.

This month’s headline model shows why the line matters. Claude Fable 5.2 started rolling out in Copilot Studio on 11 November, through Microsoft’s own model list. It appears on the Microsoft Copilot harness list behind the “Anthropic models with data retention” provider setting, which is off by default. A Microsoft 365 admin turns that on, and a Power Platform admin still has to allow the provider’s models for each environment or environment group. Deploying Fable 5.2 in your own Foundry doesn’t change that. BYOM can’t call a Claude deployment directly, because Claude in Foundry uses the Messages API, and Foundry doesn’t apply built-in content filtering to Claude models anyway. “Govern it through our Foundry” simply doesn’t apply to the model everyone’s asking about this month. The decision sits with the Microsoft 365 admin, the Power Platform admin and your model approval board.

flowchart TB    accTitle: Two meters for one Copilot Studio agent    accDescr: An agent conversation creates Copilot Credit usage, tracked in Power Platform and in Agent 365 Cost Management in preview, and BYOM prompt tokens billed as Azure consumption to the Foundry resource's subscription and tracked in Azure Cost Management. Both feed a showback to the business unit.    C["Agent conversation"]:::cs --> CC["Copilot Credits
agent messages and actions"]:::cs    C --> AZ["Azure consumption
BYOM prompt tokens"]:::az    CC --> V["Agent 365 Cost Management, preview
spending policies, limits and alerts"]:::cs    AZ --> CM["Azure Cost Management
budgets on the dedicated resource"]:::az    V --> SB["Showback to the business unit"]:::good    CM --> SB    classDef cs fill:#ede9fe,stroke:#6d28d9,color:#000    classDef az fill:#e0f2fe,stroke:#0369a1,color:#000    classDef good fill:#dcfce7,stroke:#15803d,color:#000

Two meters for one agent. Foundry model processing and eligible Copilot Studio activity are accounted for separately. A dedicated resource makes the Azure half easier to attribute; check the current licensing rules and your actual usage for the Copilot Studio half.

What Ignite changed

The Ignite announcements also cover governance and operational capabilities relevant to this design:

  • Agent 365 Cost Management (preview) covers usage-based services including Copilot Studio, with spending policies, limits, alerts and chargeback.
  • Agent 365 usage and activity insights are generally available, without an Agent 365 licence, for agents built on Microsoft platforms.
  • Dynamic Agent Risk (preview) sits alongside the agent registry, visible across the Microsoft 365 admin center, Defender, Entra, Intune and Purview.
  • Conditional Access policy plans (preview) arrive in Entra to simplify policy management at scale.
  • Model router support in AI Gateway lands on the Foundry side.

Nine go-live checks

  1. The agent stays on the standard harness. Any move to the Microsoft Copilot harness has a plan for the prompt first, because that harness has no prompt tool.
  2. The model fits. It serves chat completions, it isn’t GPT-5 or later, and its Foundry retirement date sits beyond your next review, with the replacement planned before Foundry can upgrade the deployment for you.
  3. The resource is dedicated. Its key opens only Copilot Studio’s deployments, and its policy exemptions have an owner and an end date.
  4. Roles are tight and keys rotate. Only the people who manage the connection can list keys. Regenerate the key the connection isn’t using, move the connection to it, then regenerate the other one.
  5. Instant access is reviewed. Model router’s Auto option (preview) is set per resource. Microsoft’s router reference says an empty properties.instant.modelAllowList turns off instant access, including Auto. Check the effect on other instant-access models and test this preview setting; deployed models and other access paths still need governance.
  6. Guardrails are assigned and tested. The prompt’s own moderation setting doesn’t apply to Foundry models. Check the controls supported by the selected model and API rather than assuming uniform coverage. For supported text calls, a request can override the deployment guardrail using x-policy-id; Microsoft’s guardrail guidance notes that this override isn’t available for image input. Review the policies available in the resource.
  7. The connector is allowed only where it should be. The data policy allows “Azure AI Foundry” in the environments that host approved BYOM prompts and blocks it elsewhere, and the connection holding the key is shared only with the makers who own those prompts.
  8. The network path is a decision. Test whether the documented connector can reach the endpoint with your network rules and Power Platform’s current outbound IP ranges. An API Management URL or private path is a lab test, not a design assumption, because the connector is documented for Foundry endpoints.
  9. Both meters and both logs are wired. Azure budgets and diagnostic logs on the Foundry resource, and Copilot Credit tracking and Purview audit on the Copilot Studio side.

My take

I like BYOM for what it is: a way to put a specific model, such as an open-weight or industry model, behind a single prompt, with applicable platform controls on that call. What it isn’t is a way to govern the whole Copilot Studio agent. Its orchestration, identity and sharing still need the controls in Microsoft’s governance map.

Where I push back is the reflex to drop Copilot Studio into a project on the shared platform because it looks tidy on a diagram. The documented BYOM connector needs a key, and a key turns a project boundary into a resource-wide pass. I’d rather run a dedicated Foundry resource with a reviewed key and network exception than reopen the whole platform. It’s the keyless argument from earlier this month applied the other way round: when you can’t remove an exception, contain it.

Two caveats. First, the bridge is narrow and it’s narrowing: no GPT-5 or later, no Claude, no Entra ID, and the GPT-4.1 and GPT-4o models that fit retire in 2027, while new models such as Fable 5.2 arrive on a harness with no prompt tool. Second, the connector is documented for Foundry endpoints only, so an AI gateway in this path is something to prove in a lab before you promise it to anyone.

If I were setting this up today, I’d keep BYOM for the few prompts that genuinely need a model of our own, govern everything else where Copilot Studio governs it, and look again after the next round of harness and model updates.

Key takeaways

  • Copilot Studio can call Foundry models from a BYOM prompt on the standard harness. Its primary orchestration model is selected separately.
  • BYOM gives the platform team control of the call: model version, region, guardrails, quota, logs and token cost.
  • Agent governance and evidence span Power Platform, Microsoft 365, Entra, Purview and Defender. Prompt data sent to Foundry also reaches the deployment.
  • The connection is chat completions with an API key: no GPT-5 or later, no Claude and no Entra ID.
  • Foundry keys are resource-wide, so a project in a shared resource exposes every deployment. Use a dedicated resource with time-bound policy exemptions.
  • Plan for two calendars and two meters: check Copilot Studio model migrations, manage Foundry deployments, and account for Azure processing and eligible Copilot Credit activity separately.

References

  • Microsoft Learn, Bring your own model for your prompts
  • Microsoft Learn, Azure AI Foundry Inference connector reference
  • Microsoft Learn, Select a primary AI model for your agent
  • Microsoft Learn, Model availability in Copilot Studio (Microsoft Copilot)
  • Microsoft Learn, About agents powered by the Microsoft Copilot harness
  • Microsoft Learn, Connect to a Microsoft Foundry agent (preview)
  • Microsoft Learn, Prompt model availability by region and updates
  • Microsoft Learn, Licensing and Copilot Credits
  • Microsoft Learn, Microsoft Azure VNet support overview
  • Microsoft Copilot Studio Blog, Where do I govern my Copilot Studio agents?, 11 November 2026
  • Microsoft Learn, Authentication and authorization in Microsoft Foundry
  • Microsoft Learn, How to configure guardrails and controls in Microsoft Foundry
  • Microsoft Learn, Model router API reference
  • Microsoft Learn, Model retirement schedule
  • Microsoft Learn, Claude models in Microsoft Foundry
  • Microsoft Copilot Blog, Available today: Anthropic Claude Fable 5.2 in Microsoft Copilot, 11 November 2026
  • Microsoft, Microsoft Ignite 2026 Book of News, 17 to 20 November 2026

Related posts

  • AI Agents Exploit Leaked Keys in Minutes: Go Keyless on Azure: why key authentication should be off by default, and how to prove it’s off.

  • Governance for AI Agents (Part 1): The Gap, the OWASP Agentic Top 10, and Where AGT Fits: identity, policy and audit for agents beyond a single model call.

entry.summary: Learn how Copilot Studio bring your own model connects to Microsoft Foundry, what it governs, and why resource isolation matters for API keys.
entry.title: Copilot Studio Bring Your Own Model: Microsoft Foundry Governance and Security

entry.content:
Update (2026-11-23): Claude and Codex can now be explicitly allowed

VS Code 1.147 (18 November 2026) lets admins allow the Claude and Codex harnesses by listing them in vscode.allowedHarnesses, set through file-based or MDM managed settings. Server-managed settings don't support it yet.

Sessions in those harnesses run without Copilot's managed permission, sandbox, MCP and plugin controls. They should be treated as a separate risk boundary, not as Copilot sessions with a different provider model.

TL;DR

In one week VS Code fixed ten security advisories, eight of them involving MCP servers, agent tools or the agent host, and froze the Local harness for removal in February 2027. Visual Studio moved Copilot Chat onto the Copilot harness, Copilot CLI tied its built-in MCP server to policy, and Git fixed a clone bug that an agent can trigger just by following Git’s own advice.

Treat the editor fleet like any other agent runtime. Patch to a version floor, use the Copilot harness by default because it enforces managed sandbox and permission policy, police MCP, permissions and customisations through Copilot’s managed settings, and prove it with diagnostics, telemetry and a test you expect to fail. If you allow Claude or Codex, manage their separate controls explicitly.

In a hurry? Jump to the version floor, the managed baseline or how to prove it, then come back for the why.

Three weeks ago, in Part 2 of my GitHub Copilot agents guide, I described a Copilot session as three choices: a harness, where it runs and a model. For an organisation relying on Copilot’s managed runtime controls, the choice of harness matters.

The editor used to be the place you typed code. Now it hosts an agent that starts MCP servers, calls tools, runs terminal commands and clones repositories on your behalf. That makes your editor fleet an agent runtime, and an agent runtime needs what any other runtime needs: a patch level, a supported configuration and a policy you can prove. This post is the baseline I’d hand a platform team rolling coding agents out to hundreds of developers.

The guidance below draws on release notes, advisories and docs available on 20 November 2026.

One week, four release trains

Here’s what landed between 10 and 18 November.

flowchart TB    accTitle: Coding agent releases between 10 and 18 November 2026    accDescr: On 10 November VS Code 1.145.3 fixed ten advisories, Git 2.56.1 fixed six CVEs and Visual Studio 18.12 moved Copilot Chat onto the Copilot harness. On 11 November VS Code 1.146 froze the Local harness. On 12 and 13 November Copilot CLI 1.0.110 to 1.0.112 tied the built-in MCP server to policy and made /compact and sub-agents respect the session credit limit. On 17 and 18 November VS Code 1.147, Visual Studio 18.12.1 and Copilot CLI 1.0.114 followed.    subgraph D10["10 November"]      A1["VS Code 1.145.3
ten security advisories"]:::sec      A2["Git 2.56.1
six CVEs, code execution on clone"]:::sec      A3["Visual Studio 18.12
Copilot Chat on the Copilot harness"]:::rel    end    subgraph D11["11 November"]      B1["VS Code 1.146
Local harness frozen, removal February 2027"]:::rel    end    subgraph D13["12 to 13 November"]      C1["Copilot CLI 1.0.110 to 1.0.112
MCP follows policy, credit limits hold"]:::rel    end    subgraph D18["17 to 18 November"]      E1["VS Code 1.147
allowed harnesses, regex shell rules"]:::rel      E2["Visual Studio 18.12.1
Copilot CLI 1.0.114"]:::rel    end    A3 --> B1 --> C1 --> E1    classDef sec fill:#fee2e2,stroke:#b91c1c,color:#000    classDef rel fill:#e0f2fe,stroke:#0369a1,color:#000

Four release trains, one direction. Security fixes are in red. Most of the rest moved more work onto the Copilot harness or tied the agent more tightly to policy.

Ten advisories in one patch

VS Code 1.145.3 shipped fixes for ten GitHub security advisories, all published on 10 November. Four of them sit squarely in the agent stack:

The MCP installation links advisory, CVE-2026-114171, covers crafted vscode:mcp/install links. An input definition could run a command once the user approved the install. Its CVE base score is 8.8.

The MCP elicitation notifications advisory, CVE-2026-120779, covers the fallback notification for MCP elicitation. Server-controlled text could become a clickable VS Code command link; exploitation required a user to click it. Its base score is 9.6.

The legacy SSE endpoints advisory, CVE-2026-119983, covers the MCP client’s legacy SSE transport. A server could provide an endpoint that directed later requests somewhere unintended. Its base score is 8.8.

The agent-originated local commands advisory, CVE-2026-120782, covers the Agent Host. Local-command syntax in an agent’s message could run without the expected terminal approval. Its base score is 7.8.

Four more involve agents indirectly.
