Three let a workspace start an MCP server without a trust prompt: a network workspace file treated as trusted, a __proto__ key in .vscode/mcp.json or settings.json, and a value that switched Workspace Trust off. The fourth let the agent-driven browser upload local files without path approval. The last two fixes cover the serve-web server and JavaScript debugger auto-attach.

A note on scores: the figures above are Microsoft’s base scores from the CVE records. GitHub’s advisory pages show lower temporal scores for the same issues, so your scanner may report 8.3 where the CVE record says 9.6.

flowchart TB    accTitle: Where the November VS Code advisories hit the agent stack    accDescr: A developer works in VS Code. VS Code's MCP client and the Copilot harness in the Agent Host talk to MCP servers, the Agent Host also drives the terminal and the integrated browser, and workspace configuration decides what starts. Fixes landed for MCP install links, elicitation notifications and legacy SSE endpoints, agent-originated local commands, an agent-driven browser upload, and three workspace trust bypasses that started MCP servers.    DEV["Developer"]:::user --> VS["VS Code"]:::host    VS --> AH["Agent Host
Copilot harness"]:::host    VS --> WS["Workspace configuration
mcp.json and settings.json"]:::comp    AH --> MCP["MCP servers"]:::comp    VS --> MCP    AH --> TERM["Terminal"]:::comp    AH --> BR["Integrated browser"]:::comp    MCP --- F1["Install links, elicitation
notifications, legacy SSE"]:::fix    TERM --- F2["Agent-originated
local commands"]:::fix    BR --- F3["Upload without
path approval"]:::fix    WS --- F4["Three trust bypasses
that started MCP servers"]:::fix    classDef user fill:#f1f5f9,stroke:#334155,color:#000    classDef host fill:#cce5ff,stroke:#0f172a,color:#000    classDef comp fill:#e0f2fe,stroke:#0369a1,color:#000    classDef fix fill:#fee2e2,stroke:#b91c1c,color:#000

The attack surface is the agent’s toolbelt. Eight of the ten fixes sit where the agent meets the outside world: MCP servers, the terminal, the browser and the workspace files that decide what starts.

The agent-originated command bug is the one I’d show a platform team. It lived in the Agent Host, the process that runs Copilot harness sessions, so it shows two things at once: approval only works when the runtime knows who’s asking, and the harness you pin still needs patching.

sequenceDiagram    accTitle: How an agent-originated local command could skip terminal approval before VS Code 1.145.3    accDescr: Untrusted repository instructions shape the agent's next message. Before the fix, local-command syntax in that message was treated as if the developer had typed it and ran without terminal approval. From 1.145.3 the Agent Host tracks where each message came from and handles local commands only when the developer typed them.    autonumber    participant R as Untrusted repo instructions    participant A as Agent    participant H as Agent Host    participant T as Terminal    Note over A,H: Precondition: the user granted the related session tool operation    R->>A: Instructions shape the agent's next message    A->>H: Message contains local-command syntax    alt Before 1.145.3      H->>T: Treated as typed by the developer, runs without approval    else 1.145.3 and later      H->>H: Tracks where the message came from      H-->>A: Agent text isn't handled as a local command    end

Approval only works if the runtime knows who’s asking. The fix tracks where each message came from. The advisory’s own workaround reads like the rest of this post: use the Copilot harness instead of the Local harness, keep terminal approvals on, and don’t grant session-wide permissions in repositories with untrusted instructions.

Pin: the harness is now the policy boundary

The Copilot harness has been the default for new sessions since VS Code 1.143. It’s built on the Copilot SDK and runs in the Agent Host, the process that runs Copilot sessions. VS Code 1.146 deprecated the Local harness: it’s functionally frozen and will be removed in February 2027, along with the vscode.temporaryDefaultToLocalHarness setting.

The reason matters more than the date. The 1.146 release notes say the Copilot harness “enforces managed sandbox and permission policies that the Local harness doesn’t”. The third-party harnesses are no better from a policy point of view: VS Code 1.147 notes that Claude and Codex sessions “run without Copilot’s managed permission, sandbox, MCP, and plugin controls”. Under Copilot managed settings they’re off unless you permit them with vscode.allowedHarnesses, which for now works only in file-based or MDM-managed settings. It doesn’t override temporaryAllowLocalHarness: false, so the baseline below keeps Claude and Codex off for everyone.

flowchart TB    accTitle: Which VS Code harnesses enforce your managed policy    accDescr: Under Copilot managed settings, a new session can use the Copilot harness, which enforces managed sandbox, permission, MCP and plugin controls. The Local harness is frozen and will be removed in February 2027. Claude and Codex harnesses are off unless allowedHarnesses permits them and temporaryAllowLocalHarness isn't false, and then they run without Copilot's controls.    S["New agent session
under managed settings"]:::q    S --> C["Copilot harness
Agent Host on the Copilot SDK"]:::good    S --> L["Local harness
extension host"]:::bad    S --> X["Claude or Codex harness"]:::warn    C --> C1["Enforces managed sandbox,
permissions, MCP and plugins"]:::good    L --> L1["Frozen since 1.146
removed February 2027"]:::bad    X --> X1["Off unless allowedHarnesses permits it
and temporaryAllowLocalHarness isn't false
then runs without Copilot's controls"]:::warn    classDef q fill:#f1f5f9,stroke:#334155,color:#000    classDef good fill:#dcfce7,stroke:#15803d,color:#000    classDef bad fill:#fee2e2,stroke:#b91c1c,color:#000    classDef warn fill:#fef9c3,stroke:#a16207,color:#000

Policy only binds where the harness enforces it. A permission rule that the Local harness ignores isn’t a control. Use the Copilot harness as the managed baseline, then treat any allowed provider harness as a separate boundary.

VS Code’s migration guide gives the managed settings that require it:

By default, temporaryAllowLocalHarness: false prohibits the Local, Claude and Codex harnesses. VS Code 1.147 can override the Claude and Codex part when file-based or MDM managed settings include vscode.allowedHarnesses; server-managed settings don’t support that exception yet. Requiring the Copilot harness doesn’t turn on sandboxing or add permission rules. That’s the job of the baseline further down. Since 1.143, a managed sandbox.enabled: true or a non-empty permissions.deny also requires the Copilot harness unless the temporary Local default applies.

One runtime, several clients

The Copilot SDK isn’t just VS Code’s engine. VS Code’s docs describe it as the shared agent runtime behind VS Code, Copilot CLI and the Copilot app, and Visual Studio 18.12 joined them: “Through the SDK, Copilot in Visual Studio now runs on the Microsoft Copilot harness.” The new Visual Studio chat reads AGENTS.md at the solution root, uses your organisation’s Copilot custom instructions, lets you switch individual MCP tools on and off, and keeps a separate Copilot trusted-paths list that organisations can manage through policy. That new chat is the default for eligible accounts, but it respects an account with editor preview features turned off, and developers can switch back under Tools > Options > GitHub > Copilot > Copilot Chat.

The runtime is shared. The policy channels aren’t.

flowchart TB    accTitle: Where Copilot policy comes from for each client    accDescr: GitHub enterprise and organisation policies apply to every Copilot client. Copilot managed settings, delivered from the server, MDM or a file, apply to Copilot CLI, VS Code and the Copilot app. VS Code device policies come from Group Policy, configuration profiles or a Linux policy file. Visual Studio uses its own Group Policy and MCP settings.    GH["GitHub enterprise and organisation policy
MCP servers in Copilot, Copilot CLI,
Copilot in the cloud, models, budgets"]:::gh    MS["Copilot managed settings
server, MDM or file"]:::ms    DP["VS Code device policies
ADMX, mobileconfig, policy.json"]:::dp    VP["Visual Studio Group Policy
and its own MCP settings"]:::dp    CLI["Copilot CLI"]:::client    VSC["VS Code"]:::client    APP["Copilot app"]:::client    VS["Visual Studio 2026"]:::client    GH --> CLI    GH --> VSC    GH --> APP    GH --> VS    MS --> CLI    MS --> VSC    MS --> APP    DP --> VSC    VP --> VS    classDef gh fill:#cce5ff,stroke:#0f172a,color:#000    classDef ms fill:#ede9fe,stroke:#6d28d9,color:#000    classDef dp fill:#fef9c3,stroke:#a16207,color:#000    classDef client fill:#e0f2fe,stroke:#0369a1,color:#000

Same runtime, different levers. Copilot’s managed settings reach Copilot CLI, VS Code, the Copilot app and, for some keys, Copilot in the cloud and JetBrains IDEs. Visual Studio isn’t on that list, so it needs its own Group Policy baseline alongside the GitHub policies that apply everywhere.

One more thing about levers: device policies and managed settings aren’t interchangeable. VS Code’s enterprise guidance warns that a delivered value “does not establish that every harness enforces it in the same way”, and where both set the same control, the enterprise-managed setting wins. I write the rules in Copilot’s managed settings and keep VS Code device policies for editor-only controls such as UpdateMode and ChatApprovedAccountOrganizations, rather than setting the same control in both places.

Patch: set a version floor

Here’s the floor I’d set today:

  • VS Code: 1.145.3 or later fixes ten advisories, eight of them agent-related. Version 1.147.0 is the current stable.
  • Copilot CLI: 1.0.112 or later removes the built-in GitHub MCP server when policy turns MCP off, and sub-agents respect the session credit limit. Version 1.0.114 is current.
  • Visual Studio 2026: 18.12.1, or 18.11.4 if you’re staying on 18.11. The release notes list the Git for Windows fixes under 18.11.4, so check that MSRC lists your 18.12 build for CVE-2026-111760. Version 18.12 moves Copilot Chat onto the Copilot harness.
  • GitHub Copilot for JetBrains: check the applicable MSRC update guidance for CVE-2026-83953, a local information disclosure, and confirm the fixed version for your installation.
  • Git, everywhere: 2.56.1 or the patched release for your series fixes code execution when cloning a malicious repository.

Three things make the floor stick:

  • Keep updates flowing. VS Code “releases weekly updates with new features, bug fixes, and security patches”, so a floor beats a pin. If you’ve set UpdateMode to manual or none to control rollout, you own the patch cadence, including the next Tuesday fix.
  • Set a managed minimum version. VS Code’s AI settings guide describes requiring a minimum VS Code version before AI features are available, which keeps Copilot off until the client is updated. Adding sandbox to Copilot’s managed settings also blocks connections from clients older than Copilot CLI 1.0.93, VS Code 1.141.0 and the Copilot app 1.1.26, but that’s well below this floor, so treat it as a backstop for the oldest clients.
  • Refuse stale policy. forceRemoteSettingsRefresh: true makes clients fetch server-managed settings at startup. In VS Code, Copilot features are blocked until that refresh succeeds. Deliver it by MDM or file so it applies from a device’s first start.

Police: a managed baseline

mindmap  root((Managed baseline))    Versions      VS Code 1.145.3 or later      Copilot CLI 1.0.112 or later      Git 2.56.1 or the patched series    Harness      Copilot harness by default      Local off      Claude and Codex only if explicitly allowed    MCP      Allowlist by URL or command      Denylist for known bad servers    Permissions      Bypass mode disabled      Deny and ask rules for risky operations    Sandbox and secrets      Sandbox required with no bypass      Local MCP servers inside the sandbox      Masked environment variables    Customisations      Plugin-only customisation      Approved marketplaces only    Evidence      OpenTelemetry export      Policy Diagnostics      Usage metrics and audit log

The baseline on one page. Most of it lives in one managed settings file. The rest is GitHub policy, Visual Studio’s Group Policy, a developer masking list and your patching process.

Here’s a starting managed-settings.json, built from the keys in GitHub’s reference plus the vscode harness keys and strictPluginOnlyCustomization from VS Code’s docs. Serve it from copilot/managed-settings.json in your .github-private repository. Server-managed settings only reach users who get their Copilot licence from your enterprise; device delivery applies regardless of who licensed them. Use MDM or file delivery where needed, including forceRemoteSettingsRefresh before first sign-in, and review precedence and the most-restrictive composition rules before combining sources. Native MDM uses individual string values, not the JSON file. Treat these rules as examples and replace them with your own:

To allow Claude or Codex with VS Code 1.147, add them to vscode.allowedHarnesses in file-based or MDM managed settings. Do not put that exception in server-managed settings, which don’t support the key yet. Permitting either harness only lifts the restriction. Their sessions still run without Copilot’s managed permission, sandbox, MCP and plugin controls.

What each block does, and the traps I’d watch for:

  • MCP. The “MCP servers in Copilot” policy decides whether MCP servers run at all, and it’s off by default. When you turn it on, make allowedMcpServers the main control rather than “Registry only”: GitHub’s docs say registry enforcement matches only names or IDs, which users can bypass by editing configuration files. Match by serverUrl or serverCommand, because users choose server names, and list the URLs of any Copilot connectors you use, because the allowlist blocks those too. The sample permits remote servers only; add an exact, reviewed command and arguments for each approved local server. Visual Studio is the exception: managed settings don’t reach it, but registry enforcement does from 18.4, so decide deliberately whether to keep “Registry only” for Visual Studio users. Two gaps to know: GitHub’s documentation says the allowlist doesn’t cover MCP servers defined in repository custom agent profiles; use the cloud agent firewall to restrict their required domains and verify other execution environments separately. The built-in GitHub MCP server is exempt from the allowlist and denylist, although Copilot CLI 1.0.112 removes it when organisation policy turns MCP off.
  • Install links. The 1.145.3 patch fixes the vscode:mcp/install bug. A link opens the server details editor so the user can review the configuration before installing. On supported clients, an allowlist also limits which non-default servers can be installed or run.
  • Permissions. disableBypassPermissionsMode: "disable" neuters --yolo and --allow-all in Copilot CLI and turns off chat.tools.global.autoApprove in VS Code so it can’t be re-enabled. It doesn’t block assisted permissions, so decide separately whether to set permissions.disableAssistedPermissionsMode. Rules follow deny, then ask, then allow, and once any managed rule exists, an unmatched operation asks for approval. In VS Code these granular rules apply to Agent Host sessions, which is one more reason to pin the harness. VS Code 1.147 and Copilot CLI 1.0.111 also accept regular expressions in shell rules.
  • Sandbox. failIfUnavailable with enabled makes the sandbox mandatory: if Copilot can’t enforce it, model and tool execution stop instead of running unsandboxed. allowBypass: false stops users opting out mid-session, and sandboxMcpServers puts local MCP servers inside it too. Turning the sandbox on doesn’t block outbound network access by default, so add sandbox.userPolicy.network restrictions such as allowOutbound: false where a team can live with them. On Windows, host rules and environment variable masking need local network access, so test before you set allowLocalNetwork: false.
  • Masked environment variables. This one is a developer setting, not a managed key. In VS Code 1.146, chat.agent.sandbox.credentials.envVars takes variable names, never values, and tools see placeholders; the real values are restored only in HTTPS requests to the hosts you list in injectHosts. Copilot CLI has the same idea under /sandbox. Masking only works while the sandbox is on, so the admin lever is forcing the sandbox, and the developer lever is a masking list you ship in your standard setup.
  • Customisations. strictPluginOnlyCustomization blocks standalone skills, custom agents, hooks, MCP servers and, since 1.146, canvas extensions from user and project sources, so they arrive only through plugins or managed settings. Plugin-only isn’t a marketplace allowlist, so pair it with strictKnownMarketplaces, which also switches off the built-in marketplaces. Test both against your repositories’ skills, agents, hooks, MCP configuration and instruction files before you enforce them.

Git is part of the agent runtime

Agents clone repositories, run Git commands and read Git’s error messages. On 10 November Git released 2.56.1, with backports down to 2.50.2, fixing six vulnerabilities. The one that matters most here, CVE-2026-111760, allows code execution when cloning a malicious repository. For a recursive clone, the attacker’s code can run during the clone. For a non-recursive clone, Git can report an error and suggest running git status, and following that advice runs the attacker’s code.

That’s exactly the kind of helpful hint a coding agent follows without a second thought.

flowchart TB    accTitle: Where Git runs in a coding agent fleet    accDescr: Git needs version 2.56.1 or the patched release for its series on developer laptops, in apps that bundle Git such as Visual Studio, GitHub Desktop and the Copilot app, in dev container and agent sandbox images, on self-hosted runners, and on GitHub-hosted runners, where GitHub started shipping patched images on 11 November.    G["Git 2.56.1 or the patched
release for your series"]:::good    G --> L["Developer laptops"]:::yours    G --> V["Apps that bundle Git
Visual Studio, GitHub Desktop, Copilot app"]:::yours    G --> D["Your dev container
and agent sandbox images"]:::yours    G --> S["Self-hosted runners"]:::yours    G --> H["GitHub-hosted runners
patched images from 11 November"]:::theirs    classDef good fill:#dcfce7,stroke:#15803d,color:#000    classDef yours fill:#fef9c3,stroke:#a16207,color:#000    classDef theirs fill:#e0f2fe,stroke:#0369a1,color:#000

Every place an agent can clone needs the fix. GitHub patched its own services and started shipping hosted runner images with Git 2.56.1 on 11 November. Laptops, bundled copies, custom images and self-hosted runners are yours, shown in yellow.

Prove the policy is working

A policy file proves nothing on its own. I ask three questions: did the policy arrive, does it bite, and does it cover the whole fleet?

flowchart TB    accTitle: Three layers of evidence that a coding agent policy works    accDescr: First prove delivery on a device with Policy Diagnostics and the sandbox policy view. Then prove enforcement with a canary that tries an approved action and a harmless blocked one. Then prove fleet coverage with usage metrics versions, the audit log and OpenTelemetry metrics. Drift or gaps feed back into the policy.    P["Managed settings
and policies"]:::ms    P --> E1["Delivered?
Developer: Policy Diagnostics
and /sandbox policy"]:::ev    E1 --> E2["Enforced?
a canary tries one approved action
and one harmless blocked one"]:::ev    E2 --> E3["Covered?
usage metrics versions,
audit log, OpenTelemetry"]:::ev    E3 -- "drift or gaps" --> P    classDef ms fill:#cce5ff,stroke:#0f172a,color:#000    classDef ev fill:#dcfce7,stroke:#15803d,color:#000

A delivered setting isn’t an enforced one. VS Code’s policy guide says the diagnostics report “does not prove that a restriction applies to every workflow or agent harness”. Every control gets a test you expect to fail.

  • Delivered. On a test device, run Developer: Policy Diagnostics in VS Code. It shows the applied and non-applied policy tables and the account policy gate, and Developer: Sync Account Policy forces a refresh. VS Code’s guidance pairs it with /sandbox policy in a Copilot session.
  • Enforced. Keep a canary script: open an install link for an unlisted MCP server, ask the agent to read a dummy file covered by a canary deny rule such as Read(~/copilot-canary/), start Copilot CLI with --yolo (1.0.110 and later warn when the flag is ignored), and try to start a Local harness session or a Claude or Codex session that policy should block. Never test with the real rm -rf rule. Each one should fail, every time, and the approved workflow next to it should work.
  • Covered. The Copilot usage metrics API reports last_known_ide_version, last_known_plugin_version and the last known CLI version per user, which is how you find laptops below the floor. Data arrives within two full UTC days. The dashboards don’t include Copilot CLI usage, so use the API.
  • Changed. The audit log records policy changes as copilot.cfb_enterprise_settings_changed and copilot.cfb_org_settings_changed, but those events don’t say which setting changed. Server-managed settings live in copilot/managed-settings.json in your .github-private repository, so require pull request review on that file and the commit history gives you the diff the audit log doesn’t. The log keeps 180 days, so stream it to your SIEM.
  • Observed. The managed telemetry block sends OpenTelemetry to your collector. capture.identity attributes activity to a user and machine; review all telemetry and content-capture settings separately before deploying it. Metrics such as github.copilot.tool.call.count, github.copilot.mcp.server.connection.count and github.copilot.sandbox.operation.count show trends, but GitHub describes sandbox metrics as “not a complete audit log”.
  • Spent.** User-level budgets always hard stop. Cost centre, organisation and enterprise budgets only block if “Stop usage when budget limit is reached” is ticked, and it’s off by default. Copilot CLI’s --max-ai-credits is a soft, user-set session limit, which /compact (1.0.110) and sub-agents (1.0.112) now respect.

A rollout you can run this month

flowchart TB    accTitle: Rollout plan for the coding agent baseline    accDescr: This week, patch VS Code, Copilot CLI, Visual Studio, the JetBrains plugin and Git everywhere. Over the next two weeks, pilot the managed settings with a canary group and run the proof tests. By the end of January, require the Copilot harness for everyone, ahead of the Local harness removal in February 2027. Every week after that, measure version drift, blocked actions and spend.    W1["This week · Patch
VS Code, Copilot CLI, Visual Studio,
JetBrains plugin and Git everywhere"]:::step    W2["Next two weeks · Pilot
managed settings for a canary group
and run the proof tests"]:::step    W3["By the end of January · Enforce
Copilot harness for everyone,
Local, Claude and Codex off"]:::step    W4["Every week · Measure
version drift, blocked actions and spend"]:::step    W1 --> W2 --> W3 --> W4    classDef step fill:#e0f2fe,stroke:#0369a1,color:#000

Patch first, then policy. Patching is urgent and low risk. Policy is neither: pilot it with a canary group so the first person to hit a deny rule is on your team, not a developer with a release due. Enforce the harness well before February, so the Local harness removal is a non-event.

Nine checks before you call it done

  1. Versions. Every VS Code client is on 1.145.3 or later, Copilot CLI on 1.0.112 or later, and Git on 2.56.1 or the patched release for its series, including images and runners.
  2. Harness. Sessions run on the Copilot harness, and Local, Claude and Codex are off. If a team needs Claude or Codex, treat it as a separate, documented device configuration and test what it allows, because it can’t sit alongside temporaryAllowLocalHarness: false.
  3. MCP. Servers run from an allowlist matched by URL or command, subject to the built-in server and custom agent profile exceptions. Cloud agent firewall rules restrict the required domains for those profiles.
  4. Permissions. Bypass mode is disabled, and risky operations sit in deny or ask rules.
  5. Sandbox. It’s required, it can’t be bypassed, and local MCP servers run inside it.
  6. Secrets. Developers have a standard masking list for the environment variables that hold credentials.
  7. Customisations. Plugin-only customisation and the marketplace allowlist have been tested against your repositories’ skills, agents, hooks, MCP configuration and instruction files before enforcement.
  8. Proof. A canary shows each control blocks what it should, and the usage metrics API helps identify reported clients below the floor. Last-known versions and delayed reports aren’t a complete device inventory.
  9. Visual Studio. It has its own Group Policy baseline, because GitHub doesn’t list Visual Studio as a managed settings client, and you know which developers are on the new Copilot chat.

My take

Most enterprise conversations about coding agents start with the model. I’d start with the harness. The model decides how good the suggestions are; the harness decides whether any of your policy applies. Standardise the harness before you standardise the model.

I’d also stop thinking about version pins. With weekly releases and Patch Tuesday fixes, a pin is a liability within a month. Set a floor, let updates flow above it, and use the managed minimum version and the usage metrics API to catch anything that falls behind. The Copilot harness isn’t immune either: in October, VS Code 1.141.1 fixed a flaw where it could auto-approve edits to hook and agent-definition files, and this month’s agent-originated command bug lived in the Agent Host that runs it. Pinning the harness only works alongside patching.

A few caveats. The policy surface is genuinely confusing: GitHub policies, Copilot managed settings, VS Code device policies and Visual Studio’s Group Policy overlap, and a value that reaches a device isn’t proof that every harness enforces it. Some controls, such as masking environment variables, are still developer settings. The MCP allowlist has a gap for custom agent profiles in cloud sessions. And the baseline will drift, so I’d put a monthly review in the calendar rather than treat this as a one-off.

If I had one week, I’d patch everything on Monday, turn on the managed settings for a canary group on Wednesday, and spend Friday breaking them.

Key Takeaways

  • VS Code 1.145.3 fixed ten advisories, eight of them involving MCP servers, agent tools or the agent host. Make 1.145.3 the floor, with Copilot CLI 1.0.112 and Git 2.56.1 alongside it.
  • The Copilot harness is the policy boundary. The Local harness is frozen until its removal in February 2027, and Claude and Codex sessions run without Copilot’s managed controls.
  • Put the baseline in Copilot’s managed settings: harness, MCP allowlist by URL or command, permissions, mandatory sandbox, plugin-only customisation and telemetry.
  • Visual Studio now defaults to the same runtime but sits outside managed settings, so give it its own Group Policy baseline and check which chat experience your developers actually use.
  • Patch Git wherever agents clone: a non-recursive clone plus a helpful git status hint was enough to run an attacker’s code.
  • Prove it three ways: Policy Diagnostics for delivery, a canary for enforcement, and the usage metrics API, audit log and OpenTelemetry for coverage.

References

  • Visual Studio Code, release notes for 1.145, 1.146 and 1.147, and security advisories.
  • Visual Studio Code, Move from the Local to the Copilot harness and manage AI settings in enterprise environments.
  • Visual Studio Code, sandbox Copilot agent sessions and policy diagnostics.
  • GitHub Docs, enterprise managed settings and deployment methods and precedence.
  • GitHub Docs, configure an MCP server allowlist and MCP private registry enforcement.
  • GitHub Docs, usage metrics, audit logs and OpenTelemetry reference.
  • GitHub Docs, budgets for usage-based billing.
  • GitHub, Copilot CLI releases.
  • Microsoft Security Response Center, CVE-2026-83953; GitHub Advisory Database, GHSA-5pr7-c8pm-c229.
  • Microsoft Learn, Visual Studio 2026 release notes and Copilot in Visual Studio upgrade.
  • GitHub Blog, Git security vulnerabilities announced and runner image releases.

Related posts

  • GitHub Copilot CLI vs Local vs Cloud: Agents Explained (2026): the harness, environment and model framing this post builds on.
  • AGENTS.md vs Copilot Instructions vs Cursor Rules vs CLAUDE.md: Which AI Context File to Use, and When (2026): the instruction files to test before you enforce plugin-only customisation.
  • AI Agents Exploit Leaked Keys in Minutes: Go Keyless on Azure: keeping credentials out of agent sessions in the first place.
  • Governance for AI Agents (Part 1): The Gap, the OWASP Agentic Top 10, and Where AGT Fits: policy in front of every tool call, beyond the editor.

Image Credits

  • Cover image generated by Copilot
entry.summary: Secure GitHub Copilot coding agents with a practical baseline for VS Code, MCP, sandbox policies and Git, following November 2026 security updates.
entry.title: GitHub Copilot Harness Security: Patch, Pin and Govern Your Coding Agents

entry.content:
TL;DR

A recent threat intelligence report describes an AI agent moving from searching GitHub for application secrets to exfiltrating Azure Key Vault data in five minutes. That’s one observed case, not a typical benchmark.

Use managed identities and federation instead of stored credentials, then disable key authentication once callers have migrated. Tokens can still be stolen, so least privilege, monitoring and incident response remain essential.

I spend a lot of my time in the layer between AI agents and the things they call. A model key in an app setting can look like a harmless shortcut during a proof of concept, but the gap between a leak and the response is getting harder to defend.

In a hurry? Jump to the keyless playbook or the nine checks before release, then come back for the threat and the tradeoffs. The product guidance below was checked on 15 November 2026.

What the threat intelligence report found

On 5 November, Microsoft Threat Intelligence reported that threat actors were using agentic tooling to search public GitHub repositories for exposed credentials, including application secrets and AI inference API keys. The agents analysed the results and carried out follow-on actions with little human intervention.

A stolen model key can fund someone else’s inference, while an exposed application secret can open whatever its identity is permitted to reach.

Microsoft observed large volumes of targeted searches from August 2026. In subsequent activity from 28 October, the agents signed in as service principals across multiple tenants, including customers of a vendor whose multitenant application credential was compromised at the source. They enumerated resources and targeted operations that return credentials, including storage account keys, application settings, connection strings and AI connections.

The agents also searched Azure DevOps, accessed Key Vault and Storage, and used VM Run Command. In one case, the journey from searching GitHub for client secrets to exfiltrating Key Vault data took five minutes. Elsewhere in the campaign, failed Azure Resource Manager calls were retried with supported API versions after roughly 28 to 80 seconds.

sequenceDiagram    accTitle: A composite view of the reported credential abuse    accDescr: An attacker searches public GitHub for a client secret, signs in as an application, discovers Azure resources, then reads data from Key Vault.    participant AG as Attacker agent    participant GH as Public GitHub    participant EN as Microsoft Entra ID    participant ARM as Azure Resource Manager    participant KV as Azure Key Vault    AG->>GH: Search for exposed application secrets    GH-->>AG: Credential found    AG->>EN: Authenticate as the application    EN-->>AG: Access token    AG->>ARM: Discover resources and permissions    AG->>KV: Access data permitted to the application    KV-->>AG: Data exfiltrated

This is a composite of the reported steps, not a claim that every step occurred in the five-minute case. The timing starts with the GitHub search, not with the original leak.

Microsoft has also reported ARTEX being used in different campaigns. Storm-0940 used ARTEX during a supply chain compromise, with several attacks reaching privileged cloud access in under three hours. Storm-3358 used it against financial organisations, combining it with conventional tools and vulnerabilities such as server-side request forgery (SSRF).

ARTEX is an open-source penetration testing framework, not malware by definition. The defensive problem is that the same automation can be turned against real organisations.

Why AI credentials matter

Microsoft observed repeated interest in credentials for AI services, including API keys and OAuth applications with access to Foundry Tools.

A Foundry resource key is a shared credential with coarse access and no per-user identity. It doesn’t pass through Entra authentication or its Conditional Access policies. A client secret, by contrast, can be exchanged for an Entra token representing the application; the resulting access depends on its permissions and applicable policy.

Don’t assume every provider key has the same scope. For example, the Claude Platform supports API access to Managed Agents endpoints as well as model APIs, while Foundry’s agent service requires Entra ID. Check the actual provider, endpoint and key type.

The listKeys trap

Some roles recommended for Foundry access can also retrieve resource keys. The current built-in role definitions show the difference:

  • Cognitive Services User and Foundry User, formerly Azure AI User, include accounts/listkeys/action.
  • Cognitive Services Contributor includes it as part of broader management permissions.
  • Cognitive Services OpenAI User doesn’t include that action in its own role definition.

This applies when the assignment’s scope covers the Foundry account. A separate or inherited role can still grant key access even if a role listed above doesn’t. Review effective permissions, not just one assignment.

Cognitive Services OpenAI User is a useful starting point for Azure OpenAI callers, but it isn’t an inference-only role: its data actions cover other OpenAI operations too. For a narrower custom role, select the actions your deployment actually needs and test them. Microsoft’s Foundry keyless guide shows Microsoft.CognitiveServices/accounts/MaaS/* as an example for model-as-a-service access; it isn’t a universal replacement for the OpenAI data actions.

While key authentication is enabled, an identity that can list keys may be able to obtain another usable credential. Disabling local authentication removes that key-based route into the resource once the change has propagated. It doesn’t remove excessive RBAC permissions or make an already compromised identity safe.

The wider move towards identity

The same theme is showing up outside Azure. Anthropic’s IP allowlisting is in beta for covered Claude Platform and Managed Agents endpoints. It limits where a key or federated token can be used, but not how long a stolen key remains valid. Anthropic recommends short key expiry or workload identity federation as well. Its Claude Enterprise allowlist is a separate control for the covered enterprise apps.

OpenAI’s GPT-6 Cyber system card describes restricted Daybreak Red access with identity verification and organisational controls including single sign-on, MFA and API IP allowlisting. These are useful guardrails, not a substitute for protecting the credential itself.

The IETF’s AI Identity Management System draft is an informational work in progress. It proposes a unique WIMSE identifier for each agent, expiring credentials and keeping those credentials away from the model. It calls static API keys an antipattern for agent identity.

Why rotation isn’t enough

If a credential is exposed, revoke or rotate it and investigate immediately. Deleting a commit alone doesn’t invalidate the credential, and copies can remain in history, caches, archives or logs. Keyless doesn’t mean a workload has no credentials anywhere: certificates, third-party keys and other secrets may still need rotation.

The difficulty is the response window. An access token issued at runtime has an audience, an expiry and an identity that can be authorised and audited. That is a better starting point than a long-lived shared string, but a bearer token can still be replayed until it expires. Token lifetimes and revocation behaviour vary by service, so don’t assume every token lasts only a few minutes or is immediately invalidated when an identity is disabled.

The keyless playbook for Azure

Here’s the pattern I’d start with for an AI workload. The exact identities and supported authentication methods depend on the host, model and tools.

flowchart TB    accTitle: Keyless paths for an Azure AI workload    accDescr: An application uses its managed identity to call an API Management gateway. The gateway validates the caller and uses its own managed identity to call Foundry. A pipeline deploys with OIDC. A Foundry agent uses its own identity for supported downstream tools. An external provider can use federation when supported.    P["GitHub Actions
OIDC federation"]:::caller    A["Application or agent host
managed identity"]:::identity    G["API Management
validate the caller"]:::gateway    F["Foundry model
local authentication disabled"]:::resource    I["Foundry agent
agent identity"]:::identity    T["Supported tool or storage
least-privilege access"]:::resource    X["External model provider
federation if supported"]:::resource    P -->|"deploys"| A    A -->|"Entra token"| G    G -->|"gateway identity"| F    I -->|"agent identity"| T    A -->|"federated token"| X    classDef caller fill:#fff4c2,stroke:#b7950b,color:#000    classDef identity fill:#cce5ff,stroke:#1f6feb,color:#000    classDef gateway fill:#cce5ff,stroke:#1f6feb,color:#000    classDef resource fill:#e6ffed,stroke:#2da44e,color:#000

1. Call Foundry with Entra ID

For an Azure-hosted application, attach a managed identity and assign the permissions required by the model deployment. The following Python example uses a user-assigned identity and the Azure OpenAI v1 endpoint. It follows Microsoft’s managed identity sample.

The api_key argument receives a token provider, not a stored API key. Replace the placeholders, use a deployment that supports the Responses API and configure a custom subdomain. In production, an explicit ManagedIdentityCredential avoids unexpectedly choosing a different credential from a broader discovery chain. For local development, use a developer credential instead.

Microsoft’s Foundry v1 examples request https://ai.azure.com/.default. The API Management example below requests https://cognitiveservices.azure.com as its managed identity resource. Use the audience documented for your endpoint and verify the actual request path.

2. Disable key authentication and prove it

The following Bicep illustrates a new Foundry resource with local authentication disabled and a role assignment for an existing managed identity. It doesn’t create the identity or a model deployment. The principal ID is the identity’s object ID, not its client ID.

Use a valid, available custom subdomain name. For an existing resource, incorporate the setting into its full infrastructure definition or use the documented update method. Don’t deploy an abbreviated example over a production resource without reviewing its existing settings.

The built-in Azure AI Services key access policy checks both Cognitive Services accounts and Azure AI Search. Start in audit mode to find existing resources:

After migrating callers, set the property on existing resources and consider the Deny effect to prevent new drift. Deny doesn’t remediate resources already deployed.

The control-plane setting isn’t an immediate cutoff. Microsoft says gateway configuration usually propagates in minutes but can take several hours. Check the property, confirm an Entra request succeeds, and verify that a previously working key against the same endpoint now receives HTTP 401. A wrong endpoint or an already invalid key can also produce a failure, so those checks belong together.

Handle an exposed key as an incident rather than waiting for migration. Plan any required key regeneration using the supported operations and don’t re-enable local authentication just to rotate keys.

For Storage, allowSharedKeyAccess: false rejects account and service SAS as well as Shared Key requests. A user delegation SAS for Blob Storage can still work because it’s backed by Entra ID. Check dependent services first: disabling Shared Key can break workloads such as Azure Cloud Shell storage and some Azure Files access paths.

3. Put a gateway in the middle

API Management can validate the caller’s Entra token and use its own managed identity for the Foundry request. Enable that identity and grant it the appropriate role on the model resource. This is an inbound policy excerpt, not a complete API configuration:

Configure the named values, API audience, backend and any required app roles or scopes. If you don’t want a separate API Management subscription key, disable that requirement only after the Entra policy protects the relevant operations. Review inherited policies and restrict direct access to Foundry so callers can’t bypass the gateway.

The backend sees the gateway identity, not automatically the original caller. Record the validated caller identity and correlation ID at the gateway if you need per-agent attribution, and don’t log bearer tokens. Quotas and usage logging also need explicit policies.

4. Federate your pipelines

GitHub Actions can exchange an OpenID Connect token for Azure access through a federated credential on an Entra application or user-assigned managed identity. The identifiers below aren’t client secrets, even though they’re stored in GitHub Secrets:

Configure the federated credential before running the job, and restrict its issuer, audience and subject to the intended repository and branch or environment. An environment-based subject doesn’t itself restrict the branch, so use GitHub environment protection rules where needed. Check GitHub’s current subject format rather than assuming every repository uses the same one.

5. Give agents their own identities

Microsoft Entra Agent ID represents an agent instance with its own identity under an agent identity blueprint. Credentials are configured on the blueprint, not stored as a client secret on each agent identity. Microsoft recommends federation with managed identities or certificates rather than client secrets for production blueprints.

The current Foundry agent model provisions a unique blueprint and identity for an agent’s default instance. The blueprint has a service-managed federated credential, and the new agent identity starts without downstream permissions. Grant only the access each supported tool needs. Other tool connections can use a project managed identity or a delegated user identity instead, so check the actual authentication mode.

Give each agent an owner and sponsor, and use a distinct identity where the platform supports it. A Conditional Access policy targeting a blueprint applies to its agent identities, but delegated calls are evaluated against the user. Disabling a blueprint prevents new authentication by its identities; already issued tokens can remain valid until expiry.

Conditional Access for agents requires Microsoft 365 E7, or Microsoft Agent 365 paired with Entra ID P1 or Microsoft 365 E3. Risk-based agent policies require the additional licensing described in Microsoft’s guidance. The default inactivity policy needs no licence, but it is a preview feature. Once enabled, it notifies at 60 days, disables at 90 and deletes at 455 days of inactivity. Exclude genuinely seasonal agents where appropriate.

6. Stop new secrets being created

Entra application management policies can block new passwords and symmetric keys on applications and service principals, with managed exceptions. In the Entra admin centre, look under Enterprise apps and Application policies for Block password addition. This doesn’t revoke secrets that already exist.

For automation, Microsoft’s Graph example uses the beta endpoint. Read the current policy first and preserve any existing restrictions in both collections:

Catch mistakes before and after a push too. GitHub scans public repositories for supported secrets, and push protection can block supported secrets before they land. Eligible enterprises can enable public monitoring for credentials associated with their people in public repositories beyond those they own.

Give coding assistants the same rules in AGENTS.md or .github/copilot-instructions.md: don’t write secrets into code or tests, use managed identity for deployed Azure workloads, and use the supported agent identity creation path when an agent needs its own identity.

7. When a provider only takes keys

If the provider supports workload identity federation, use it. The Claude Platform’s Azure guide describes exchanging an Entra token from a managed identity for an Anthropic token bound to a service account. It requires an audience app registration and federation rules that match the intended issuer, audience and identity. The upstream managed identity token can live longer than the provider token, so protect both.

For a provider that only accepts static keys, keep the key in Key Vault and let a gateway inject it from a Key Vault-backed named value. Restrict provider access to the gateway’s egress addresses where supported, and set expiry, spending limits and alerts. An allowlist containing a shared proxy is weaker: someone with the leaked key may be able to use that proxy too.

Claude on Microsoft Foundry is a Foundry deployment; the Claude Platform IP allowlist doesn’t cover that path. Apply the controls supported by the actual endpoint.

Spotting abuse in the logs

Microsoft’s report is also a useful detection guide. Start with failed and successful service principal sign-ins, unexpected token requests across multiple resources, and unusual Key Vault secret reads. Default tool user agents can provide context, but they are easy to change and shouldn’t be a blocking rule by themselves.

This Defender XDR hunting query looks for one source address with mixed results across at least three service principals in an hour:

The table requires Entra ID P2. An empty result without the required data isn’t evidence of safety. This query groups events; it doesn’t prove that a failure preceded a success or that both involved the same application. Investigate the sequence and account for legitimate shared egress addresses and expired credentials.

Microsoft also suggests decoys and other deception controls. Used carefully, they can give defenders a useful signal while drawing automated activity away from real assets.

Nine checks before release

  1. A previously working key fails after the Foundry setting propagates, while an Entra request to the same endpoint succeeds.
  2. Each caller has the correct endpoint, token audience and resource permissions. Role assignments can take time to propagate.
  3. Effective permissions are reviewed, including inherited roles and listkeys access. Use the narrowest role that supports the required operations.
  4. Production code uses a deliberate credential, such as ManagedIdentityCredential, and doesn’t expose tokens to the model.
  5. Existing client secrets have been inventoried and removed or governed. Block new password additions where the organisation is ready.
  6. Storage dependencies have been checked before disabling Shared Key, including account and service SAS.
  7. Pipelines use restricted federation, with protected environments or branches as appropriate.
  8. Each supported agent has an accountable owner, sponsor and appropriately scoped identity. Test Conditional Access and lifecycle policies with their licensing and preview limitations in mind.
  9. Sign-in and resource diagnostics are available before cutover, with alerts and an incident response path for suspicious activity.

My take

The ARTEX reports change the maths on a model key kept in an app setting “just for now”. One observed attacker got from a GitHub search to Key Vault data in five minutes. Rotation is still necessary when something leaks, but it can’t be the only defence.

Keyless moves risk rather than removing it. A compromised host, or SSRF against an exposed local token endpoint, can still put a managed identity token in the wrong hands. Network controls, least privilege and monitoring still matter. Conditional Access coverage and licensing also differ between agent identities, user-delegated access and managed identities.

If I had one week, I’d audit AI resources that still accept keys, move the highest-risk callers to managed identities, disable local authentication where the dependencies are ready, and prove both the token and key paths. Then I’d start the next agent with an identity and an owner from day one.

Key takeaways

  • Microsoft observed one agent go from a GitHub secret search to Key Vault data exfiltration in five minutes.
  • Replace stored credentials with managed identities and federation where supported, then disable the old authentication path.
  • Review effective RBAC permissions: some Foundry roles can list resource keys, and inherited assignments still count.
  • A gateway’s backend identity isn’t automatically the original caller’s identity. Preserve attribution in gateway logs without recording tokens.
  • Treat agent identity, lifecycle, licensing and detection as part of the rollout, not an afterthought.

References

  • Microsoft Threat Intelligence, Threat actors use agentic AI tooling to find and abuse exposed secrets
  • Microsoft Security Research, Storm-0940 uses ARTEX in a supply chain compromise
  • Microsoft Learn, Azure built-in roles for AI and machine learning
  • Microsoft Learn, Configure keyless authentication for Foundry Models
  • Microsoft Learn, Disable local authentication in Foundry Tools
  • Microsoft Learn, Prevent Shared Key authorisation for Azure Storage
  • Microsoft Learn, Authenticate and authorise LLM APIs with API Management
  • Microsoft Learn, Authenticate to Azure from GitHub Actions with OpenID Connect
  • Microsoft Learn, Agent identity concepts in Microsoft Foundry
  • Microsoft Learn, Conditional Access for agents
  • Claude Platform Docs, Workload Identity Federation
  • IETF, AI Identity Management System, Internet-Draft, work in progress

Related posts

  • Governance for AI Agents, Part 1: identity, policy and audit beyond the credential layer.
  • MCP Goes Stateless: routing and correlation at an AI gateway.
  • Microsoft Foundry Cross-Region with Private Endpoints, Part 1: network isolation as another layer.
  • AGENTS.md vs Copilot Instructions vs Cursor Rules vs CLAUDE.md: where to put instructions for coding agents.

Image Credits

  • Cover image generated by Copilot
entry.summary: Microsoft saw an AI agent move from a GitHub secret search to Key Vault data theft in five minutes. Learn how keyless Azure AI reduces the risk.
entry.title: AI Agents Exploit Leaked Keys in Minutes: Go Keyless on Azure

entry.content:
Update (2026-11-23): Claude and Codex can now be explicitly allowed

VS Code 1.147 (18 November 2026) lets admins allow the Claude and Codex harnesses by listing them in vscode.allowedHarnesses, set through file-based or MDM managed settings. Server-managed settings don't support it yet.

Sessions in those harnesses run without Copilot's managed permission, sandbox, MCP and plugin controls. See the VS Code 1.147 release notes before enabling them.

TL;DR

The four agent types I described in January are no longer the right map for VS Code. Choose a harness, where the session runs and a model, then set the role and permissions.

The Copilot harness is now the default. It shares a runtime with other Copilot products and runs through the Agent Host, so a session can outlive its editor window, but not a stopped host.

Cloud sandboxes let work continue without your laptop. Under GitHub AI Credit billing, sub-agents consume tokens at their own models’ rates, so context isolation is still useful, but it isn’t free.

Comparing GitHub Copilot CLI vs Local vs cloud? They aren’t three equivalent agent types. Copilot CLI is a terminal interface, Local is a VS Code harness, and cloud describes where the agent’s tools run. The Copilot SDK is the programmable way to embed the Copilot runtime in your own application, not another execution location.

This is Part 2 of my GitHub Copilot agents guide: the current comparison, including what changed since the original four types.

In a hurry? Jump to the updated decision guide, then come back for the architecture and the money bit.

Ten months is a long time in agent land

When Part 1 went out on 10 January, I split GitHub Copilot agents into Local, Background, Cloud and Sub-agents. It was a useful way to explain the workflows, but it mixed together where an agent ran, how you interacted with it and how it delegated.

Since then, VS Code has moved to weekly releases, GitHub has rebuilt Copilot billing, and the old boxes have stopped lining up with the controls in front of us.

The better mental model is one Copilot engine with many cockpits, alongside other providers’ harnesses. This post is a November 2026 snapshot, checked against the primary sources on 3 November, covering VS Code 1.144 and GitHub’s 28 October cloud rollout.

What happened to the four types

The biggest change isn’t a rename. The old categories have been pulled apart into choices you can make separately.

%%{init: {"htmlLabels": false, "flowchart": {"htmlLabels": false, "nodeSpacing": 15, "rankSpacing": 30, "padding": 10}}}%%flowchart TB    accTitle: From four agent types to three separate choices    accDescr: January's Local, Background, Cloud and Sub-agent categories mixed several concepts. November separates the harness, execution environment and model, with Copilot as the default harness.    JAN["January: four types
Local, Background,
Cloud and Sub-agents"]    NOV["November: three choices
Harness
Environment
Model"]    DEFAULT["Copilot is the default
Local remains for migration"]    JAN -->|"separate the concepts"| NOV --> DEFAULT    classDef historical fill:#f6f8fa,stroke:#8c959f,color:#000,stroke-dasharray:5 5    classDef focus fill:#cce5ff,stroke:#1f6feb,color:#000    classDef data fill:#fff4c2,stroke:#b7950b,color:#000    class JAN historical    class NOV focus    class DEFAULT data

The work we used to divide between Local and Background is converging on the Copilot harness. It became the default for new sessions in VS Code 1.143. Local remains available for editor workflows and integrations that haven’t migrated yet.

The coding agent became Copilot cloud agent, and research, plans and branch-only work joined the original pull request workflow. The newer cloud experience defaults to a managed sandbox where that environment choice is offered.

Sub-agents haven’t disappeared. They’re still isolated workers, but the delegation tool depends on the harness, and their model calls are metered under AI Credit billing.

Two things also need correcting rather than presenting as new features. You could already steer the coding agent while it worked in October 2025. And VS Code’s Autopilot arrived in 1.111 in March 2026, not January. I’ve added notes to Part 1 rather than quietly rewriting its history.

The new mental model: harness, environment, model

Start a session by separating the agent loop from the machine running its tools and the model answering its requests.

%%{init: {"htmlLabels": false, "flowchart": {"htmlLabels": false, "nodeSpacing": 15, "rankSpacing": 30, "padding": 10}}}%%flowchart TB    accTitle: The choices that define an agent session    accDescr: Choose a harness, an execution environment and a model. Then choose the role and permission settings supported by that harness. Not every combination is available.    H["Harness
Copilot, Local,
Claude or Codex"]    E["Environment
this computer or container
remote host or cloud"]    M["Model access
Copilot, provider credentials
or supported local models"]    R["Then: role and permissions
within that harness"]    H --> E --> M --> R    classDef focus fill:#cce5ff,stroke:#1f6feb,color:#000    classDef output fill:#e6ffed,stroke:#2da44e,color:#000    classDef data fill:#fff4c2,stroke:#b7950b,color:#000    class H focus    class E output    class M,R data

These are separate choices, not a promise that every combination exists. Cloud is an execution target for the Copilot harness, not a fifth harness. Local only lives in the editor’s Chat view.

The naming is a trap worth calling out: Local is a harness name, not a synonym for running on your machine. Copilot, Claude and Codex can also run tools on your machine. None of that guarantees local model inference or that your code stays offline.

Changing the model doesn’t change the harness either. A Claude model inside a Copilot session still uses Copilot’s agent loop, tools and customisations. Selecting the Claude harness is a different decision.

Copilot: the default starting point

The Copilot harness uses the Copilot SDK and runs through the Agent Host. Use it for day-to-day coding, background work and sessions you want to open in both the editor and the Agents window.

In the Session Target control, choose Copilot, then the model and built-in agent. Ask researches without making changes, Agent implements and validates, and Plan researches an approach for review, also available through /plan. Custom agents appear in the same picker.

Local: the editor-bound migration option

Local uses VS Code’s earlier built-in harness in the extension host. Its session belongs to the editor window, so closing that window stops ongoing work. It isn’t available in the Agents window.

Keep it when an integration still depends on Local-specific tools or customisations, not because the word sounds more private. Before migrating, check tool availability, MCP configuration and hooks rather than assuming the files mean the same thing in both harnesses.

Claude and Codex: different harnesses, not just models

Claude integrates Anthropic’s Claude Agent SDK. Codex uses OpenAI’s integration, either through its extension or the experimental Agent Host route. They retain their own agent behaviour and provider-specific configuration.

Claude support is enabled by default where policy permits it. Codex requires opting into an integration; the Agent Host route has its own authentication requirements, including Pro+ for the Copilot-backed option.

There is an important enterprise caveat: the Claude and Codex harnesses are disabled by default when Copilot enterprise-managed settings apply, including managed permission or sandbox settings. In VS Code 1.147, file-based or MDM managed settings can allow one or both through vscode.allowedHarnesses; server-managed settings don’t support that exception yet. Separate provider credentials don’t bypass the policy. Allowed Claude and Codex sessions still don’t inherit Copilot’s managed permission, sandbox, MCP or plugin controls.

The harness guide is the source to check when a target is missing from your picker.

One Copilot engine, many cockpits

This is the architectural change that makes the rest less confusing. VS Code’s Copilot harness, the CLI, the Copilot app, cloud sessions and Copilot code review share the Copilot runtime. Claude and Codex remain separate harnesses.

%%{init: {"htmlLabels": false, "flowchart": {"htmlLabels": false, "nodeSpacing": 15, "rankSpacing": 30, "padding": 10}}}%%flowchart TB    accTitle: Copilot interfaces share a runtime that applications can also use    accDescr: VS Code, Copilot CLI, the Copilot app, cloud sessions and code review share the Copilot harness. The SDK exposes that engine to custom applications.    CLIENTS["Copilot clients
VS Code, CLI and app
cloud sessions
and code review"]    RUNTIME["Shared Copilot harness
agent loop, tools
and customisations"]    SDK["Copilot SDK
embed in your own app"]    CLIENTS -->|"share"| RUNTIME    RUNTIME -->|"exposed through"| SDK    classDef focus fill:#cce5ff,stroke:#1f6feb,color:#000    classDef data fill:#fff4c2,stroke:#b7950b,color:#000    classDef output fill:#e6ffed,stroke:#2da44e,color:#000    class CLIENTS output    class RUNTIME focus    class SDK data

The Copilot SDK became generally available on 2 June, with TypeScript, Python, Go, .NET, Rust and Java SDKs. By default, an SDK drives the Copilot CLI in server mode over JSON-RPC. An experimental in-process transport is also available, so a separate CLI process is the default architecture, not the only one.

Standard SDK use needs a Copilot subscription, including the Free tier for personal use. Bring your own key is a separate route that can work without a Copilot subscription, with usage billed by that provider.

Sharing a runtime makes instructions, skills, custom agents, hooks and plugins more portable. It doesn’t make every surface identical. Tools, model access, permissions, discovery locations and supported customisations still differ. The migration guide is more useful than copying configuration until the errors stop.

Prompt files are a particular migration concern: workflows that depend on the Local harness’s prompt files should move reusable procedures into skills for the Copilot harness. Copilot Memory is another shared capability across supported surfaces, but it isn’t a promise that all personal settings or session history automatically synchronise.

One SDK default deserves attention before embedding it in a tool: it exposes the CLI’s first-party tools by default, similar to --allow-all. Execution is still governed by the SDK’s permission handler. Configure that handler and the available tools deliberately rather than treating an embedded agent as a harmless text-completion API.

The Agent Host: sessions that outlive the window

The Agent Host is a dedicated process that owns sessions, their terminals and their changes. The editor window is a client of that process, not the place the whole agent has to live.

%%{init: {"htmlLabels": false, "flowchart": {"htmlLabels": false, "nodeSpacing": 15, "rankSpacing": 30, "padding": 10}}}%%flowchart TB    accTitle: Clients connect to an Agent Host running beside the code    accDescr: The editor, Agents window and browser connect to an Agent Host. The host owns session state and runs harnesses beside the workspace.    CLIENT["Editor, Agents window
or browser"]    HOST["Agent Host
session state
terminals and changes"]    HARN["Harness adapters
Copilot, Claude and Codex"]    CODE["Code and tools
this computer, a container
or a remote host"]    CLIENT -->|"Agent Host Protocol"| HOST    HOST --> HARN --> CODE    classDef focus fill:#cce5ff,stroke:#1f6feb,color:#000    classDef output fill:#e6ffed,stroke:#2da44e,color:#000    class HOST,HARN focus    class CLIENT,CODE output

Clients communicate through the open Agent Host Protocol. Version 1.0 arrived with VS Code 1.144. The host owns the authoritative state, so several clients can observe and steer the same session instead of each creating a copy.

The distinction that matters in practice is session lifetime.

Close a project or editor window, and a Copilot harness session can keep working while its Agent Host remains running. Quit the VS Code application that manages that local host, and the work stops. Put the laptop to sleep, and local work doesn’t magically continue elsewhere.

A remote session can continue if its remote machine and serving process stay running. A cloud sandbox doesn’t depend on your laptop, although the service still manages its availability and lifecycle. Being able to reopen a conversation isn’t proof that its agent kept working while its host was stopped.

For an overnight job, choose a host that will actually stay available. Window independence is not machine independence.

Connected windows can lend tools to a session, including extension and browser capabilities. Those tools need their lender to stay connected, even if the host itself can keep going.

For a standalone host, the documented command is code agent host; --tunnel exposes it through a dev tunnel. GitHub Environments, currently in preview, lets you register an existing machine and access supported sessions from other Copilot clients. Registration doesn’t provision compute or move your workspace. Your machine still has to stay on.

Handoffs have changed

Part 1 described a smooth Local to Background to Cloud escalation path. That isn’t a general pipeline inside the current VS Code experience.

%%{init: {"htmlLabels": false, "flowchart": {"htmlLabels": false, "nodeSpacing": 15, "rankSpacing": 30, "padding": 10}}}%%flowchart TB    accTitle: A VS Code Local session can hand off, but not through an unlimited chain    accDescr: A Local session can carry its history to Copilot, Claude or experimental Codex. Those sessions cannot hand off again to another harness or the cloud.    LOCAL["VS Code Local session"]    DEST["Copilot, Claude or
experimental Codex"]    STOP["No further handoff
start a cloud session
when you need the cloud"]    LOCAL -->|"history and context"| DEST --> STOP    classDef focus fill:#cce5ff,stroke:#1f6feb,color:#000    classDef data fill:#fff4c2,stroke:#b7950b,color:#000    classDef warning fill:#ffd6d6,stroke:#c0392b,color:#000    class LOCAL data    class DEST focus    class STOP warning

A Local session can hand off to Copilot, Claude or the experimental Codex integration, carrying its conversation history and context. Those destination sessions can’t then hand off to another harness or to the cloud. Starting a new cloud session is a separate operation; it doesn’t automatically copy your local uncommitted changes.

The terminal CLI still supports /delegate, or a prompt beginning with &. That delegates a task to Copilot cloud agent, creating a branch and draft PR. It isn’t the same operation as selecting another harness in VS Code.

For an interactive CLI session whose tools run in a cloud sandbox, start it with:

That starts a new cloud session rather than moving the current local conversation. Once a cloud sandbox session exists, supported clients can reconnect to the same session. Continuing a session, handing off a task and starting another session are three different things.

The cloud side: Copilot cloud agent and cloud sandboxes

The cloud agent has grown beyond “assign an issue and wait for a PR”. You can ask for research, approve a plan before implementation, iterate on a branch and request a PR when you’re ready.

The newer connected experience also changes where that work runs. Check the selected environment before starting, because the default and available choices still depend on the client and workflow.

%%{init: {"htmlLabels": false, "flowchart": {"htmlLabels": false, "nodeSpacing": 15, "rankSpacing": 30, "padding": 10}}}%%flowchart TB    accTitle: Choose Actions when the repository needs Actions-specific capabilities    accDescr: Use Actions for Actions setup steps, runner customisation or Windows. Otherwise, a managed Linux cloud sandbox is the default where offered.    START["Need Actions-specific
setup, runners or Windows?"]    ACTIONS["Actions"]    CLOUD["Cloud sandbox"]    START -->|"yes"| ACTIONS    START -->|"no"| CLOUD    classDef focus fill:#cce5ff,stroke:#1f6feb,color:#000    classDef output fill:#e6ffed,stroke:#2da44e,color:#000    classDef data fill:#fff4c2,stroke:#b7950b,color:#000    class START focus    class CLOUD output    class ACTIONS data

Cloud sandboxes: the new default where offered

A cloud sandbox is a GitHub-hosted Linux environment with its own workspace. It can keep working without your machine, saves a snapshot when stopped and can resume across supported Copilot clients.

Unlike Actions-based agent sessions, sandboxes don’t have the one-hour total running-time limit. They can also work across repositories in one organisation, or across repositories owned by your personal account. Access and organisation policies still apply.

The connected cloud experience and sandboxes became generally available on paid Copilot plans on 28 October. Entry points include GitHub.com, Mobile, the CLI, the Copilot app, VS Code, Slack and Teams. Availability in a service doesn’t mean every client’s integration has the same maturity.

Actions: still needed for some repositories

Choose Actions when the repository needs copilot-setup-steps.yml, Actions-specific setup such as OIDC sign-in, larger or self-hosted runners, or a Windows environment. Those settings don’t automatically transfer into a cloud sandbox.

Actions-based agent sessions still have a 59-minute execution limit and are scoped to one repository. GitHub also documents a one-branch, one-pull-request-per-task limitation. A sandbox’s broader repository access isn’t a promise of unlimited PR creation within one task.

Remote environments: your compute, your lifecycle

A registered machine or VM is another option when you need an environment you control. Unlike a managed sandbox, you maintain the machine, dependencies and uptime.

Automations can initiate recurring work on schedules or repository events, subject to feature availability, eligible repositories and policy. A cloud automation doesn’t need your laptop; an automation running locally still needs its host.

Security checks are defaults, not an absolute guarantee

Part 1 called security validation non-negotiable. The current security documentation says repository administrators can disable individual validation tools.

By default, the cloud agent uses CodeQL, secret scanning and checks of new dependencies against the GitHub Advisory Database. The validation doesn’t require a GitHub Advanced Security licence. Keep it enabled, inspect the results and review the code yourself. Automated scanning isn’t proof that a change is safe.

Claude and Codex are also available as third-party coding agents on GitHub, currently in public preview and subject to account policies. They receive security validation and consume AI credits plus Actions minutes. Don’t confuse those hosted agents with simply selecting one of their models inside Copilot.

Sub-agents: the same context benefit, a different bill

The useful part of Part 1 still stands. A worker can investigate a bounded question in its own context and return a focused answer, without filling the main thread with every file read and intermediate result.

%%{init: {"htmlLabels": false, "flowchart": {"htmlLabels": false, "nodeSpacing": 15, "rankSpacing": 30, "padding": 10}}}%%flowchart TB    accTitle: Isolated workers return focused results to the main agent    accDescr: The main agent delegates independent research and review tasks to workers with their own context. Focused results return to the main agent for implementation. Each worker's model calls contribute to usage.    MAIN["Main agent
assigns scoped tasks"]    RESEARCH["Researcher
own context"]    REVIEW["Reviewer
own context"]    RESULTS["Focused results
not every intermediate step"]    NEXT["Main agent
implements and validates"]    MAIN --> RESEARCH & REVIEW    RESEARCH & REVIEW --> RESULTS --> NEXT    classDef focus fill:#cce5ff,stroke:#1f6feb,color:#000    classDef data fill:#fff4c2,stroke:#b7950b,color:#000    classDef output fill:#e6ffed,stroke:#2da44e,color:#000    class MAIN,NEXT focus    class RESEARCH,REVIEW data    class RESULTS output

The delegation mechanism now depends on the harness. Copilot uses its native task tool; Local uses runSubagent, exposed through the agent tool set. Claude and Codex manage their own provider-native sub-agents.

That is more than a spelling change. When migrating a coordinator, review its tool list, prompts and expected arguments. Don’t mechanically replace runSubagent with task and assume the contracts match.

Give a research worker a smaller job and model

For a Local harness example, create .github/agents/repo-researcher.agent.md with a read-only tool list and a model suited to lightweight research:

This is a Local harness example, not a universal configuration for all four harnesses. Choose an available model from your picker and compare its current price with the parent model. user-invocable: false hides the worker from the picker without preventing agent invocation.

Local’s model selection order is an explicit tool-call preference, then the custom agent’s model, then Auto if chat.subagents.defaultToAuto is enabled and applicable, then the parent model. Explicit and agent-configured selections can’t exceed the parent’s cost tier. Auto routing has separate rules, so that isn’t a universal guarantee that a worker can never use a pricier model.

Local invocations are stateless and don’t inherit the conversation history. Supply the goal, necessary context, allowed actions and expected result. Nested Local sub-agents are off by default; enabling chat.subagents.allowInvocationsFromSubagents permits nesting up to five levels.

Make the cost visible

Enable chat.subagents.showCreditUsage to show credit usage in the worker’s response pill and hover details. It is hidden by default. In the Agents window, you can inspect a worker’s model, elapsed time and active tool call.

Delegation adds model usage and coordination. Use it when separate context, independent work or a cheaper model is worth that overhead. A quick lookup doesn’t need a miniature organisation of agents.

Guardrails: permissions, Autopilot and sandboxing

There are three separate controls here, and confusing them is an easy way to grant more autonomy than you meant to.

%%{init: {"htmlLabels": false, "flowchart": {"htmlLabels": false, "nodeSpacing": 15, "rankSpacing": 30, "padding": 10}}}%%flowchart TB    accTitle: Permissions, Autopilot and terminal sandboxing are separate controls    accDescr: Permission levels govern approvals. The workflow mode controls how autonomously the agent continues. Terminal sandboxing is a separate layer and does not cover every tool.    PERM["Approvals
Manual, Assisted
or Allow all"]    AUTO["Workflow
Agent or Autopilot"]    SBX["Terminal sandbox
file and network limits"]    LIMIT["Other tools need
their own controls"]    PERM -->|"combine with"| AUTO    AUTO -->|"separate layer"| SBX    SBX --- LIMIT    classDef focus fill:#cce5ff,stroke:#1f6feb,color:#000    classDef data fill:#fff4c2,stroke:#b7950b,color:#000    classDef warning fill:#ffd6d6,stroke:#c0392b,color:#000    class PERM focus    class AUTO,SBX data    class LIMIT warning

In Copilot harness sessions, Manual permissions follows your configured approval rules. Assisted uses an LLM judge to assess tool calls and asks you about those it doesn’t approve. Allow all runs tools without confirmation.

Assisted became generally available in VS Code 1.144 and requires Folder isolation. Worktree sessions always use Allow all. A worktree separates Git changes; it doesn’t isolate the agent from the rest of your machine.

Autopilot is an agent mode in the Copilot harness, not another permission level. It auto-approves tools, retries errors and answers questions that would otherwise block progress. In the Local harness, Autopilot is still selected as a permission level. That harness-specific difference matters when following older instructions.

Sandboxing is separate again. An enabled terminal sandbox restricts file system and network access even under Allow all or Autopilot. It doesn’t cover every tool, so it isn’t a substitute for tool and URL controls. Local terminal sandboxing is in preview on macOS, Linux and WSL2, and experimental on Windows.

Neither Assisted nor Autopilot guarantees good judgement. Both can make mistakes, and their model usage belongs in your cost planning too.

The money bit: from premium requests to AI credits

GitHub moved Copilot to usage-based billing on 1 June 2026. One GitHub AI Credit is $0.01 USD, and metered model usage is priced from input, output and cached tokens at the selected model’s rates.

The important unit is no longer just the prompt you typed. An agent task can make many model calls, with more calls in its workers.

%%{init: {"htmlLabels": false, "flowchart": {"htmlLabels": false, "nodeSpacing": 15, "rankSpacing": 30, "padding": 10}}}%%flowchart TB    accTitle: Every model call in an agent task contributes to usage    accDescr: Main-agent and worker model calls consume input, output and cached tokens at each model's rates. These costs draw from the AI Credit allowance and permitted additional usage.    PROMPT["One user task"]    CALLS["Main and worker
model calls"]    TOKENS["Input, output
and cached tokens
at each model's rates"]    AI["GitHub AI Credits
included allowance,
then permitted extra usage"]    PROMPT --> CALLS --> TOKENS --> AI    classDef focus fill:#cce5ff,stroke:#1f6feb,color:#000    classDef warning fill:#ffd6d6,stroke:#c0392b,color:#000    class PROMPT,CALLS focus    class TOKENS,AI warning

Under legacy premium-request billing, user prompts or cloud agent sessions were the relevant units, with model multipliers. Tool calls made within an agent’s work weren’t each a new user request. That’s the context behind Part 1’s advice about effectively free sub-agents.

Under AI Credit billing, worker model calls consume usage at their own models’ rates. A shell command isn’t itself a model call, but its output can become input to the next one. Repeated context and long conversations still count, although cached input may have a different price.

Check the billing model before comparing numbers

Some existing annual Pro and Pro+ subscribers chose to remain on legacy premium-request billing until their annual plan ends. Those accounts are an exception to the general migration, not evidence that worker model calls are free on usage-based plans.

Inline code completions and next edit suggestions aren’t billed in AI credits. Nor are responses actually run by the experimental on-device model. A local harness calling a hosted model is not that on-device exception.

Copilot Fusion also isn’t free routing. It bills the models it uses at their standard rates, with the current 30% paid-plan discount running through 30 November 2026.

Treat model usage and cloud execution as separate budgets

Cloud sandboxes have compute, allocated-memory and stopped-snapshot-storage meters. Compute and memory can draw from the shared included compute entitlement also used by eligible Actions runners. That isn’t your AI Credit allowance.

GitHub announced sandbox billing would begin in November 2026. Check the sandbox billing documentation for the applicable rates and controls. Stopping a sandbox stops compute and memory metering, but retained snapshots still consume storage.

An AI Credit budget alone doesn’t cap sandbox spending. Configure the relevant product or SKU budget too, and enable its stop-usage option when you need a hard limit rather than an alert.

What I’d do about it
