Give workers cheaper models when the task allows it, keep their briefs bounded and avoid sending the same large context to several agents without a reason. Keep the main thread focused rather than paying a frontier model to repeatedly reread everything.

For teams, included usage is pooled: Business contributes 1,900 AI credits per seat per month and Enterprise contributes 3,900. User-level budgets cap total consumption, including usage drawn from the pool; spending limits at other levels can control additional charges. Those are different controls, so check which one you’re setting.

The point isn’t to avoid delegation. It’s to stop treating delegation, Fusion and Autopilot as invisible work outside the meter.

Part 1’s decision guide, rewritten

Pair on code or plan a change

Start with the Copilot harness in the Chat view. Use Ask to understand the code, Plan to review an approach and Agent to implement it. Choose a different harness for its behaviour or integrations, not simply because you want one of its provider’s models.

Keep working after closing an editor window

Use an Agent Host-backed Copilot session and keep VS Code and the host running. If the requirement is “keep working with my laptop shut”, choose a remote machine that stays on or a cloud sandbox instead.

Fix an issue overnight and review it in the morning

Use a cloud session with clear acceptance criteria. Ask for a plan first when the approach needs review, or ask explicitly for a pull request. Select Actions if the repository depends on Actions-specific setup or runners.

Work on several features without mixing the changes

Use separate sessions and worktrees in the Agents window. This isolates Git changes, not security permissions. Compare the extra model usage with the value of independent work.

Research without filling the main context

Use a bounded sub-agent on an appropriate cheaper model. Give it enough context to work independently and ask for a concise result. For a small lookup, stay in the main session.

Reuse a provider workflow, schedule a job or embed an agent

Choose Claude or Codex when you need their native harness and policy permits it. Use an automation for a recurring job, selecting a host that will be available when it runs. Use the Copilot SDK to put the Copilot runtime inside your own application.

Keep Local only for a workflow that still needs it while you migrate.

How we got here

The release dates make the pace easier to appreciate:

  • 25 February: the Copilot CLI became generally available.
  • 9 March: VS Code 1.111 began weekly Stable releases and introduced Autopilot.
  • 1 April: the renamed cloud agent added branch-only work and plans.
  • 1 and 2 June: AI Credit billing went live, followed by Copilot SDK general availability.
  • 17 June: the Copilot app became generally available.
  • 15 July: VS Code 1.129 began rolling out the Agent Host.
  • October: 1.143 made the Copilot harness the default; 28 October brought the connected cloud experience and VS Code 1.144 with AHP 1.0.

Those changes explain why a January comparison table now needs more than a few renamed columns.

Honest limits

Cloud sandboxes are generally available, but VS Code’s cloud-session integration still has experimental settings and account requirements. The Dev Container and direct Codex integrations also have their own maturity and setup constraints.

The Copilot harness doesn’t yet expose every Local tool or customisation. Enterprise policy can restrict harnesses, models, permissions and environments, or move a Local session to Copilot so the runtime can enforce the policy.

The docs describe several overlapping generations of workflows. When checking sub-agents and permissions, use the documentation for your actual harness. When checking cloud behaviour, distinguish managed sandboxes from Actions-based sessions.

This will date again. Treat the dates, preview labels and discounts as a snapshot, not permanent promises.

My take

The headline isn’t any single feature. It’s convergence. In January I was explaining four agents with four rulebooks. Today the useful questions are which harness should run the loop, where its tools should run and which model should do the thinking.

For Copilot, one engine with many cockpits is a much better mental model. Just don’t mistake a common engine for identical capabilities everywhere, or a persistent conversation for compute that never stops.

The bit I’d flag to every team lead is cost. Sub-agents remain a useful context-management tool, but every worker needs to earn its model usage. Give it a bounded job, choose its model deliberately and turn the credit meter on.

Key takeaways

  • Choose the harness, execution environment and model separately. Local is a harness name, not a privacy or offline guarantee.
  • Agent Host sessions can outlive an editor window, but they still need a running host. Use remote or cloud compute for work that must outlive your laptop.
  • Cloud sandboxes bring resumable sessions and broader repository scope; Actions remains necessary for some setup and runner requirements.
  • Delegation tools and permission semantics depend on the harness. Review integrations rather than relying on old tool names.
  • Under AI Credit billing, the main agent and its workers all contribute model usage. Cloud execution has separate meters and budget controls.

References

  • Choose an agent harness, VS Code
  • Agent Host architecture, VS Code
  • Use subagents, VS Code
  • Manage approvals and permissions, VS Code
  • VS Code 1.144 release notes
  • VS Code 1.147 release notes
  • GitHub Copilot SDK: architecture, authentication and tools
  • Copilot on GitHub.com and GitHub Mobile: environments and limitations
  • Cloud sandboxes: defaults, setup compatibility and lifecycle
  • Billing for cloud and local sandboxes
  • AI Credit billing for individuals
  • AI Credit billing for organisations and enterprises
  • Legacy billing exceptions for existing annual plans

Related posts

  • Part 1: The Four Types of GitHub Copilot Agents, preserved with update notes as a historical snapshot.
  • AGENTS.md vs Copilot Instructions vs Cursor Rules vs CLAUDE.md, for the context files and customisations around the agent.

Image Credits

  • Cover image generated by Copilot
entry.summary: Compare GitHub Copilot CLI, Local and cloud agents in 2026. Learn where the Copilot SDK fits, how sessions run, and what sub-agents and AI Credits cost.
entry.title: GitHub Copilot CLI vs Local vs Cloud: Agents Explained (2026)

entry.content:
GitHub Universe 2026 brought a stack of updates across Copilot, developer workflows, automation, security and platform engineering. I built a more entertaining way to catch up.

SHIP IT is a 3D arcade game with five sectors and all 41 announcements from Universe 2026. Fly through the sectors, collect announcement cores, blast the blockers and beat each boss with what you learned.

GitHub Universe 2026, playable

Ready, player one?

Open the game, launch your mission and discover the announcements on the way to the main branch.

Play SHIP IT

No download. No sign-in. Keyboard and touch controls included.

Your mission

Each sector turns a major Universe theme into an arcade run. Collecting a core unlocks the announcement behind it, including the problem it solves, how it works, why it matters, availability and official links.

Miss an announcement and it circles back once. Finish a sector and you face a short quiz boss. Every answer, right or wrong, reveals the correct update, so the game keeps moving even when you miss one.

The Announcement Guide keeps everything you unlock in this browser. If you want the straight recap, open the Guide and turn on Show every announcement.

How to play

  • Use the left and right arrows or A and D to steer, then hold Space to fire.
  • Press Enter to start or continue, 1, 2 or 3 to answer a boss question and F for fullscreen.
  • On a phone or tablet, swipe to steer and tap to fire. On-screen controls appear automatically.

I designed and built SHIP IT as an independent interactive recap of GitHub Universe 2026. It is not an official GitHub product.

References

  • GitHub Universe 2026 recap
  • GitHub Universe 2026: Evolving every layer of the stack
  • GitHub Universe 2026 changelog collection
  • Octoverse 2026
  • GitHub Copilot app: The agent-native desktop experience

Image Credits

  • Cover image generated by Copilot

entry.content:
Update (2026-11-23): Azure AI Gateway is now generally available

Azure AI Gateway became generally available on 17 November 2026 as its own resource type, Microsoft.ApiManagement/aigateways, in 17 regions including Australia East but not New Zealand North. Paid billing starts on 1 January 2027, and resources created in the old AI Gateway tier of API Management keep working only until 15 January 2027.

Model Router, Private Link, VNet integration, Agent Hooks and tool threat protection are still preview, and API Management workspaces still don't support MCP servers. See the GA announcement and migration guidance for the details.

TL;DR

MCP 2026-07-28 removes the initialize handshake and protocol-level sessions, so each request can reach any server replica. For Azure gateways, the useful part is routing and rate limiting per tool from validated headers, without parsing JSON bodies.

Keep application state explicit, protect retry state and check streaming and tracing before removing affinity. Azure’s dedicated AI Gateway reached GA on 17 November 2026; if you piloted the old preview tier, re-create it before 15 January 2027.

Running a remote MCP server behind a load balancer used to come with an awkward question: which instance remembers this client? If the server issued an Mcp-Session-Id and kept its session in memory, you needed affinity, shared storage or a deployment small enough to avoid the problem.

The 28 July specification release changes that model. Every request describes itself. A tool call no longer needs a handshake before it can do useful work, and the next call doesn’t have to find the same process.

I spend a lot of my time in the layer between agents and the things they call. From there, the interesting question isn’t just what changed in MCP. It’s what we can simplify in the gateway, what we can finally do per tool, and which responsibilities haven’t gone away.

In a hurry? Jump to the gateway checklist or the eight checks before go-live.

Updated 23 November 2026: the SDK sign-in guidance and AI Gateway migration notes below reflect the GA service and documentation checked on that date.

One request, before and after

The biggest change is easiest to see on the wire. This compares a session-based deployment of the previous revision, 2025-11-25, with the new one.

sequenceDiagram  accTitle: One tool call before and after MCP 2026-07-28  accDescr: In a legacy deployment with in-memory sessions, the agent initialises a session tied to one instance. In the new revision, a self-describing POST can land on any instance.  autonumber  participant AG as Agent  participant LB as Load balancer  participant A as Instance A  participant B as Instance B  rect rgb(246, 248, 250)    Note over AG,B: Before: 2025-11-25 with an in-memory session    AG->>LB: POST initialize    LB->>A: route    A-->>AG: InitializeResult and Mcp-Session-Id abc    AG->>LB: POST notifications/initialized, session abc    LB->>A: must reach A    AG->>LB: POST tools/call, session abc    LB->>A: must reach A again    A-->>AG: result    Note over LB,B: If A disappears, B doesn't know session abc  end  rect rgb(230, 255, 237)    Note over AG,B: After: 2026-07-28    AG->>LB: POST tools/call
version, method, name and _meta    LB->>B: any ready instance    B-->>AG: resultType complete  end

In the older deployment, the first tool call takes three POSTs: initialize, notifications/initialized and the call itself. Once the server creates an in-memory session, later requests have to find that state.

Older revisions already allowed servers to omit session IDs. The distinction is that 2026-07-28 removes both the handshake and protocol-level sessions, rather than leaving session behaviour to each server.

Here’s a complete example of the new request shape. The protocol version and client capabilities travel in params._meta; the method and tool name are mirrored into HTTP headers.

Three details in the Streamable HTTP specification matter at the gateway:

  • MCP-Protocol-Version must match the version in _meta. Mcp-Method is required on requests, and Mcp-Name is required on tools/call, resources/read and prompts/get.
  • A server must reject missing, malformed or mismatched required headers with HTTP 400 and JSON-RPC error -32020, HeaderMismatch.
  • Servers must implement server/discover for clients that want capabilities up front. Clients don’t have to call it before doing useful work.

Client identity in clientInfo is descriptive metadata, not authentication. Don’t turn a caller-supplied agent name into an authorisation decision.

The release on one page

The TypeScript, Python, Go and C# SDKs supported the new revision on release day. The change is broader than removing one session header.

mindmap  root((MCP 2026-07-28))    Stateless core      No initialize handshake      No Mcp-Session-Id      Version and capabilities per request      Optional server/discover call    Routing headers      Mcp-Method      Mcp-Name      Mcp-Param headers via x-mcp-header    Cache hints      ttlMs freshness      cacheScope public or private      Deterministic tools/list order    Trace context      traceparent, tracestate, baggage      Carried in _meta    Server to client      Multi Round-Trip Requests      subscriptions/listen stream      No resumable SSE    Authorisation      Validate iss when present      Credentials bound to issuer      DCR deprecated for CIMD    Extensions and deprecations      Tasks move to an extension      Roots, Sampling, Logging deprecated      Legacy HTTP+SSE deprecated

Tasks move out of the core into the formal extensions framework, alongside extensions such as MCP Apps. Roots, Sampling and Logging are deprecated, not immediately removed; new implementations shouldn’t build on them.

For gateway operators, the practical changes are independent requests, visible routing information, explicit cache hints and a different way to continue work when a tool needs more input.

What you can remove, and what you can’t

A server keeping transport sessions in memory had three common deployment choices.

Session affinity kept requests on one replica. In Azure Container Apps, affinity is cookie-based and requires single revision mode with HTTP ingress. API Management backend-pool session awareness also uses cookies. Neither is automatically a routing mechanism for Mcp-Session-Id, so the client had to preserve the right cookies too.

A shared session store let replicas find the same state, with an event store if you also wanted resumable streams. That solved a problem, but added infrastructure, latency and another access boundary.

One replica avoided cross-replica coordination altogether. It also left the workload dependent on that replica.

%%{init: {"htmlLabels": false, "flowchart": {"htmlLabels": false, "nodeSpacing": 15, "rankSpacing": 30, "padding": 10}}}%%flowchart TB  accTitle: Removing protocol session infrastructure  accDescr: Legacy deployments needed affinity or shared session storage to recover session state. The new protocol lets a load balancer send each request to any ready replica without a protocol session store.  subgraph OLDWAY["Before: find the session state"]    direction TB    C1["Agent"] --> LB1["Load balancer
session-aware routing"]    LB1 --> A1["Instance A"]    LB1 --> B1["Instance B"]    A1 --- S1[("Shared session store
if replicas share state")]    B1 --- S1  end  subgraph NEWWAY["After: any request, any ready instance"]    direction TB    C2["Agent"] --> LB2["Load balancer
plain round robin"]    LB2 --> A2["Instance A"]    LB2 --> B2["Instance B"]    LB2 --> D2["Instance C"]  end  classDef historical fill:#f6f8fa,stroke:#8c959f,color:#000,stroke-dasharray:5 5  classDef focus fill:#cce5ff,stroke:#1f6feb,color:#000  classDef output fill:#e6ffed,stroke:#2da44e,color:#000  classDef data fill:#fff4c2,stroke:#b7950b,color:#000  class C1,LB1,A1,B1 historical  class S1 data  class C2,LB2 focus  class A2,B2,D2 output

With 2026-07-28, you can remove affinity and storage that existed solely for MCP transport sessions. Container Apps can scale in without stranding a protocol session, multiple revisions can participate in traffic splitting, and API Management pools can use ordinary round robin, weighted or priority routing.

That doesn’t make an application stateless. A basket, browser session or report still needs somewhere to live. Return an explicit handle from one tool and accept it as an argument on the next. Treat the handle as a name, not a credential: authorise access on every call, and put its lifetime in the tool description so the model can see it.

There’s also no promise that an interrupted request did nothing. A broken response stream loses the in-flight response, and a retry is a new request with a new ID. Side-effecting tools need an application-level idempotency key or a way to check the original outcome before repeating the action.

Route and govern each tool from the headers

This is the change I’m most interested in. Mcp-Method and Mcp-Name let a gateway make per-tool decisions without buffering and parsing the JSON body.

A server can also mark selected tool parameters with x-mcp-header. Conforming clients mirror those values into Mcp-Param-{Name} headers. For example, "x-mcp-header": "Region" on a region parameter produces Mcp-Param-Region.

Don’t mirror passwords, tokens or personal data. These values become visible to network intermediaries.

The trust boundary matters more than the convenience. A client can put a harmless tool name in a header and a destructive one in the body. The backend must compare them before execution, and the gateway must only rely on those headers for protocol revisions whose servers enforce that comparison.

%%{init: {"htmlLabels": false, "flowchart": {"htmlLabels": false, "nodeSpacing": 15, "rankSpacing": 30, "padding": 10}}}%%flowchart TB  accTitle: Per-tool routing from validated MCP request headers  accDescr: The gateway checks the protocol version before using method and name headers for routing. The selected MCP backend must validate the headers against the body before executing a tool.  REQ["POST /mcp
version, method and name"]  VER{"Validated revision
2026-07-28?"}  LEGACY["Reject or use a legacy endpoint
without header-based policy"]  METHOD{"Mcp-Method"}  LIST["tools/list
client caching"]  LISTEN["subscriptions/listen
streaming settings"]  NAME{"Mcp-Name"}  HEAVY["run_report
report pool, tighter limit"]  STD["Other tools
standard pool and limit"]  CHECK["MCP server
validate headers against body
before execution"]  REQ --> VER  VER -->|"no"| LEGACY  VER -->|"yes"| METHOD  METHOD -->|"tools/list"| LIST  METHOD -->|"subscriptions/listen"| LISTEN  METHOD -->|"tools/call"| NAME  NAME -->|"run_report"| HEAVY  NAME -->|"other tool"| STD  HEAVY --> CHECK  STD --> CHECK  classDef focus fill:#cce5ff,stroke:#1f6feb,color:#000  classDef output fill:#e6ffed,stroke:#2da44e,color:#000  classDef data fill:#fff4c2,stroke:#b7950b,color:#000  classDef warning fill:#ffd6d6,stroke:#c0392b,color:#000  class REQ,VER,METHOD,NAME focus  class LIST,LISTEN,HEAVY,STD output  class CHECK data  class LEGACY warning

Here’s the core pattern as an API Management policy at MCP server scope on supported classic or v2 tiers. Replace the backend ID and tool name with your own. The inherited inbound policy must already enforce your authentication and authorisation requirements; the counter key below is a throttling bucket, not proof of identity.

This deliberately limited example uses plain ASCII names and rejects Base64-encoded names. A general implementation must decode the specification’s =?base64?...?= sentinel format before comparing Mcp-Name or mirrored parameters. Otherwise an encoded run_report could miss the stricter branch.

The report pool must expose the same tool contract advertised by discovery and enforce the same header and body validation. Keep incompatible protocol revisions in separate pools. If you serve older clients, give them a compatible endpoint rather than weakening the version gate.

At MCP server scope, policies apply across the server’s tools. Per-tool behaviour comes from conditions like these, not from assuming that each tool has its own REST operation policy.

Keep the response body out of that policy. Microsoft’s MCP guidance warns that accessing context.Response.Body forces buffering and can break streaming. Check that the inherited forward-request uses buffer-response="false" for SSE; the example inherits backend policy rather than replacing it.

Cache hints aren’t an HTTP response cache

Results from tools/list, prompts/list, resources/list, resources/read and resources/templates/list now carry ttlMs and cacheScope. The first is a freshness hint in milliseconds; the second controls whether shared intermediaries may cache the result.

Tool lists may vary with the caller’s authorisation, even though they must no longer vary with connection state. Keep caller-specific results private, partition caches by authorisation context and return tools in a deterministic order.

API Management’s built-in cache-lookup policy only performs response lookups for GET requests. MCP messages use POST. It won’t automatically become an MCP cache because the result contains ttlMs.

For this design, let the client honour the hints and leave the gateway out of response caching. A protocol-aware shared cache is a separate implementation, not something cacheScope: "public" creates for you.

When a tool needs more input

Sometimes a tool needs a confirmation, a missing parameter or an answer from the client’s model. Older revisions sent server-initiated requests such as elicitation/create, sampling/createMessage or roots/list down a held-open stream.

Multi Round-Trip Requests, or MRTR, replace that exchange. The server returns resultType: "input_required", its questions in inputRequests and, optionally, opaque requestState. The client gathers the answers and retries the original call with a new JSON-RPC ID, the answers in inputResponses and exactly the state it received.

MRTR applies to tools/call, resources/read and prompts/get.

sequenceDiagram  accTitle: A multi round-trip request across two instances  accDescr: Instance A asks for user input and returns protected request state. The client gathers consent, then sends a new request with the answer and unchanged state. Instance B verifies the state and completes the tool call.  autonumber  participant U as User  participant AG as Agent  participant GW as Gateway  participant A as Instance A  participant B as Instance B  AG->>GW: tools/call delete_files, id 1  GW->>A: any ready instance  A-->>GW: input_required
inputRequests and requestState  GW-->>AG: passed back unchanged  AG->>U: Delete 3 files?  U-->>AG: Yes  AG->>GW: tools/call delete_files, id 2
inputResponses and unchanged requestState  GW->>B: another ready instance  Note over B: Verify integrity, caller,
expiry and original request  B-->>GW: resultType complete  GW-->>AG: result

The first request can land on A and the retry on B. In a self-contained implementation, the replicas don’t need to share the original request’s in-memory state.

They do need to agree on how to trust requestState. The MRTR specification treats it as attacker-controlled input. If it influences authorisation, resource access or business logic, protect its integrity, for example with HMAC or AEAD, and reject failed verification.

Bind it to the authenticated caller, a short expiry and the original request. Those checks limit replay; they don’t guarantee single use. A one-time approval or redemption still needs server-side enforcement of that invariant.

On Azure, I’d keep the protection key in Key Vault, let each replica access it through managed identity and overlap current and previous keys during rotation. A retry routed to the reporting pool must reach a replica that understands the state and can verify it.

Don’t confuse a follow-up request for consent with proof of consent. The client must actually obtain the user’s answer, and the server still has to authorise the operation.

One trace from agent to tool

The specification now reserves traceparent, tracestate and baggage in _meta, using W3C Trace Context and Baggage formats. Several implementations already used those names; the convention now has a standard home.

There are still two propagation paths. MCP carries context in the body, while HTTP intermediaries work with headers. API Management’s Application Insights diagnostic supports W3C correlation, which injects Trace Context headers.

I’d instrument the agent’s HTTP client and propagate the same trace ID through both the HTTP header and MCP metadata. That’s the same trace ID, not a requirement to freeze the complete traceparent value: parent span IDs change as services create child spans.

%%{init: {"htmlLabels": false, "flowchart": {"htmlLabels": false, "nodeSpacing": 15, "rankSpacing": 30, "padding": 10}}}%%flowchart TB  accTitle: Trace propagation through API Management to an MCP server  accDescr: The agent supplies HTTP and MCP trace context. API Management creates correlated gateway telemetry and forwards HTTP context. The MCP server continues the downstream HTTP parent, with all telemetry exported to Application Insights.  AG["Agent
starts trace 0af7..."]  GW["API Management
W3C correlation
gateway and dependency spans"]  SRV["MCP server on Container Apps
OpenTelemetry instrumentation"]  DS["Downstream API or database"]  AI[("Application Insights
shared trace ID")]  AG -->|"traceparent header
and _meta.traceparent"| GW  GW -->|"downstream traceparent
and x-correlation-id"| SRV  SRV -->|"child trace context"| DS  AG -.->|"agent spans"| AI  GW -.->|"gateway telemetry"| AI  SRV -.->|"server and tool spans"| AI  classDef focus fill:#cce5ff,stroke:#1f6feb,color:#000  classDef output fill:#e6ffed,stroke:#2da44e,color:#000  classDef data fill:#fff4c2,stroke:#b7950b,color:#000  class GW focus  class AG,SRV,DS output  class AI data

Make the server’s parent-selection behaviour explicit. To preserve the gateway as part of the parent chain, HTTP server instrumentation should continue the downstream HTTP context rather than replacing it with the older agent parent still in _meta. Check how your MCP instrumentation handles both, and avoid creating duplicate root spans.

I keep a correlation ID alongside tracing because it’s useful in a support ticket. These sections belong inside an existing <policies> document, merged with its current inbound and outbound sections.

Treat a caller-supplied correlation ID as untrusted diagnostic text, never an identity or an access token. The trace record reaches Application Insights only when its severity meets the diagnostic’s configured verbosity.

For the Application Insights tables, this KQL query brings the journey back in time order:

Use the corresponding AppRequests, AppDependencies and AppTraces schema if you query the Log Analytics workspace tables instead.

One MCP-specific setting is easy to miss: if Application Insights or Azure Monitor diagnostics are enabled at All APIs scope, set frontend response payload bytes to log to 0. Logging the response body can interfere with streaming, just as reading it in a policy can.

Azure AI Gateway isn’t just another policy editor

Microsoft introduced the AI Gateway tier in public preview on 27 July. On 17 November, it reached general availability as a standalone Azure service with its own Microsoft.ApiManagement/aigateways resource type.

The October change makes the naming more important: the dedicated AI Gateway product and AI gateway capabilities in API Management service are related, but they aren’t the same resource or management model.

With the dedicated product, applications use model aliases and MCP endpoints while the platform team manages backend connections. A federated MCP server can combine remote MCP servers, OpenAPI-described APIs and built-in connectors.

%%{init: {"htmlLabels": false, "flowchart": {"htmlLabels": false, "nodeSpacing": 15, "rankSpacing": 30, "padding": 10}}}%%flowchart TB  accTitle: A dedicated AI Gateway for models and tools  accDescr: Applications authenticate to AI Gateway. Model aliases route to registered model backends, while federated MCP endpoints combine remote servers, OpenAPI APIs and connectors. Gateway telemetry goes to a configured destination.  APP["Agents and apps"]  GW["AI Gateway
caller access and AI policies"]  MOD["Model aliases
registered model backends"]  TS["Federated MCP server
one governed endpoint"]  R1["Remote MCP server"]  R2["OpenAPI API"]  R3["Built-in connector"]  OT[("Configured telemetry
Application Insights or OTLP")]  APP -->|"Entra runtime access
or gateway runtime key"| GW  GW --> MOD  GW --> TS  TS --> R1  TS --> R2  TS --> R3  GW -.-> OT  classDef focus fill:#cce5ff,stroke:#1f6feb,color:#000  classDef output fill:#e6ffed,stroke:#2da44e,color:#000  classDef data fill:#fff4c2,stroke:#b7950b,color:#000  class GW focus  class APP,MOD,TS,R1,R2,R3 output  class OT data

Backend authentication is separate from caller access. A managed identity or stored backend credential determines what the gateway can do upstream; it doesn’t automatically limit each caller to that caller’s own downstream permissions.

The current concepts guide also makes an important boundary explicit: runtime API keys grant gateway-wide access. Separate keys help attribution and rotation, but don’t create per-tool least privilege. Use separate gateways where trust boundaries require them.

The AI-focused policy cards aren’t the XML policies shown earlier. Check the controls supported by your actual resource type rather than assuming a card from the July launch is available on the replacement.

The October resource migration

From 14 October, AI Gateway moved from the AIGateway SKU of Microsoft.ApiManagement/service to Microsoft.ApiManagement/aigateways.

The migration guidance, checked on 4 November, says existing AIGateway SKU resources work until 15 January 2027 and are then permanently removed. New resources using that older representation can’t be created.

Migration creates a new resource, not an in-place type change. Applications need its new runtime hostname under ai.gateway.azure.com and a new runtime key. Key-based requests change from api-key to Authorization: Bearer <key>. Read the hostname from the resource; don’t construct it yourself.

Resource-scoped role assignments must be recreated. A new system-assigned identity also needs its own permissions to backends and telemetry destinations.

The migration guide lists Private Link and VNet integration as preview capabilities, no content safety policy support and no ability to change the virtual network or subnet after creation. Those aren’t small details if your deployment assumes private ingress or a particular safety control.

The GA service is available in 17 regions, including Australia East and Southeast Asia but not New Zealand North. The freemium tier includes 10,000 requests per gateway each month; paid billing starts on 1 January 2027.

Where should your MCP servers sit?

I’d start with workload requirements, not with the newest portal.

%%{init: {"htmlLabels": false, "flowchart": {"htmlLabels": false, "nodeSpacing": 15, "rankSpacing": 30, "padding": 10}}}%%flowchart TB  accTitle: Choosing between API Management service and dedicated AI Gateway  accDescr: APIM-only XML policy logic or an MCP server in an APIM workspace points to API Management service. Otherwise, check Azure AI Gateway's region, networking and preview feature requirements.  Q1{"Need APIM-only XML policy
or workspace MCP?"}  Q2{"Can the request path use
one of 17 AI Gateway regions?"}  Q3{"Can the remaining preview
features and limits fit?"}  CL["API Management service
appropriate production tier
MCP support and XML policies"]  AGT["Azure AI Gateway
managed AI gateway service"]  Q1 -->|"yes"| CL  Q1 -->|"no"| Q2  Q2 -->|"no"| CL  Q2 -->|"yes"| Q3  Q3 -->|"no"| CL  Q3 -->|"yes"| AGT  classDef focus fill:#cce5ff,stroke:#1f6feb,color:#000  classDef output fill:#e6ffed,stroke:#2da44e,color:#000  classDef data fill:#fff4c2,stroke:#b7950b,color:#000  class Q1,Q2,Q3 focus  class CL output  class AGT data

For New Zealand and Australian customers, the region question can settle it before policy features do. Australia East is supported, but New Zealand North is not. A gateway in another region still puts prompts and tool payloads through that region, so review the whole request path against your residency obligations.

For production MCP traffic that needs established API management controls, I’d keep the supported classic or v2 service tier that meets those requirements. The Developer tier is not a production SLA choice.

For an AI-focused service without an APIM-only requirement, evaluate the dedicated gateway against its regions, networking, remaining preview features and price. Microsoft’s product comparison confirms that existing AI workloads in API Management remain supported; adopting the dedicated product doesn’t require moving everything.

Clients must know who issued their credentials

The authorisation changes are less visible than the new transport, but matter just as much for agents connecting to several servers.

Authorisation servers should include iss in their responses, following RFC 9207. When present, clients must check it against the recorded issuer before redeeming an authorisation code.

Stored client credentials belong to the issuer that minted them. Clients must key them by issuer, must not reuse them with another authorisation server and must register again when that server changes.

Clients also declare an appropriate application_type during Dynamic Client Registration. DCR itself is deprecated in favour of Client ID Metadata Documents, while remaining available for backwards compatibility.

sequenceDiagram  accTitle: Credentials stay bound to their issuer  accDescr: A client compares discovered authorisation metadata with the issuer recorded for its credentials. It uses those credentials only with the matching issuer and never sends them to a different server.  autonumber  participant C as MCP client  participant M as MCP server  participant ISS as Recorded issuer  participant OTHER as Other issuer  C->>M: tools/call  M-->>C: 401 and resource metadata  Note over C: Compare discovered issuer
with recorded credential issuer  alt issuer matches    C->>ISS: token request with bound credentials    ISS-->>C: access token  else issuer differs    C--xOTHER: stored credentials never sent    Note over C: A different issuer needs
a separate trusted registration  end

A governed gateway protected by a known Entra issuer can reduce the number of issuers an agent needs to trust. That only helps if clients validate the issuer and the gateway validates tokens and tool access correctly.

SDK sign-in fixes: update checked 4 November 2026

The SDK advisories make this concrete. The official Python and TypeScript SDKs had OAuth clients that let a malicious or compromised MCP server influence where credentials were sent.

For Python’s issuer-binding advisory, the fixes are mcp 1.30.0 and 2.2.0 or later. Upgrading alone isn’t enough for ClientCredentialsOAuthProvider or PrivateKeyJWTOAuthProvider: configure issuer= as well. Clear registrations stored without an issuer so the client registers again, or bind pre-registered records to their legitimate issuer.

For TypeScript’s issuer-binding advisory, the fixes start at @modelcontextprotocol/sdk 1.31.0 and @modelcontextprotocol/client 2.2.0. Bundled providers need expectedIssuer; stored credentials need issuer, or must be cleared. Custom OAuthClientProvider implementations must persist the issuer passed to their save methods. If you import @modelcontextprotocol/core directly, update that too.

A separate TypeScript cross-origin redirect advisory is fixed in SDK 1.32.0 and client 2.3.0. Those higher versions address both advisory sets, but don’t remove the issuer configuration requirements. Configure final endpoints rather than restoring unrestricted redirect following.

Only complete new interactive sign-ins for servers you trust. If an affected client may have sent credentials to an untrusted destination, rotate the exposed secret or signing key and revoke its tokens. These advisories concern affected HTTP clients, not every MCP server built with those SDKs.

Eight checks before go-live

API Management’s existing-server guide specifies MCP 2025-06-18 or later over Streamable HTTP or SSE. That minimum is not evidence that every 2026-07-28 interaction works through your chosen configuration. The guide currently supports tools and resources for external servers, but not prompts, and doesn’t support MCP server capabilities in workspaces.

Run these checks through the actual endpoint, policies and backends you intend to use. For a federating gateway, test its public MCP surface as well as each upstream connection; federation isn’t necessarily transparent proxying.

1. A call gets through without a handshake

Send tools/call with the required headers and _meta, without initialize. Expect a successful response with resultType: "complete" and no transport session minted along the path.

2. Required headers reach the validating component

Verify MCP-Protocol-Version, Mcp-Method, Mcp-Name and applicable Mcp-Param-* values. On a proxy path, confirm they arrive unchanged. If a federation layer rewrites a request, verify that it creates matching upstream headers and metadata.

3. Header and body disagreements are refused

Send Mcp-Name: get_weather with a body calling another tool. Expect HTTP 400 and the server’s -32020 error. Also test missing required headers, mismatched versions and encoded names. No tool should execute when validation fails.

4. A continuation can reach another replica

Use three replicas without affinity and a tool returning input_required. Confirm the retry succeeds on a different replica. Also try modified, expired and wrong-caller requestState; those must fail before the action runs.

5. Progress isn’t buffered

Use a slow tool that supports notifications/progress, and request progress with _meta.progressToken. Events should arrive while the tool runs, not in a burst at the end.

API Management documents buffer-response="false" on forward-request for SSE backends. Check inherited policies and disable frontend response body logging at All APIs scope.

6. A listen stream survives quiet periods

Where the server supports subscriptions, open subscriptions/listen and leave it idle beyond four minutes. Confirm keep-alive comments preserve the stream, or the client reconnects and re-establishes the subscription correctly.

The forward-request documentation notes that network infrastructure can drop idle connections after about 240 seconds. The MCP specification encourages periodic SSE comments on long-lived streams. This is not resumable SSE with Last-Event-ID.

7. The trace joins up

Send one trace ID through the HTTP and MCP contexts. Check operation_Id across agent, gateway and server, then inspect the parent-child relationships. Sharing a trace ID is necessary, but it doesn’t prove the span tree is correct.

8. Cache hints survive at the public surface

Check tools/list for sensible ttlMs and cacheScope. For caller-filtered catalogues, verify private scope and cache isolation. A federated server may generate its own catalogue and hints rather than copy a backend’s values.

For self-hosted deployments, Microsoft’s open-source MCP Gateway now documents a 2026-07-28-only path, with no legacy handshake or transport sessions. Its migration guide is a useful implementation reference, not a compatibility guarantee for managed API Management or dedicated AI Gateway.

Put numbers behind the scaling argument

I haven’t run a new benchmark for this article. This is the harness I’d use to measure the difference rather than assume a latency improvement.

%%{init: {"htmlLabels": false, "flowchart": {"htmlLabels": false, "nodeSpacing": 15, "rankSpacing": 30, "padding": 10}}}%%flowchart TB  accTitle: A benchmark design for session-based and stateless MCP  accDescr: A k6 client runs the same tool-call mix against session-based and stateless servers with the same replica count, equivalent gateway limits and comparable instrumentation. A replica is removed during each run to measure recovery.  K6["k6 load generator
same tool-call mix"]  APIM["API Management
equivalent routing and limits"]  subgraph RUN1["Run 1: 2025-11-25 with in-memory sessions"]    ACA1["Container Apps, 3 replicas
client preserves affinity cookies"]  end  subgraph RUN2["Run 2: 2026-07-28"]    ACA2["Container Apps, 3 replicas
no affinity"]  end  AI[("Application Insights
throughput, p95, errors
and replica distribution")]  K6 --> APIM  APIM --> ACA1  APIM --> ACA2  APIM -.-> AI  ACA1 -.-> AI  ACA2 -.-> AI  classDef historical fill:#f6f8fa,stroke:#8c959f,color:#000,stroke-dasharray:5 5  classDef focus fill:#cce5ff,stroke:#1f6feb,color:#000  classDef output fill:#e6ffed,stroke:#2da44e,color:#000  classDef data fill:#fff4c2,stroke:#b7950b,color:#000  class K6,APIM focus  class ACA1 historical  class ACA2 output  class AI data

Keep the tool implementation, load, replica count, limits and telemetry settings comparable. Use a version-aware comparison policy, not the earlier example’s single-revision gate, and confirm the legacy client actually preserves affinity cookies and session IDs.

Warm the backends first. As with the APIM fan-out benchmark, cold scale can tell a convincing but misleading story.

Partway through each run, remove a replica. Measure throughput, p95 latency, error rate, request distribution and recovery time.

With sessions held only on that replica, legacy clients have to establish new sessions. The stateless side has no transport session to recover, but in-flight calls can still fail and side effects can still have an uncertain outcome. That’s the distinction to measure, not a claim that stateless means zero disruption.

What to change at your gateway

  1. Remove affinity and storage used solely for 2026-07-28 transport sessions, after checking application state and draining legacy traffic.
  2. Gate mirrored-header policy by supported protocol version, and validate or decode header values before using them.
  3. Route and rate-limit per tool, while keeping header and body validation on every executing backend.
  4. Preserve streaming: no response body access in MCP policy, no frontend response body logging at All APIs scope, and no response buffering for SSE.
  5. Protect requestState across replicas, overlap keys during rotation and enforce one-time consumption where required.
  6. Join HTTP and MCP trace propagation deliberately, then inspect the span tree rather than only the trace ID.
  7. Give subscriptions/listen keep-alives and reconnection handling; don’t assume old SSE resumability still exists.
  8. Let clients honour cache hints, isolate caller-specific catalogues and bind OAuth credentials to their issuer.
  9. Run the eight checks through the real gateway before go-live.

My take

The best part of this release is what it lets us stop doing. A remote MCP tool server can behave much more like an ordinary HTTP workload, without transport sessions deciding which replica gets the next request.

For gateways, the headers are the real prize. They make routing, metering and policy per tool practical without buffering bodies. That only works as a trust boundary when the server enforces the header and body contract.

The remaining state is more visible, not magically gone. Application handles, retry protection, consent and idempotency still deserve proper design.

I’d keep production traffic on the gateway that meets its actual operational requirements and account for the dedicated AI Gateway migration and remaining preview features where they apply. The protocol simplification is useful either way.

Key takeaways

  • MCP 2026-07-28 removes the handshake and protocol sessions, not application state or the possibility of interrupted calls.
  • Header-based policy needs a compatible revision, correct value decoding and backend validation before execution.
  • MRTR can continue on another replica, but integrity protection alone doesn’t make an approval single-use.
  • Streaming, trace parentage, cache isolation and issuer-bound credentials belong in the go-live gate.
  • Dedicated AI Gateway is a separate GA resource. Re-create old preview-tier gateways before 15 January 2027 and account for the remaining preview features.

References

  • MCP 2026-07-28 changelog

  • Multi Round-Trip Requests and request-state security
  • MCP tools: catalogues, caching and mirrored parameters
  • Expose and govern an existing MCP server in API Management
  • API Management forward-request policy
  • API Management and Application Insights integration
  • Azure AI Gateway general availability announcement
  • AI Gateway concepts: federation, runtime access and identities
  • AI Gateway region availability and scaling
  • Migrate from the AI Gateway tier to the dedicated resource
  • MCP server limitations in API Management workspaces
  • Python SDK OAuth issuer-binding advisory
  • TypeScript SDK OAuth issuer-binding advisory
  • TypeScript SDK cross-origin redirect advisory

Related posts

  • APIM Backend Fan-out: Shared Backend + rewrite-uri vs One Backend Per API (A Real Benchmark)
  • Governance for AI Agents: The Gap, the OWASP Agentic Top 10, and Where AGT Fits
  • Microsoft Foundry Cross-Region with Private Endpoints, Part 1
